Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 40, verse 1:

﴿Ḥā Mīm﴾

The discussion of this is like the discussion of its counterparts among the disjointed letters (al-ḥurūf al-muqaṭṭaʿah) at the beginnings of the surahs, and that most of them are followed by mention of the Qur'an and what refers to it, as a challenge to the deniers to show their inability to produce its like. This was already discussed at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah, where we mentioned that the letters whose names end in a extended vowel (al-ḥurūf allatī asmāʾuhā mamdūdatu al-ākhir) are pronounced in these openings in shortened form by dropping the hamzah, for lightness, since in the state of pausing they are like the name (ḥā) in this surah, the name (rā) in (Alif Lām Rā), and the name (yā) in (Yā Sīn).

﴿The revelation of the Book is from Allah, the Almighty, the All-Knowing.﴾

What is said about it is like what is said about the opening of Surat al-Zumar. It may be added here that the intended addressees of this statement (khabar) are the polytheists who deny that the Qur'an was sent down from Allah. Thus, stripping the statement of emphasis (al-mu'akkid) takes it out of what the apparent requirement (muqtada al-zahir) would call for, by treating the denier as if he were not a denier, because there surround it such proofs that, if he reflects upon them, he would refrain from his denial. So it was fitting that he should not deny that.

[p. 79]

**Commentary of Ibn ʿĀshūr (al-Taḥrīr wa al-Tanwīr) on Sūrah 40, verse 3:**

﴿The Forgiver of sin, the Accepter of repentance, severe in punishment, the Possessor of bounty. There is no god but Him; to Him is the final return.﴾

Six attributes (nuʿūt, sing. naʿt, "descriptive epithets") follow the Name of Allah, all of them definite (maʿārif). Some are definite by the definite article (al-), and others by being in construct (iḍāfah) with a noun that is itself definite by the article.

The description of Allah with the two attributes al-ʿAzīz (the Mighty) and al-ʿAlīm (the All-Knowing) here contains an allusion (taʿrīḍ) that those who deny the revelation of the Book are overcome and subdued by Him, and that Allah knows what their souls conceal, so He will call them to account for it. It also signals that the Qur'an is the speech of the Mighty, the All-Knowing, so no one other than Allah is able to produce its like, and no one other than Allah knows how to bring the like of it.

This is the point of difference between this verse and its counterpart at the beginning of Sūrat al-Zumar, where the attribute al-ʿAzīz al-Ḥakīm (the Mighty, the Wise) occurs. Yet the attribute of knowledge (al-ʿIlm) can accommodate what some of the possible meanings of the attribute al-Ḥakīm in Sūrat al-Zumar accommodate. And both attributes can also accommodate what was accommodated there by way of the inimitability of the Qur'an (iʿjāz al-Qurʾān).

Mentioning these two attributes also signals that Allah knows best where to place His message, and that He does not follow the whims of people regarding whom they nominate for it from among their elders. [Allah says:] ﴿And they said, "Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man from the two cities?"﴾ (Zukhruf: 31).

By following the two great attributes with these descriptions, ﴿the Forgiver of sin, the Accepter of repentance, severe in punishment, the Possessor of bounty﴾, there is an alignment (tarshīḥ) with that allusion, as if it were saying: If you have sinned by disbelieving in the Qur'an, then the remedy for your sin is within your reach, because Allah is established as having the attributes of accepting repentance and forgiving sin. Just as He forgave the nations that repented and accepted their faith, He will forgive whoever among you repents.

The placement of (Ghāfir, "Forgiver") before (Qābil al-Tawb, "Accepter of repentance"), even though the second is consequent upon the first in occurrence, is for the sake of hastening the announcement of it to whoever prepares to remedy his situation. Thus the description ﴿the Forgiver of sin, the Accepter of repentance﴾ is an allusion toward encouragement (targhīb), and the two epithets ﴿severe in punishment, the Possessor of bounty﴾ are an allusion toward warning (tarhīb).

[Page 80]

Al-tawb (التَّوْبُ) is the verbal noun of tāba (to repent). Al-tawb with the letter *tāʾ* (التَّوْبُ), al-thawb with *thāʾ* (الثَّوْبُ), and al-awb (الأوْبُ) all carry the same meaning of return, that is, return to the command of Allah and obedience to it after having distanced oneself from it. The attribute (Qābil al-Tawb, "Accepter of repentance") is joined to (Ghāfir al-Dhanb, "Forgiver of sin") by the conjunction *wa* (and), and it was not separated from it as the two attributes (al-ʿAlīm, "the All-Knowing" and Ghāfir al-Dhanb) were separated, and as the attribute (Shadīd al-ʿIqāb, "severe in punishment") was. This indicates a magnificent point, which is that the sinner who repents is granted two mercies together: that Allah accepts his repentance and makes it an act of obedience for him, and that He erases through it the sins from which he has repented and over which he has regretted, so that he becomes as though he had never committed them. This is a bounty from Allah.

His saying (Shadīd al-ʿIqāb, "severe in punishment") is a clear declaration of threat (waʿīd) against denying the Qur'an, because its coming after His saying ﴿The revelation of the Book is from Allah﴾ (Ghāfir: 2) indicates that this is the intended meaning of this utterance, through the implications (mustatbaʿāt) of the compositional structures.

What is meant by (Ghāfir, "Forgiver") and (Qābil, "Accepter") is that He is described by their meanings in the past (fīmā maḍā), since the intended meaning is not that He *will* forgive and *will* accept. The active participle in both is cut off from resembling the verb, and it does not operate as a verb. Therefore it acquires definiteness through the construct phrase (iḍāfah), which brings it closer to the nouns, and this is the interpretation that fits here and no other.

The word (Shadīd, "severe") is an adjectival form (ṣifah mushabbahah) in construct with its agent, and it has come as a description of the divine name Allah. This is on the basis that the definite article attached to the agent of the adjective stands in place of the definiteness of the adjective itself. Thus it does not contradict what is well known in speech, namely the agreement of the epithet and the noun described in definiteness. As for the adjective mushabbahah acquiring definiteness through the construct phrase, this is the view of the Kufan grammarians (nuḥāt al-Kūfah), extending the principle of definiteness by construct. Sībawayh (the grammarian) permits adjectives in construct to acquire definiteness by the construct, except the adjective mushabbahah, because its construct is in fact with its agent in meaning. The original of what the adjective mushabbahah is joined to is that it was an agent, so its construct with it is merely a verbal lightening, and the matter is simple.

Al-ṭawl (الطَّوْلُ) is applied to abundance of bounty and abundance of wealth, and it is applied to power (qudrah), as in al-Qāmūs (the dictionary). Its apparent application is general, and Tāj al-ʿArūs (the lexicon) confirmed it and made it part of the meaning of this verse.

[Page 81]

The occurrence of (ḏhū al-ṭawl, "Possessor of bounty") together with (Shadīd al-ʿIqāb, "severe in punishment") and its pairing with the two attributes ﴿the Forgiver of sin, the Accepter of repentance﴾ serves to indicate a warning of the punishment of the Hereafter from the attribute (Shadīd al-ʿIqāb), and a warning of the punishment of this world from the attribute (ḏhū al-ṭawl), as in His saying ﴿Or We show you what We have promised them, for indeed We are Able over them﴾ (Zukhruf: 42), and His saying ﴿Say: Indeed Allah is Able to send down a sign﴾ (Anʿām: 37).

He follows this with what indicates the oneness of God (waḥdāniyyah), and with [the statement] that the final destination (al-maṣīr), that is, the place of return, is to Him. This is a recording of the invalidity of association (shirk) and a corruption of their denial of resurrection (al-baʿth).

Thus the sentence ﴿There is no god but Him﴾ is in the position of a descriptive clause (ṣifah). Then he follows that with the sentence ﴿to Him is the final return﴾ as a warning of resurrection and recompense. Since the attributes ﴿the Forgiver of sin, the Accepter of repentance, severe in punishment﴾ have been enumerated, hope and fear have been stirred up in the discourse, so it is fitting that they perceive that the final destination is either to His reward or to His punishment, and let them weigh their souls so as to place them where their condition indicates.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase in (ilayhi al-maṣīr, "to Him is the final return") is for emphasis and for the sake of observing the rhyme (fāṣilah, verse-ending) with two letters: a soft letter (ḥarf līn) and a consonant letter (ḥarf ṣaḥīḥ), as in: al-ʿAlīm, al-Bilād, and ʿIqāb.

The opening of this sūrah has included what points to the comprehensive aims of its subject matter, and fits the discussion of the polytheists' denial of the Qur'an. It indicates that they have taken pride in their strength and status, and that this will vanish from them, just as it vanished from nations that were stronger than them. So this opening has fulfilled the full completeness required in the openings of topics, what is called barāʿat al-maṭlaʿ (excellence of the opening) or barāʿat al-istihlāl (excellence of the introduction).

*Istiʾnaf bayani* (an explanatory resumptive clause) arising from His words ﴿The revelation of the Book is from God, the Mighty, the All-Knowing﴾ [Ghafir: 2], which implies that the Qur'an's being sent down from God is a matter beyond doubt, as has already been stated. So in the minds of the listeners there arises the question: what is the matter with these disputers over the truthfulness of the Qur'an's attribution to God, that the evidences of its descent from God have not convinced them? The answer is given: none dispute the truthfulness of the Qur'an except those who disbelieved in God. Since the disbelief of those who deny the Qur'an was already a known matter, informing about them that they are disbelievers was not intended to convey their being characterized by disbelief. Therefore it must be that the statement is not used to convey its benefit, neither by its explicit wording nor by its implicit meaning. The implicit meaning of the restriction, namely that those who believe do not dispute the signs of God, is also a known and established matter. Thus it is permissible to take "those who disbelieved" as referring to the very ones who dispute the signs of God, and their disbelief as their disbelief in God's oneness due to their associating partners with Him. The meaning then is: there is no wonder in their disputing God's signs, for they have committed what is greater, namely *shirk* (associating partners with God), in the manner of His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿The People of the Book ask you to bring down to them a Book from heaven. They had asked Moses for something greater than that, and said: Show us God openly﴾ [al-Nisa': 153].

It is also permissible to take "those who disbelieved" as referring to all disbelievers in God, from earlier and present times. That is, disputing God's signs is only a matter of the character of the people of disbelief and polytheism, and the disputing of the polytheists of Makkah is a branch of the disputing of all disbelievers. This is then an argument from the general to the particular. On both interpretations, this sentence has been left without being conjoined to the preceding one.

The disputing (*mujadalah*) meant here is disputing in falsehood, as indicated by the context. Thus the phrase "in the signs of God" means "concerning the truthfulness of the signs of God," as indicated by His saying ﴿The revelation of the Book is from God, the Mighty, the All-Knowing﴾ [Ghafir: 2]. Therefore it is necessary to supply an omitted noun (*mudaf*) which the context indicates, just as His saying, may He be exalted, concerning Abraham, peace be upon him, indicates ﴿He disputes with Us concerning the people of Lot﴾ [Hud: 74], meaning: concerning the destruction of the people of Lot. The form *mufa'alah* here (in *yujadilu*) is for emphasis of the action from one side, to convey repetition, like *safara* (he travelled) and *ʿafahu Allah* (God granted him well-being). They shift and vary in fabrication and repeatedly return to denial and to speaking falsely, such as their saying "fables of the ancients," "manifest sorcery," "the saying of a soothsayer," "the saying of a poet"; they do not cease from this. Among disputing is their insistence upon the Messenger (ﷺ) by asking him to bring them signs as they propose, such as their saying "We will not believe you until you cause a spring to gush forth for us," and their saying ﴿Why has an angel not been sent down to him to be a warner with him?﴾ [al-Furqan: 7], and so on.

The use of the preposition *fi* (in) as a locative with *al-jidal* (disputing), and its attachment directly to the signs themselves rather than to their states, as in His saying ﴿who disputes in the signs of God﴾, has a great eloquence, because the locative sense encompasses all kinds of disputing. The object of the preposition was made to be the signs themselves without specifying their aspect, whether their truthfulness, their occurrence, or their kind. Thus His saying "in the signs of God" encompasses disputing in all its types and in its varied objects and conditions. The intended meaning is disputing in falsehood, as is shown by the comparison of their situation with that of those of whom it is said "and they disputed with falsehood." If disputing in truth is intended, the verb of disputing is then restricted by what indicates it.

The meaning is: none disputes in the signs of God as to whether they are from God, for the Qur'an challenged them to produce its like, and they were unable to. Their disputing is only fabrication and concealment of their inability to do so, and a clinging to obstinacy. Thus their disputing, after the challenge that preceded it, indicates that disbelief has taken firm hold of them and that they are stubborn. By this the intended benefit of this statement is achieved; otherwise, their being disbelievers is already known.

The Divine Name (*ism al-jalalah*, "God") appears explicitly in His saying ﴿who disputes in the signs of God﴾, rather than saying "in His signs," in order to make the matter of their disputing grave by explicit mention, for mentioning the Divine Name signals the gravity of their disputing and disbelief, and in order to further emphasize the esteem of the Qur'an.

His saying ﴿So let not their movement about the lands deceive you﴾ is made a consequence (*tafriʿ*) of the content of ﴿none disputes in the signs of God except those who disbelieved﴾. This is because, as you know, the implication of that sentence is that those who dispute the signs of God are the people of disbelief. Such a matter is apt to stir in the soul of one who sees them in comfort and blessing the question of how God leaves them in that state, and to suppose that they have become secure from God's punishment. Therefore the answer is given as a consequence: ﴿So let not their movement about the lands deceive you﴾, meaning: this is only a gradual leading on (*istidraj*) and a measure of God's forbearance and mercy towards them for a time. Or its meaning is: We know that they dispute Our signs out of persistence in disbelief, so let not their movement about the lands make you imagine that We will not hold them to account for that.

*Al-ghurur* (deception) is a person's thinking something good while it is in fact its opposite. It is said: *gharraka* (he deceived you), when he made you think what is evil to be good. Deception may take place by speech or by making the appearance of ugliness look fair.

*Al-taqallub* (movement, shifting) is the variation of conditions, and it is a metonymy for the attaining of what is loved and desired.

*Al-bilad* (the lands) means the earth, and here it is meant as the present world, as a metonymy for life.

The one addressed by the prohibition in His saying ﴿So let not deceive you﴾ may be unspecified, so that it encompasses everyone for whom the movement of those who disbelieved about the lands is apt to deceive. On this reading the prohibition runs according to its literal sense, i.e., directed to those from whom deception is expected. A similar usage is common in their speech. Ka'b ibn Zuhayr said:

*So let not what it promises and wishes deceive you,*
*for hopes and dreams are misleading.*

It is also permissible that the address is directed to the Prophet (ﷺ), with the prohibitive form being figurative, representing the state of the Prophet (ﷺ) in his impatience for the punishment of the disbelievers by the state of one who has been deceived by their movement about the lands while they were safe. This is like His saying ﴿Leave them to eat and enjoy themselves and be diverted by hope; they will come to know﴾ [al-Hijr: 3].

The meaning is: let not their enjoyment of various blessings and pleasures in their lives make you imagine that We will not hold them to account for their disputing in Our signs. Or: let that not make you imagine that We do not know what they are upon, and so We did not hold them to account for it. This is by treating the one who knows as if he were ignorant, in order to express the intensity of the grief of the Messenger (ﷺ) over the persistence of their disbelief and the repetition of their harm. This is like His saying ﴿And do not think that God is unaware of what the wrongdoers do﴾ [Ibrahim: 42]. In the same sense is His, may He be exalted, saying ﴿Let not the movement of those who disbelieved about the lands deceive you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 196], ﴿A brief enjoyment; then their refuge is Hell, and wretched is the resting-place﴾ [Al 'Imran: 197], which were discussed in Al 'Imran.

The Qur'an verse ﴿كَذَّبَتْ قَبْلَهم قَوْمُ نُوحٍ﴾ and what follows it explain the phrase ﴿فَلا يَغْرُرْكَ تَقَلُّبُهم في البِلادِ﴾ [Ghafir: 4], in terms of the sequence of clauses that follows it, namely ﴿فَأخَذْتُهم فَكَيْفَ كانَ عِقابِ﴾. The meaning is: earlier nations denied their messengers just as these people denied you, and they disputed falsely with their messengers just as these people disputed with you. ﴿فَأخَذْتُهم﴾ means "so I seized them." ﴿فَكَيْفَ كانَ عِقابِ﴾ means "how then was My punishment of them?" That is, "you have seen how I punished them; similarly, these people will be punished after I have granted them respite until I seize them."

Al-Ahzab is the plural of hizb (with a kasra on the ḥāʾ and a sukun on the zāy). It denotes a group of people who share the same attitude in some matter, whether belief, action, or custom. Here it refers to the nations, each of which was united in its religion. So each nation was a hizb in what it agreed upon.

In His saying ﴿مِن بَعْدِهِمْ﴾ ("after them") there is an indication that the people of Nuh were also a hizb. They adhered to the worship of idols: Yaghuth, Ya'uq, Nasr, Wadd and Suwa'. Likewise, each nation that denied the messengers was a hizb united in religion: ʿĀd was a hizb, Thamud was a hizb, the People of the Thicket (Ashab al-Aykah) were a hizb, and the people of Nuh were a hizb. The meaning is that they all shared in denying the messengers, even though some of the nations differed from others in their religions.

The combination of ﴿قَبْلَهم﴾ ("before them") and ﴿مِن بَعْدِهِمْ﴾ ("after them") contains the embellishment of tibāq (antithesis) in the speech.

Al-Hamm means resolve or intention. Its proper construction is with the preposition bāʾ when applied to meanings, because resolve is an inward act that relates only to meanings, as in His saying the Exalted: ﴿وهَمُّوا بِما لَمْ يَنالُوا﴾ ["and they resolved upon what they did not attain," al-Tawbah: 74]. It is not transitive to essences (dhawāt). So when it is transitive to a noun denoting an essence, a meaning that is connected with that essence must be supplied, as indicated by the context, as in His saying: ﴿ولَقَدْ هَمَّتْ بِهِ﴾ ["she certainly desired him," Yusuf: 24], meaning she desired to lie with him. Sometimes after a noun denoting an essence, something is mentioned that indicates the meaning which is intended, as in His saying here ﴿لِيَأْخُذُوهُ﴾ ("to seize him"), meaning the resolve to seize him. The use of this style is for the purpose of brevity (ijmāl) followed by detail (tafṣīl). Similar to it is the connection of verbs of the heart to nouns, as in ẓanantuka jāʾiyan ("I thought you were coming"), meaning I thought your coming.

The verb akhadha is used metaphorically to mean dealing with a thing by punishment, torment, killing and similar forms of retribution. He the Exalted said: ﴿فَأخَذَهم أخْذَةً رابِيَةً﴾ ["So He seized them with a overwhelming seizure," al-Haqqah: 10]. A captive is called akhīdh, and a slain person is also called akhīdh.

This verb was chosen here to include the various things each nation intended against its messenger, whether killing or other harm, as the Exalted said: ﴿وإذْ يَمْكُرُ بِكَ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا لِيُثْبِتُوكَ أوْ يَقْتُلُوكَ أوْ يُخْرِجُوكَ﴾ ["And when those who disbelieved plotted against you, to confine you or kill you or expel you," al-Anfal: 30].

The meaning is that the earlier disbelieving nations did not limit themselves to denying the Messenger, but went beyond that to harm, through the intention to kill, as God related about Thamud: ﴿قالُوا تَقاسَمُوا بِاللَّهِ لَنُبَيِّتَنَّهُ وأهْلَهُ ثُمَّ لَنَقُولَنَّ لِوَلِيِّهِ ما شَهِدْنا مَهْلِكَ أهْلِهِ وإنّا لَصادِقُونَ﴾ ["They said, 'Swear to one another by God that we will surely attack him and his family by night; then we will say to his heir, "We did not witness the destruction of his family, and indeed we are truthful."'" al-Naml: 49]. The disbelievers of Quraysh also conspired against the Messenger of God (ﷺ) on the night of Dar al-Nadwa to kill him, by having a group from all their clans strike him with swords, a single blow from one man, so that his kinsmen from Banu Hashim would not be able to seek vengeance for him. So God seized the nations as a punishment for them for their resolve against their messengers, and He destroyed them and uprooted them.

From the connection of His saying ﴿فَأخَذْتُهم﴾ to His saying ﴿وهَمَّتْ كُلُّ أُمَّةٍ بِرَسُولِهِمْ لِيَأْخُذُوهُ﴾ it is understood that there is a warning to the polytheists that their resolve to kill the Messenger (ﷺ) is the final limit of the respite granted to them. When they firmly resolve upon that, God will seize them, as He seized the nations that denied before them when each nation resolved against its messenger to seize him. For when Quraysh resolved to kill the Messenger (ﷺ), God delivered him from them through the Hijra, and then He enabled him over them on the day of Badr.

What is meant by ﴿كُلُّ أُمَّةٍ﴾ ("each nation") is each nation among the hizb groups mentioned.

The pronoun in ﴿وجادَلُوا بِالباطِلِ﴾ ("and they disputed with falsehood") refers to ﴿كُلُّ أُمَّةٍ﴾.

The purpose of enumerating the crimes of the earlier nations (denying the messengers, resolving to kill them, and disputing with falsehood) is to make the state of the polytheists, about whom He revealed ﴿ما يُجادِلُ في آياتِ اللَّهِ إلّا الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا﴾ ["None dispute concerning the signs of God except those who disbelieve," Ghafir: 4], comparable to the state of the earlier nations, so that the threat applies to their condition most completely in His saying ﴿فَأخَذْتُهم فَكَيْفَ كانَ عِقابِ﴾.

The bāʾ in His saying ﴿بِالباطِلِ﴾ ("with falsehood") expresses accompaniment (mulābasa), meaning they disputed while accompanied by falsehood; so the prepositional phrase is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to the pronoun. Or the bāʾ expresses instrument, with falsehood treated as an instrument for their disputation, so the adverbial phrase is loose (laghw), connected to ﴿جادَلُوا﴾.

Restricting ﴿جادَلُوا﴾ with the qualification that it was "with falsehood" requires restricting what was stated without qualification in His saying ﴿ما يُجادِلُ في آياتِ اللَّهِ إلّا الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا﴾ [Ghafir: 4].

Idḥāḍ (refutation) means invalidating an argument, as God the Exalted said: ﴿حُجَّتُهم داحِضَةٌ عِنْدَ رَبِّهِمْ﴾ ["their argument is invalid in the sight of their Lord," al-Shura: 16].

The meaning is that they presented falsehood in the form of truth and embellished it with sophistry in the form of proof, in order to invalidate the proofs of truth. That suffices as a reproach for their disbelief.

He based on His saying ﴿فَأخَذْتُهم﴾ the statement ﴿فَكَيْفَ كانَ عِقابِ﴾, just as He based His saying ﴿فَلا يَغْرُرْكَ تَقَلُّبُهم في البِلادِ﴾ [Ghafir: 4] on the clause ﴿ما يُجادِلُ في آياتِ اللَّهِ إلّا الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا﴾ [Ghafir: 4]. So the direction of the interrogation here follows the same pattern as the direction of the address there.

Here al-akhdh means overpowering.

The interrogative in ﴿فَكَيْفَ كانَ عِقابِ﴾ is used to express wonder at the state of the punishment. That implies that the one addressed by the question has witnessed that seizing and punishment. It is based on witnessing the traces of that seizure when many pass by their dwellings on journeys, as indicated by His saying the Exalted: ﴿وإنَّها لَبِسَبِيلٍ مُقِيمٍ﴾ ["and indeed it is on a road that remains," al-Hijr: 76], and similar verses, and on hearing reports of the descent of punishment upon them and their description. So He placed all the addressees in the position of those who witnessed the descent of the punishment upon them. Thus this interrogative contains confirmation and affirmation of the content of the clause ﴿فَأخَذْتُهم﴾.

It is also possible that this interrogative carries the meaning of taqrīr (affirmation by question), on the basis that the purpose of the statement from His saying ﴿كَذَّبَتْ قَبْلَهم قَوْمُ نُوحٍ﴾ through to ﴿فَأخَذْتُهم﴾ is an allusive (taʿrīḍ) threat to the polytheists of Quraysh, by alerting them to what befell the nations before them, since they are like them in associating partners with God and in denial. Therefore the interrogation about what befell their counterparts is an affirmation to them of that.

The yāʾ of the first person is omitted from ﴿عِقابِ﴾ for lightness, with the kasra indicating it.

"And thus the word of your Lord has come into effect against those who disbelieved, that they are the companions of the Fire."

The conjunction "wa" (و) is coordinating, joining this to the clause "so how was My punishment" [Ghafir: 5]; that is, "and in like manner the word of your Lord has come into effect." The thing pointed to by "thus" (dhalika) is the verbal noun drawn from the phrase "the word of your Lord has come into effect," in the manner established on more than one occasion, the first of which was at the words of the Exalted, "And thus We made you a midmost community" [al-Baqarah: 143], in Surat al-Baqarah. This indicates that the thing compared has reached the utmost degree of the quality of resemblance, such that if anyone wished to compare it, he would compare it only to itself.

You may also take the thing pointed to as the seizing (al-akhdh) derived from the phrase "so We seized them" (fa-akhadhtuhum): that is, "and in like manner as the seizing by which God seized the people of Noah and the confederates after them, the words of God have come into effect against those who disbelieved." Thus it is understood, from the comparison of the realization of God's words against those who disbelieved with that seizing, [that]

Page 88

that seizing was itself a realization of God's words, that is, a confirmation of what He had informed them of regarding the threat. Accordingly, by "those who disbelieved" is meant all the disbelievers, so the statement is a generalization after a specification, and it is therefore a concluding summation (tadhyil), because the "confederates" (al-ahzab) are the well-known peoples whose stories have been mentioned, so "those who disbelieved" is more general.

On this reading the comparison in "And thus the word of your Lord has come into effect" operates according to the original principle of comparison, which requires a difference between the compared and the thing compared to it, and it is not of the kind of His saying, "And thus We made you a midmost community" [al-Baqarah: 143] and its like.

It is also permissible that the intended sense of "those who disbelieved" is the same as the intended sense of His earlier saying, "None dispute concerning the signs of God except those who disbelieve" [Ghafir: 4]; that is, "like the seizing of the people of Noah and the confederates, the word of your Lord has come into effect against the disbelievers of your people," meaning the words of threat have come into effect against them if they do not desist from their disbelief.

"The words of God" are His statements which He revealed to the messengers concerning the threat against those who denied, and "against those who disbelieved" is connected to "has come into effect."

His saying, "that they are the companions of the Fire," may be a substitute (badal) for "the words of your Lord," a substitute that is identical to it (badal mutabiq), so that the pronoun in "that they" refers to "those who disbelieved," meaning: it has come into effect against them that they are the companions of the Fire. In this there is an indication that God does not punish the community of the Muhammadan call by total annihilation (al-isti'sal), because He intended to bring forth from among them a generation of believers.

It is also permissible that the particle of causation, the lam (lam al-ta'lil), is omitted, in accordance with the common practice of omitting it before "anna," and the meaning is: "because they are the companions of the Fire." In that case the pronoun in "that they" refers to everything mentioned before it: the people of Noah, the confederates after them, and those who disbelieved.

Al-Jumhur read the word "kalimat Rabbika" in the singular. Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Abu Ja'far read it in the plural form. The singular here is equivalent to the plural, because what is meant by it is the genus (al-jins), as indicated by the fact that the pronoun governed by "'ala" is attached to the verb "haqqat," which is a plural pronoun; so the word is necessarily a genus that applies truly to a multiplicity, in accordance with the multiplicity of the times of the words of threat and the multiplicity of the threatened peoples.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 40, verse 7:

﴿Those who bear the Throne and those around it glorify their Lord with His praise, and believe in Him, and ask forgiveness for those who believe: "Our Lord, You encompass all things in mercy and knowledge, so forgive those who repent and follow Your way, and protect them from the punishment of the Blazing Fire."﴾

This is a fresh, independent resumption (isti'naf ibtida'i), necessitated by the shift from mention of the threat, which points to the blame of those who disbelieved, to praise of the believers. The speech on the tongues of the angels is like the speech on the tongues of the messengers, since all of it is from the revelation of God, and there is a contrasting relationship (munasabah mudadda) between the two states and the two statements.

It may also be an explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani) arising from the threat against those who dispute the signs of God: a questioner might ask about the state of those who do not dispute the signs of God but believe in them.

In this verse, He singled out a group of angels described with attributes that imply the elevation of their rank, as a means of drawing attention to the status of the believers for whom this noble group of angels asks forgiveness. Otherwise, God has ascribed such seeking of forgiveness to angels in general, in His saying in Surat al-Shura: ﴿And the angels glorify their Lord with His praise and ask forgiveness for those on the earth﴾ [al-Shura: 5], meaning among the believers, by the indication of His saying after it: ﴿And those who have taken protectors other than Him - Allah is Guardian over them﴾ [al-Shura: 6].

﴿Those who bear the Throne﴾ are those entrusted with carrying the Throne which encompasses the heavens, and it is the greatest of the heavens; for this reason it is attributed to God in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And above them, on that Day, eight will bear the Throne of your Lord﴾ [al-Haqqah: 17].

And "those around it" (man hawlahu) are a group of angels who surround the Throne, affirming its greatness. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And you will see the angels surrounding the Throne, glorifying with the praise of their Lord﴾ [al-Zumar: 75]. There is no need to delve into their number: ﴿And none knows the hosts of your Lord except Him﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 31].

The report about the two categories of angels, that they glorify and believe in Him, is a preparation and paving for the report about them that they ask forgiveness for those who believe, and that is the purpose of the report; so what contributes to the realization of the acceptance of their seeking forgiveness was placed before it, since it issues from those whose habit is glorification and whose attribute is faith.

The form of the present tense in "yusabbihuna, yu'minuna, and yastaghfiruna" indicates the renewal and repetition of that, and this suggests that what is meant is that they do that in this world, as is most fitting to His saying ﴿So forgive those who repent﴾ and His saying (﴿And admit them to gardens of perpetual residence which You have promised them﴾ [Ghafir: 8]) and His saying ﴿And whoever You protect from evil deeds﴾ [Ghafir: 9], etc. He said in the other verse ﴿and ask forgiveness for those on the earth﴾ [al-Shura: 5], meaning among the believers, as has preceded.

The meaning of the renewal of faith derived from "wa yu'minuna" is the renewal of its consideration in the souls of the angels; otherwise faith is a firm bond in the souls, and its renewal occurs only through the renewal of its evidences and effects.

The benefit of reporting about them that they believe, although it is known on the part of the angels, is to honor the matter of faith by making it the state of the angels, and to allude to the polytheists that they were not like the most noble of the kinds of created beings, like His saying, exalted is He, concerning Abraham: ﴿And he was not of the polytheists﴾ [al-Baqarah: 135].

The clause ﴿Our Lord, You encompass all things in mercy and knowledge﴾ explains "they ask forgiveness," and in it there is an omitted statement indicated by the manner of speech in their saying "Our Lord." The preposition "bi" in "bi-hamdi rabbihim" is for accompaniment, meaning they glorify God with a glorification accompanied by praise, and the object of "yusabbihuna" was omitted because the complement attached to it indicates it.

What is meant by "those who believe" (alladhina amanu) is the believers who are known, and they are the believers in Muhammad (ﷺ), because they are the intended ones in this context, although it is applicable to all believers.

The angels' supplication for the believers opens with the vocative, because that is more conducive to humility and more hopeful for response, and they turned to God by praising the vastness of His mercy and knowledge, because the vastness of mercy is among what makes one hopeful for the answering of forgiveness, and the vastness of knowledge relates to the firmness of the faith of those who believe.

The meaning of vastness in the two attributes is the abundance of their objects, and the mention of the vastness of knowledge is a metonymy for their certainty of the truthfulness of the faith of the believers; it is thus like the saying of one who says: "You know that they believed in You and affirmed Your oneness."

In describing Him with the wide mercy and wide knowledge, the transferred specification (tamyiz muhawwal 'an al-nisbah) was used, because of the hyperbole in its structure, by ascribing the vastness to the essence apparently, as if His essence itself is what encompassed. This is a general statement which makes the listener look forward to what follows, so after it comes the specification that clarifies the relation of vastness, that it is on the side of mercy and on the side of knowledge. This is the benefit of specification of relation in Arabic speech, because detail after generality establishes the attribute in the soul, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the head has blazed with grey hair﴾ [Maryam: 4].

What is meant is that mercy and knowledge encompass every existent now, that is, in this world, and that is the context of the supplication as preceded. So there is no existent in this world except that it has received a portion of God's mercy, whether the believer or the disbeliever, the human or the animal.

"Kulla shay'" (every thing) means every existent, and it is general, specified by reason in relation to mercy; that is, every thing is in need of mercy, and these are the existents that have perception by which they distinguish the agreeable and the disagreeable, the beneficial and the harmful, among humans and animals, since there is no benefit in mercy's relation to stone, tree, and the like.

As for knowledge, the generality is on its proper footing, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Should not He who created know?﴾ [al-Mulk: 14].

Since the context of this supplication is that it occurs in this world, as preceded, what might be said is dispelled: that God's mercy does not encompass the polytheists on the Day of Resurrection, since they are in everlasting punishment. Thus there is no need to specialize the generality of "every thing" regarding the vastness of mercy by means of specifying evidences that are separate, which require that God's mercy not encompass the polytheists after the reckoning.

Upon this preparation there branches the intimate address to God, exalted is He, with what is sought through it, which is asking forgiveness for those who repent, because if He has known the truthfulness of the repentance of those among them who repented, and His mercy has encompassed every thing, then they deserve that His mercy include them, since they are worthy of it.

The object of "fa-ighfir" is omitted for knowledge, meaning: forgive them what they repented of, that is, the sins of those who repented.

What is meant by repentance is abandoning acts of disobedience, and the greatest of them is associating partners with God.

Following the way of God is doing what He commanded them and avoiding what He forbade them. The guidance resembles the path which God laid out for them and pointed them to, so when they act upon it, it is as if they followed the way and walked in it until they reached the goal.

﴿And protect them from the punishment of the Blazing Fire﴾ is coordinated with "fa-ighfir," so it is part of the consequence, since forgiveness requires this protection, because forgiveness of a sin is non-punishment for it. God has made the punishment of the Blazing Fire the recompense of sinners, but they reinforced the implicational indication with the direct indication, to show eagerness for the sought matter.

Al-Jahim: the intensity of blazing; and Jahannam was named the abode of recompense for sins.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 40, verses 8–9:

﴿Our Lord, and admit them to gardens of perpetual residence which You have promised them, and those who were righteous among their fathers and their spouses and their descendants. Indeed, You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise.﴾ ﴿And protect them from the evils [of consequence]; and whoever You protect from evils on that Day – You have had mercy on him. And that is the great attainment.﴾

The repetition of the call (nida') within the sentences of supplication is a parenthetical insertion for emphasis, by increasing the humble entreaty. This is an ascent from the request for their protection from punishment to the request for their admission into the place of bliss.

Al-'Adn (perpetual residence) means abiding, i.e., eternity.

The supplication for them to be given this, while they are certain that they are promised it, is a display of good manners (ta'addub) with Allah the Exalted, because He is not questioned about what He does. As was mentioned in Surat Al 'Imran, His saying ﴿Our Lord, and grant us what You promised us through Your messengers﴾ [Al 'Imran: 194].

It is possible that what is meant by their saying "and admit them" is: hasten for them the entry.

It is also possible that this is a preface to their saying ﴿and those who were righteous among their fathers and their spouses and their descendants﴾, for those [fathers, spouses and descendants] were not explicitly promised it. And "those who were righteous" (man salah) is a conjunction (ataf) upon the object pronoun in "admit them".

The meaning is a supplication that Allah make them, together with those [righteous ones], to be in dwellings close to one another, as was mentioned in His saying the Exalted ﴿They and their spouses are in shade﴾ [Ya-Sin: 56] in Surat Ya-Sin, and His saying ﴿We shall join them with their descendants﴾ [al-Tur: 21] in Surat al-Tur.

The relationships in this verse are arranged in their natural order, for fathers are the earliest in relation to children, then spouses, then descendants.

The sentence ﴿Indeed, You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise﴾ is a parenthetical insertion between the supplications, to exhaust the desire for response, by the cause of the angels' love for the people of righteousness, due to the affinity between their souls and angelic souls.

The coupling of this sentence with the emphatic particle is for giving it importance. And "inna" in such a context functions as the causal fa' (fa' of causation), meaning: Your might and Your wisdom are what embolden us to ask this of Your majesty. Might requires independence from benefiting from precious things; so when He promised the righteous the Garden, there was nothing He would withhold from that, so no delay issues from Him; and wisdom requires treating the doer of good with good.

They followed the request for deliverance from punishment and the bliss of the abode of reward with a supplication for safety from the generality of everything that would distress them on the Day of Resurrection, by their saying ﴿And protect them from the evils﴾. It is a comprehensive supplication, since "sayyi'at" here is the plural of sayyi'ah, which is a state or a deed that distresses the one with whom it is connected, like what is in His saying ﴿So Allah protected him from the evils of what they plotted﴾ [Ghafir: 45] and His saying the Exalted ﴿And if an evil befalls them, they attribute it to Musa and those with him﴾ [al-A'raf: 131]. It is formed on the pattern fay'alah for intensifying the attribute's inherence in the one described, like qayyim, sayyid and sayqal. So the meaning: protect them from everything that would distress them.

The definiteness in "al-sayyi'at" is for the genus, which is capable of conveying comprehensiveness. Its occurrence in a context resembling negation, namely the act of protection, conveys the generality of the genus. Moreover, the nature of supplication requires the generality of the genus even without a negating lam, as in the saying of al-Hariri:

O people of this abode, may harm be averted from you.

And in the hadith: "O Allah, give the one who spends a replacement, and the one who withholds a loss," meaning every spender and every withholder.

The purpose is to convey to these believers the highest degrees of good pleasure and acceptance on the Day of Recompense, such that punishment does not reach them, they remain in the midst of bliss, and nothing troubling afflicts them, such as rebuke and disgrace.

This meaning has come in many verses, such as His saying ﴿So Allah protected them from the evil of that Day﴾ [al-Insan: 11].

The sentence ﴿And whoever You protect from evils on that Day – You have had mercy on him﴾ is a concluding appendage (tadhyil), meaning: whoever is protected from evils on the Day of Resurrection has been reached by Allah's mercy, i.e., mercy has reached him in its completeness; so the verb "rahimtahu" is intended to magnify its source.

This intended meaning is indicated in this verse by His saying ﴿And that is the great attainment﴾ [al-Nisa': 13], since what was mentioned of the protection from evils is pointed to with a demonstrative for honoring and magnifying. The attainment is described as "great" because it is an attainment of bliss pure from the turbidities that diminish the sweetness of the blessing.

And the tanwin of "yawma'idhin" is a substitute (iwad) for the genitive that was omitted, meaning: on the day when You admit them into gardens of perpetual residence.
