[Page 95]

The contrast between the angels' request for the believers, who will receive pure bliss on the Day of Resurrection, and the rebuke and reproach that the polytheists will receive on that day, along with their pleas for pardon that will be rejected, implies that the promise of answering the angels' supplication for the believers is understood. Omitting mention of it is a form of brevity (ījāz).

The shift from this to explaining what will befall the polytheists on that day is a form of the wise approach (al-uslūb al-ḥakīm), because His saying ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved will be called out to﴾ and the verses that follow are a resumption for explanation (istīnāf bayānī), as if a questioner had asked about the acceptance of the angels' supplication for the believers, and the answer was given that what matters more is to ask about its opposite. In this style there is an allusion and an indication that the most important point of all these verses is the admonition of the people of polytheism. This refers back to His saying: ﴿And thus the word of your Lord has come true against those who disbelieved, that they are companions of the Fire﴾ [Ghafir: 6]. The intended meaning of "those who disbelieved" here is the polytheists of Makkah, for they are the ones addressed by these reports, as was mentioned just before in His saying: ﴿and they seek forgiveness for those who believed﴾ [Ghafir: 7].

The meaning is that the angels will call out to them, conveying from the Lord of Majesty. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Those are called from a far place﴾ [Fussilat: 44], which is a distance from the rank of majesty. That is, they will be called out to while they are in Hell, as His saying indicates: ﴿Is there any way to get out?﴾ [Ghafir: 11].

The lām in ﴿the aversion of Allah﴾ is the lām of oath. Maqt means intense hatred.

The phrase "when you were called" (idh tud'awna) is a temporal adverbial complement of ﴿your aversion toward yourselves﴾.

Idh is a temporal particle for past time, meaning: at the time when you were being called to faith through the Messenger ﷺ, and that was in this world, as indicated by the verb "you were called." The imperfect form is used in tud'awna and takfurūn to indicate the repetition of their being called to faith and the repetition of their disbelief, that is, its renewal.

The meaning of ﴿your aversion toward yourselves﴾ in this context is that they did toward themselves what resembles aversion, since they deprived themselves of the excellence of faith and the goodness of its laws, and they accepted for themselves the religion of disbelief after being alerted to the error in it and its bad end. So their act was like the act of a person who harms and plots against someone he hates. This is like the saying: "So-and-so is the enemy of himself." In the hadith of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, that 'Umar said to some women of Quraysh who were asking the Prophet ﷺ and demanding a great deal, and when 'Umar entered they hastened to cover themselves: "O enemies of themselves! Do you feel awe of me and not of the Messenger of Allah?" (ﷺ).

So maqt is used figuratively for little reflection on what harms. The phrase ﴿when you were called to faith and you disbelieved﴾ has indicated the basis of this figurative usage, so the core of the statement is "and you disbelieved." The mention of "they are called out to" implies an omitted statement, whose estimated meaning is: "Those who disbelieved are hated by Allah and are called out to, [being subjected to] the aversion of Allah, etc."

[Page 96]

The meaning of "the aversion of Allah" is His hatred of them. It is a metonymy (majāz mursal), applied to treating them with the effects of hatred, such as humiliation and punishment. This is closer to the reality of hatred, because what is meant is its effect, which is treatment with punishment. This usage is as common as its parallels that are attributed to Allah, whose true meaning is impossible for Him. This report is used for rebuke and reproach.

"Greater" (akbar) means more severe and more harmful in effect. Applying "greatness" to it is a metaphor, because greatness is a quality of physical bodies, but its use for strength in abstract matters has become common. Since their aversion toward themselves deprived them of faith, which is the cause of salvation and righteousness, and since Allah's anger against them brought them into punishment, Allah's hatred of them was more severe and more painful than their aversion toward themselves, because the intensity of pain is stronger than being deprived of good.

The first aversion is close to His saying: ﴿Those are the ones who bought error in exchange for guidance, so their trade did not profit﴾ [al-Baqarah: 16], and the second aversion is close to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the disbelievers' disbelief increases them only in aversion before their Lord﴾ [Fatir: 39], which is the aversion of punishment. This is the interpretation of the verse that fits the coherence of its wording. Among the scholars of tafsir there are other interpretations of it, some closer and some further from what we have mentioned, so review them and form your judgment about them.

"Your selves" (anfusakum) is governed by the aversion of Allah, and "your aversion" (maqtikum) is the object of both verbal nouns, which are annexed to their agents.

The verb "you were called" (tud'awna) is put in the passive form for the sake of knowing the agent, since it is clear that the caller is the Messenger ﷺ or the messengers, peace be upon them.

The connection of "and you disbelieved" (fatakfurūn) to "you were called" with the particle fa indicates that they followed the call with disbelief, that is, with a renewal of their earlier disbelief and with its public declaration, without giving themselves the pause of reflection and contemplation on what they were called to.

[Page 97]

﴿They said, "Our Lord, You caused us to die twice and You gave us life twice, so we have acknowledged our sins. Is there any way out?"﴾

This is an answer to the call they were addressed with from God, the Exalted. He related their speech in the manner of reported dialogue, omitting the conjunction. They hoped that their acknowledgment of their sins would be a means of granting them some exit from the punishment, an exit of some sort, so that they might rest from it, even for a portion of time. This is because the call addressed to them from God gave them the impression that it implied turning toward them.

The purpose of the acknowledgment is their acknowledgment of the second life, because they had been denying it. As for the two deaths and the first life, they were mentioned incidentally (idmaj) as part of the argument within the core of the acknowledgment, out of a desire to ingratiate themselves. That is, "We have become certain that the second life is true." This is an allusion (ta'rid) that their confession is sincere, without equivocation or affectation, because it results from evidence. For this reason, their saying ﴿so we have acknowledged our sins﴾ is made a consequence of this statement by joining it with the causal particle فاء (fa') in their words.

By "one of the two deaths" is meant the state in which the fetus is flesh without life in the earliest stage of its formation, before the spirit is breathed into it. Applying the term "death" to that state is a figurative usage (majaz). This is the preference of al-Zamakhshari and al-Sakkaki, based on the view that the true meaning (haqiqa) of death is the cessation of life in a living being after it has been characterized by life. Thus applying it to the absence of life before life has come into it is a metaphor (isti'ara). However, this is so widespread in the Qur'an that it has come to equal the literal usage. Therefore there is no difficulty in using the word أمتنا (amatna) in both its literal and figurative senses. In that verb there is thus a combination of the literal and the subordinate metaphor (isti'ara tabi'iyya), following from the operation of metaphor in the verbal noun. There is no objection to this, since it occurs and is found in eloquent speech, like the use of a homonym in both its meanings. As for those who do not restrict the meaning of death to occurring after life, the application of "death" to the state before characterization by life is clear to them. This was discussed in the Almighty's words ﴿And you were dead, and He gave you life﴾ [al-Baqara: 28] in Surat al-Baqara. Moreover, applying "death" to the state before the breathing of the spirit in this verse is more fitting, because it gives precedence to the second death.

As for the second death, it is the commonly known death at the end of the life of a human being and an animal.

By "the two lives" is meant the first life, at the breathing of the spirit into the body after the beginning of its formation,

[Page 98]

and the second life, which occurs at resurrection. This is equivalent in meaning to the Almighty's words ﴿And you were dead, and He gave you life; then He causes you to die, then He gives you life, then to Him you will be returned﴾ [al-Baqara: 28].

The word اثنتين (ithnatayn) in both places is in the accusative as an adjective to an omitted absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq). The estimated sense is: "two deaths" and "two lives." Thus, in the estimation of "two deaths," the literal term is given precedence over the figurative term according to those who restrict the meaning of death.

Many exegetes have raised the objection that there is a third life not mentioned here, namely the life in the grave, which is indicated by the hadith of the questioning in the grave. This is a hadith well known among Muslims since the time of the early generations. Whether the questioning in the grave requires the full life of the body is open to possibility. It may be interpreted as the questioning of the soul of the deceased at its body, or as the life of part of the body, or because it is a temporary life, lasting only for the duration of the questioning, during which the one characterized by it does not have the actions of the living in this world. It was not counted, especially since the speech is intended as a preparation for the request for their exit from Hell. By this it is known that the verse has no connection to being used as evidence for the existence of life during questioning in the grave.

The statement ﴿so we have acknowledged our sins﴾ branches off from their statement ﴿and You gave us life twice﴾, on the basis that one of the two lives was the cause of their sins coming into being, among whose roots was their denial of resurrection. When they saw resurrection with their own eyes, they became certain that they were sinners, since they had denied it, and sinners for what they had committed in great number of sins, due to their deception by safety from being held accountable after the immediate life.

So the clause ﴿so we have acknowledged our sins﴾ is a performative utterance of confession of sins. For this reason the past tense is used in it, as is the general practice of declarative forms used performatively, like the forms of contracts, such as بعت (ba'tu, "I sold"). The meaning is: "We acknowledge our sins."

They treated this acknowledgment as a kind of repentance, supposing that repentance would be beneficial on that day. For this reason they built upon it ﴿Is there any way out?﴾. The interrogative is used entirely in the sense of proposal and entreaty, seeking the removal of the punishment. The request of the people of the Fire for an exit or for lightening, even for a day, is repeated in the Qur'an.

[Page 99]

The interrogative with the particle هل (hal) is used in the sense of entreaty.

The particle من (min) is superfluous, serving to emphasize the generality inherent in the indefinite noun, so as to convey their seeking every way out. The nature of the superfluous من is that it occurs in negation and what has the meaning of negation, not in affirmation. However, the interrogative with هل (hal) specifically has been counted among the positions where the superfluous من is used to emphasize generality, as in the Almighty's words ﴿and it says, "Is there any more?"﴾ [Qaf: 30]. This was discussed at the Almighty's words ﴿Then do we have any intercessors who will intercede for us?﴾ [al-A'raf: 53] in Surat al-A'raf. The reason that هل (hal) is specifically associated with the occurrence of the superfluous من in the item asked about by it is that the use of interrogation with it came to be very frequent in the sense of negation. The superfluous من is then used to emphasize the negation and to make explicit the generality of the negation. Thus its occurrence after هل (hal) became light on the tongues of the users of the language.

The indefiniteness of خروج (khurooj) is for the sense of kind, out of gentleness in the request. That is: "to some kind of exit, few or many," because every exit from which they would benefit would be a rest from the punishment, as in their saying ﴿Call upon your Lord to lighten the punishment for us by a day﴾ [Ghafir: 49].

The word سبيل (sabil) means "road," and it has been used metaphorically for the means by which the desired matter is attained. Usage has varied widely in the applications of sabil, tariq (road), maslak (path), and reaching, for means and for the attainment of the aim.

The indefiniteness of سبيل (sabil) is like the indefiniteness of خروج (khurooj); that is, "a means, however it may be, whether by right or by pardon, by lightening or otherwise."

Al-Zamakhshari said in the Kashshaf: "This is the speech of one overcome by despair and hopelessness." He means that in their being satisfied with some exit there is an indication that they regard the occurrence of an exit as improbable.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 40, verse 12:

﴿That is because, when Allah alone was invoked, you disbelieved, but when others were associated with Him, you believed. So judgment belongs to Allah, the Most High, the Most Great.﴾

He turned away from their request (for release) by denying them any escape, and turned instead to mentioning the cause of their falling into the punishment. Since they already knew it, and had said ﴿So we acknowledge our sins﴾ [Ghafir: 11], the reiteration of the reproach after their plea for forgiveness was a metaphor for the continuation of this state and the non-granting of their request to be released from it, in a manner that conveys their humiliation.

This was reinforced by His saying ﴿So judgment belongs to Allah, the Most High, the Most Great﴾.

The reference of (That) is to their state of punishment, which was announced by His saying ﴿They will be called: Surely Allah's aversion to you is greater than your aversion to yourselves﴾ [Ghafir: 10], and what followed it of their saying ﴿Is there any way out?﴾ [Ghafir: 11].

The bā' in (bi-annahu) is causal, meaning: because of your disbelief when Allah was invoked alone.

The pronoun in (bi-annahu) is the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n), and it is explained by what follows it, His saying ﴿when Allah alone was invoked, you disbelieved, and when others were associated with Him, you believed﴾. Thus the cause is the content of the statement, whose sum is: because of your disbelief in Divine Unity and your belief in associating partners.

(Idhā, "when") is used here for past time, because the invoking of Allah and their disbelief in His Unity took place in the worldly life. The invocation that occurred, together with their disbelief in it, was the cause of their falling into punishment.

The use of the present form in both verbs, ﴿and when others are associated with Him, you believe﴾, is understood as past by the context preceding it. The choice of the present form in both verbs indicates the repetition of this from them in the worldly life, for its repetition has an effect in multiplying the punishment for them.

Invocation (du'ā') means calling out and addressing. Both meanings are used for it, and du'ā' is also applied to worship, as will come at His saying ﴿And your Lord said: Call upon Me, I will respond to you﴾ [Ghafir: 60] in this surah. So the meaning is: when Allah was proclaimed in your hearing with a proclamation indicating that He is one God, like the Qur'anic verses that indicate the proclamation of Allah's Unity. Thus invocation here means declaration and mention, and for this reason it is paired with ﴿you disbelieved, and when others are associated with Him, you believe﴾. Invocation in this sense is more general than invocation in the sense of asking for needs, but it includes it, or (it means) when Allah is worshipped alone.

The meaning of "you disbelieved" (kafartum) is: you renewed disbelief. This may occur either through utterances from them in which they deny Allah's sole divinity, or through a fresh consideration and remembrance of their gods. The meaning of "when others are associated with Him, you believe" is: if there issues forth what indicates association with Allah, from the sayings of their leaders and companions that indicate a plurality of gods; or, if He is associated with in worship, you believe, that is, you renew belief in a plurality of gods in your hearts, or you confirm that with statements of affirmation and augmentation. The complements of (kafartum) and (tu'minu) are omitted, being indicated by what precedes them. The estimated sense is: you disbelieved in His Unity, and you believe in the partners.

In the first condition the particle (idhā) is used, whose condition usually indicates the certainty of its occurrence, pointing out that invoking Allah alone is a matter certain among the believers, which their days and gatherings never lack, along with what (idhā) conveys of desire for the realisation of the content of its condition.

In the second condition the particle (in) is used, which originally implies non-certainty of the occurrence of its condition, or that its condition is a supposed matter, although association is in fact established. This treats the established as if it were the doubtful and supposed, to draw attention to the fact that the proofs of the invalidity of association are clear with the least reflection and contemplation. So their established association is placed in the position of the supposed, because the context contains what uproots the content of the condition from its root, and so it is fit only to be supposed, in the manner in which the known is supposed to exist, or the impossible is supposed to be possible.

The alif and lam in (al-ḥukm, "the judgment") are for the genus.

The lam in (lillāhi, "belongs to Allah") is for ownership, meaning: the genus of judgment belongs to Allah. This indicates the restriction (qaṣr) of this genus to being Allah's, as was discussed earlier at His saying (al-ḥamdu lillāh, "all praise is for Allah") in Surat al-Fatiha. It is a true restriction, since on the Day of Resurrection there is no judgment for anyone other than Allah, the Exalted.

By this verse the Ḥarūriyya held fast on the day of Ḥarūrā' when the armies of Kufa and Syria converged on arbitration (taḥkīm). The Ḥarūriyya rebelled against 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and said: "There is no judgment but Allah's." They took the definite article as generic and the form as restrictive, and fixed their gaze on this verse while ignoring many others. 'Ali said when he heard it: "A word of truth by which falsehood is intended." People were thrown into confusion, and the arbitration was not completed.

The choice of the two attributes, the Most High (al-'Ali) and the Most Great (al-Kabir), is mentioned here because their meaning is suitable to their being deprived of exit from the Fire, that is, because Allah's judgment against them of eternal abiding in the Fire is not to be annulled. For loftiness in His attribute is a figurative, relational loftiness, in the sense of nobility of rank and perfection; He is the Most High in all degrees of perfection essentially. Among what this requires is complete loftiness and complete justice, and therefore He does not judge except by what wisdom and justice require.

The attribute of Greatness is likewise figurative greatness, which is the strength of the attributes of His perfection, for the Great is strong, and He is the Absolutely Self-Sufficient. Both attributes are formed on the pattern of the attributive adjective (al-ṣifa al-mushabbaha) to indicate firm, essential attribution. A judgment is only accepted as annulled for one of two reasons: either because it does not follow what its cause requires, namely annulment on account of opposition to truth, and this is contrary to the attribute of Most High; or because it is tyranny and exceeds its bounds, and this is contrary to the attribute of Most Great, for it implies independence from tyranny.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 40, verse 13:

﴿He it is who shows you His signs and sends down for you provision from the sky. Yet none is mindful except one who turns back in repentance.﴾

This is a fresh, independent resumption (isti'naf ibtida'i), turning to address the Messenger (ﷺ) and the believers after the description of the torment that the polytheists face and the supplications they make that will not be answered. The indication of this is His saying: "even though the disbelievers may be averse."

The reason for the shift is the two attributes, the Most High (al-'Ali) and the Great (al-Kabir), because the clause "He shows you His signs" suits the attribute of loftiness, and the clause "and sends down for you provision from the sky" suits the attribute of greatness in the sense of absolute self-sufficiency (al-ghani al-mutlaq).

The signs (al-ayat) are the proofs of His existence and His oneness: the great manifestations that appear to people in this world, as in His saying: ﴿It is He who shows you the lightning, as a fear and as a hope﴾ [al-Ra'd: 12], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth and the alternation of the night and the day are signs for people of understanding﴾ [Al 'Imran: 190].

The sending down of provision from the sky is the descent of rain, because rain is the cause of provision, and it is itself a sign, and a favour (imtinan) is combined with it. For this reason both matters are followed by His saying: ﴿Yet none is mindful except one who turns back in repentance.﴾

The form of the present tense in "He shows you" (yurikum) and "sends down" (yunazzilu) indicates that the showing is a renewed showing and the sending down is a renewed sending down, and this only occurs in the world. It is therefore established that the address is a new address, intended for the believers, and is not part of the continuing address to the polytheists in Hell. This is further confirmed by His saying: ﴿So call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion, even though the disbelievers may be averse﴾ [Ghafir: 14].

The two verbs "shows" (yuri) and "sends down" (yunazzilu) are transitive to the pronoun of the addressees, who are the believers, because they are the ones who benefited from the signs and believed, and who benefited from the provision and gave thanks through acting in obedience. Others are therefore placed in the position of those not intended by the signs, since they did not benefit from them, as He said: ﴿And these are the parables We present to the people, but none understands them except those of knowledge﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 43]. Thus He made those who lack knowledge like one who does not reason or comprehend.

For this reason, the showing of the signs and the sending down of provision for them are concluded with His saying: ﴿Yet none is mindful except one who turns back in repentance﴾, that is, whoever believes and renounces polytheism, because polytheism prevents its adherents from fairness and from exercising reflection on the proofs.

Al-inabah means repentance (al-tawbah). The use of the present tense indicates that the repentance that achieves the desired goal is the renewed and repeated repentance. Since the addressees were already turning back to Allah, His saying "none is mindful except one who turns back in repentance" implies by necessary implication (dalalat al-iqtida') that they saw the signs, found assurance in them, recognised the measure of the blessing, and gave thanks for it. Thus there is a customary correlation (talazum 'adi) between turning back in repentance and being mindful. For this reason the clause "Yet none is mindful except one who turns back in repentance" is a concluding clause (tadhyil).

The placement of "for you" (lakum) before the object of "sends down," which is "provision" (rizqan), serves the completeness of the favour, by making the sending down of provision for the sake of people. Had the prepositional phrase been postponed, it would have become an attribute of "provision," and it would not convey that the sending down was for the sake of the addressees; rather it would convey that the provision is suitable for the addressees. Between the two meanings there is a vast difference. Thus placing the prepositional phrase before the object of the verb is contrary to what the apparent structure requires, since the object ought to precede other complements of the verb; it departs from that apparent order only for this subtle purpose.

Making the sending down of provision for the sake of the addressees, who are the believers, indicates that Allah intended their honour first, and that the benefit of others from the provision is a benefit by way of following them, because they are the ones who occupy the place of Allah's good pleasure.

From this verse arises the question of the disagreement between the Ash'ariyyah, with al-Maturidi, and the Mu'tazilah, on whether the disbeliever is a recipient of blessing (mun'am 'alayh) or not. According to al-Ash'ari, the disbeliever is not a recipient of blessing in this world, nor in religion, nor in the Hereafter. Al-Qadi Abu Bakr al-Baqillani and al-Maturidi said: he is a recipient of a worldly blessing, not a religious one nor an otherworldly one. The Mu'tazilah said: he is a recipient of a worldly and religious blessing, but not an otherworldly one.

As for al-Ash'ari, he did not take into account the apparent pleasures that the disbeliever obtains in life, because that is only respite and lure (imla' wa istidraj), since their outcome is painful torment, and so they do not deserve the name of blessing. I say: if he were argued with on the basis that these are obtained by them incidentally (taba'an), then they are delights (la'adhdhat) and not blessings, because a blessing is a delight whose purpose is the benefit of the one to whom it reaches, as I indicated a moment ago.

As for al-Baqillani, he considered the apparent pleasures and did not prevent them from being blessings even if their consequences are pains, and the verses of the Qur'an bear witness to his view.

As for the Mu'tazilah, they went further and claimed that the disbeliever is a recipient of religious blessing, and by this they meant that Allah enabled the disbeliever with the blessing of the capacity to reflect, which leads to knowledge of Allah and of the attributes that are necessary for Him.

What has settled as the view of the verifying scholars (al-muhaqqiqun) among the theologians is that this disagreement is verbal (lafzi), because it does not look at the reality of the disbeliever's state in the world and in religion. Rather, each side looked at what surrounds the disbeliever's circumstances in that blessing, and so the dispute returned to a disagreement over the terms agreed upon and their connotations, regarding the realities of what is intended by them.

[Page 105]

This is a consequence of what they witnessed of the signs and of the provision poured out upon them, and of their being those who are hoped to be reminded. That is: since you are at this rank, "so call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion." The fa' here carries the sense of the *fa' fasiha* (the fa' that implies an unstated condition), as was mentioned earlier at His saying: ﴿And none remembers except those who turn back in repentance﴾ [Ghafir: 13].

The meaning is: Allah has shown you His signs and sent down provision for you, and none remembers except those who turn back in repentance, and you are among them. So call upon Allah, sincere to Him, so as to multiply the motives for that worship.

The *du'a'* (calling, supplication) here means proclamation, the remembrance of Allah, and invoking Him. It also includes supplication in the sense of asking for one's needs, the general encompassing the specific. It was mentioned just above that *du'a'* is applied to worship.

The imperative is used to express a request for continuity, because the believers had already called upon Allah sincerely to Him. So the intended meaning is: persist in that, even if the disbelievers dislike it. The disbelievers' dislike of this on the part of the believers would prompt them to try to turn them away from it by every means they could find, and it is feared that this might tempt a group of the believers. Thus "dislike" is a *kinaya* (metonymy) for opposition and obstruction, since these two accompany dislike, for the nature of one who dislikes is that he does not endure patiently the continuation of what he dislikes. Accordingly, the command ﴿So call upon Allah, sincere to Him﴾ is akin to the command in His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾ [An-Nisa': 136].

The name of Allah (Allah) is stated explicitly in ﴿So call upon Allah﴾ because the speech is a consequence that introduces a new purpose, so it was made independent of what precedes it.

The explanation of ﴿sincere to Him in religion﴾ has already been given in the commentary on His saying ﴿So worship Allah, sincere to Him in religion﴾ [Az-Zumar: 2] at the beginning of Surat az-Zumar.

The clause ﴿even if the disbelievers dislike it﴾ occupies the position of a *hal* (circumstantial qualifier) relative to the subject of "call upon" (ud'u).

The *law* here is *wasliyya* (the "even if" of inclusion), which indicates that its condition is the furthest of the states in which the regulating verb of the circumstance is meant to be restricted. That is: worship Him in every state, even in the state of the disbelievers' dislike of that, because the disbelievers' dislike of it, while the believers are among them and in the lands under the authority of the disbelievers, is a likely cause for it to turn them away from calling upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion. This has the same sense as His saying: ﴿So proclaim what you are commanded﴾ [Al-Hijr: 94]. The detailed treatment of this *law* has already been given at His saying ﴿So never will there be accepted from any of them the earth filled with gold, even if he should ransom himself by it﴾ [Al 'Imran: 91] in Surat Al 'Imran.

[Page 106]

﴿Exalted in ranks, Lord of the Throne, He sends down the Spirit by His command upon whomever He wills of His servants, that he may warn of the Day of Meeting﴾ ﴿the Day when they will come forth, with nothing of them hidden from God﴾ [Ghafir: 15–16].

"Exalted in ranks" (*rafī' al-darajāt*) is a predicate of an omitted subject, which is the pronoun of the Name of Majesty (God) in His saying "so call upon God" (﴿so call upon God﴾). It is not a second predicate after His saying ﴿He is the One who shows you His signs﴾ [Ghafir: 13], because the discourse here concerns a new purpose. Omitting the subject in such a case is an omission of continuity (*ḥadhf ittibā'*) owing to the usage of omitting its like. This is what al-Sakkakī (d. 626 AH) named it, after the sentence has been preceded by a discourse about the omitted element, as in the verse of ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr, or Ibrāhīm ibn al-ʿAbbās al-Ṣūlī, or Muḥammad ibn Saʿīd the secretary:

*I shall thank ʿAmr if my death is delayed, for favours bestowed without reminder, even if they are great.*

*A youth whose wealth is not hidden from his friend, nor does he display complaint when his sandal slips.*

"Exalted" (*rafī'*) may be an attribute in the form of the *ṣifa mushabbaha* (the adjective of quality, a stable attribute). The definite article in "the ranks" (*al-darajāt*) is a substitute for the genitive complement. The original sense is: "whose ranks are exalted." When the description of what belongs to His affairs is transferred to become a description of His essence, the construction of the genitive is adopted, the *ṣifa mushabbaha* is made a predicate of the pronoun of the Name of Majesty, and the agent of the attribute is made a genitive complement. This is one of the states of the *ṣifa mushabbaha*: one says "so-and-so is good in his deed," and also "good of deed"; thus His saying "Exalted in ranks" is interpreted as an attribute of His essence.

"The ranks" (*al-darajāt*) is used metaphorically for glory and greatness. Its plural form signals the abundance of greatnesses, in view of the attributes of God's glory, which cannot be enumerated. The meaning is that He is worthy of having the supplication directed to Him sincerely.

It is possible that "Exalted" (*rafī'*) is among the forms of intensity (*mubālagha*), meaning one who raises ranks abundantly for whomever He wills. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿We raise in ranks whom We will﴾ [al-Anʿam: 83]. Its genitive relation to "the ranks" is of the type of the genitive of the object, so it refers to the attributes of God's acts.

The purpose is to make them steadfast in worshipping God, sincerely devoted to Him in religion, by encouraging them through mention of God raising their ranks, as in His saying: ﴿God will raise those among you who believe and those who have been given knowledge, by degrees﴾ [al-Mujadila: 11], in the Surah of al-Mujadila.

[Page 107]

"Lord of the Throne" (*dhū al-ʿarsh*) is a second predicate, and it contains an indication that the raising of ranks from Him varies, just as His created beings on high vary in greatness and nobility, up to the Throne, which is the highest of created beings. It is as if it were said: He who raised the heavens and raised the Throne, what do you imagine His raising of the ranks of His worshippers to be, according to the levels of their worship and sincerity?

The clause "He sends down the Spirit by His command" is a third predicate, or a partial substitute (*badal baʿḍ*) for the clause "Exalted in ranks." For among the raising of ranks is that He raises some of His servants to the rank of prophethood, and that is the greatest raising of ranks with respect to His servants. Thus the partial substitute here is the most important of the individuals of what is substituted.

"Sending down" (*al-ilqāʾ*): its literal meaning is throwing a thing from the hand to the ground. It is used metaphorically for giving when it is unexpected, and this is frequent in the Qur'an. He said: ﴿So they cast to them the word, "You are indeed liars"﴾ [al-Naḥl: 86], ﴿and they will cast to God on that day their submission﴾ [al-Naḥl: 87]. It is borrowed here for revelation, because it comes suddenly, without anticipation, like the casting of a thing to the ground.

"The Spirit" (*al-rūḥ*) means the Sharīʿa (divine law). The literal sense of "the spirit" is that by which a living being among created things is alive. It is used metaphorically for what is precious among matters, and for revelation, because by it people's spiritual life is sustained, which is their perfection and the ordering of their affairs. Just as life is used metaphorically for faith and knowledge, so too the Spirit, which is the cause of life, is used metaphorically for the perfection of souls and their safety from evil dispositions. The Spirit is also applied to the angel, as He said: ﴿So We sent to her Our Spirit, and it appeared to her as a man in every respect﴾ [Maryam: 17].

"From" (*min*) in "by His command" (*min amrihi*) is for the beginning, meaning "by His command," so "command" is in its apparent sense. It is possible that "from" is partitive, an adverbial phrase of location functioning as a qualifier of the Spirit, meaning: some of His affairs which no one knows except whom He approves; "command" then means "affair," i.e., the wondrous affairs. It has also been said that "from" is explicative, and that "command" is the Spirit itself, but this is remote.

This verse indicates that prophethood is not acquired, because it began with His saying

[Page 108]

﴿So call upon God, sincerely devoted to Him in religion﴾ [Ghafir: 14], then it was followed by His saying "Exalted in ranks," which indicates that worshipping God with sincerity is a cause of the raising of ranks. Then it was followed by His saying ﴿He sends down the Spirit by His command﴾. The verb of sending down was used, along with the Spirit being "from His command," and with the relative clause "upon whomever He wills of His servants." This indicates that this is by His sole choice and knowledge, as He said, Exalted is He: ﴿God knows best where to place His message﴾ [al-Anʿam: 124].

This relates to His saying at the beginning of the Surah: ﴿We have sent down to you the Book with the truth, so worship God, sincerely devoted to Him in religion﴾ [al-Zumar: 2]. He commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to be sincere in worship, as a consequence of the sending down of the Book to him, and He addressed the people concerning this in His saying ﴿So call upon God, sincerely devoted to Him﴾ [Ghafir: 14], then followed it with His saying "Exalted in ranks."

He has presented the Throne and the prophets to them as two examples of the raising of ranks among the worlds and among rational beings. In this there is an allusion that belittles the polytheists, when they said ﴿Shall we follow a single man from among us?﴾ [al-Qamar: 24], and ﴿They said, "Why was this Qur'an not sent down to a great man from the two towns?"﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 31], and they said ﴿We will not believe until we are given the like of what was given to the messengers of God﴾ [al-Anʿam: 124].

He moves from the mention of prophethood to warning of the Day of Recompense, so that the description of the Day of Recompense, whose discussion had been interrupted since His saying ﴿That is because, when God alone was invoked, you disbelieved﴾ [Ghafir: 12], returns, and so on.

"Warning" (*al-indhār*) is information containing a caution against what is harmful, and it is the opposite of giving good news (*al-tabshīr*), which is information containing what brings joy. Its unaugmented verb is *nadhira*, like *ʿalima*; one says: *nadhira bi-l-ʿaduww* ("he perceived the enemy") and so he was wary of him.

The *hamza* in *andhara* is for transitivity. Its proper usage is that it should not take a direct object with the *hamza* except one object, which is the one who was the agent of the unaugmented verb, and that it should take the matter reported by means of the preposition *bi-* (with); one says *andhartuhum bi-l-ʿaduww* ("I warned them of the enemy"). However, in usage it became customary to imply in it the sense of caution, so they made it transitive to a second object, and this is the usage of the Qur'an. As for His saying at the beginning of al-Aʿrāf ("that you may warn thereby"), the *bāʾ* there indicates cause or a figurative instrument, and is not for transitivity. The pronoun in "thereby" refers to the Book.

The concealed pronoun in "that he may warn" (*li-yundhira*) refers to the Name of Majesty from His saying "so call upon God" [Ghafir: 14]. The better view is that it refers to the relative "whomever" (*man*), so that the one upon whom the Spirit was cast warns his people; and because

[Page 109]

in this there is a smooth transition to mention of the greatest Messenger (ﷺ), who is poised for warning, unlike the earlier messengers, for whom the present-tense form is unsuitable. It also favours making the Name of God explicit in His saying ﴿Nothing of them is hidden from God﴾ [Ghafir: 16], as will come.

"The Day of Meeting" (*yawm al-talāq*) is the Day of Gathering. It is called the Day of Meeting because all people meet in it, or because they meet their Lord in a figurative meeting, that is, they stand in His presence and before His command directly, as He said: ﴿Those who do not hope for meeting Us﴾ [Yunus: 7], meaning, those who do not hope for the Day of Gathering. "The Day of Meeting" is in the accusative as a second object of *yundhira*, and the first object is omitted because it is evident, i.e., "that he may warn the people."

There is paronomasia (*jinās*) between "the Meeting" (*al-talāq*) and "casts down" (*yulqī*).

"Al-talāq" is written in the Muṣḥaf without a *yāʾ*. Nāfiʿ, and Abū ʿAmr in one transmission from him, read it with a kasra and without a *yāʾ*. The rest read it with a *yāʾ*, because it occurs in connected speech, not at pause, so there is no reason to drop the *yāʾ* except treating connection as pause, which is rare in prose, so it is restricted to what is heard. The transmission of Nāfiʿ and Abū ʿAmr suffices as a hearing.

"The Day when they will come forth" (﴿yawma hum bārizūn﴾) [Ghafir: 16] is a substitute for "the Day of Meeting." "They are coming forth" is a nominal sentence, and the noun it is attached to is a temporal adverb in the future, which is permissible in the most preferred view without any need for an elided element.

The pronoun of absence refers to "the disbelievers" in His saying ﴿and even if the disbelievers dislike it﴾ [Ghafir: 14].

The clause "nothing of them is hidden from God" [Ghafir: 16] is an explanation of the clause "they are coming forth," and the meaning is that their outward and inward states are clear, for this is what His saying "nothing of them" requires.

The explicit mention of the Name of Majesty is because making it explicit is more clear, given the distance of its referent from what follows it, namely His saying ﴿upon whomever He wills of His servants﴾; and because the more evident view is that the pronoun in "that he may warn" refers to "whomever He wills."

The meaning of "of them" (*minhum*) is "from their totality," i.e., from the totality of their conditions and affairs. For this reason the plural pronoun was preferred, because it contains a generality suitable for the implicit construction of a fitting genitive complement for the context. The word "thing" (*shayʾ*) was also preferred, because of its extreme generality. He did not say "nothing of them is hidden from God, not one (*aḥad*)," or "nothing of anyone is hidden from God," meaning a part of his body; so the meaning is: nothing of their conditions, whether outward or inward, is hidden from God.

Ibn 'Ashur on Qur'an 40:16:

﴿Whose is the dominion today? It belongs to Allah, the One, the Subduer.﴾

It is a *maqul* (the object of speech) of an omitted saying, and the verb of saying was omitted from the context of the sea. The estimated reading is: Allah says, "Whose is the dominion today?" The omitted verb of saying is therefore a clause in the position of a circumstantial phrase (*hal*), or a *istinaf bayani* (explanatory resumptive clause) answering the question of one who asks what happens after they emerge before Allah.

The interrogative is either *taqriri* (affirmative, seeking acknowledgment), so that the tyrants among the people of the Gathering (*mahshar*) bear witness against themselves that in this world they were wrong in what they claimed for themselves of dominion for their idols, when they attributed to them control over realms of the earth and the heavens. This is like the claim of the Greeks regarding the god of the sea, the god of war and the god of wisdom, and the claim of the Copts of Egypt regarding the god of the sun, the god of death and the god of wisdom, and the claim of the Arabs regarding the restriction of certain idols to certain tribes, such as al-Lat for Thaqif, Dhu al-Khalasa for Daws, and Manat for al-Aws and al-Khazraj. Likewise is what they claimed for themselves of authority over people which no one else shares, like the words of Pharaoh: ﴿I know of no god for you other than myself﴾ [al-Qasas: 38], and his saying: ﴿Does not the dominion of Egypt belong to me, and these rivers flow beneath me?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 51]; and the titling of the Persian Kisras for themselves with the title "King of Kings" (*Shahanshah*), and the titling of the kings of India for themselves with the title "King of the World" (*Shah Jahan*). This meaning is explained by what is in the hadith describing the Day of Gathering: «Then Allah will say: I am the King; where are the kings of the earth?», an interrogative intended to frighten them from appearing on that day, meaning: where are they today? Why did they not appear with their greatness and their arrogance?!

It is also permissible that the interrogative be a metaphor for arousing eagerness for the answer that follows it, because the nature of one who hears a question is that he awaits its answer, so the answer settles more firmly in his soul upon hearing it. And the arousing of eagerness does not escape even if the interrogative is considered as affirmative. Close to this is the verse: ﴿And when My servants ask you concerning Me, indeed I am near. I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me﴾ [al-Baqarah: 186].

The phrase "today" (*al-yawm*), defined by the article *al-*, refers to the present day, and its presence is relative to the reported saying, i.e., the day on which this saying is uttered, as is the case with time-nouns used as adverbs when they are defined by *al-*.

The clause ﴿for Allah, the One, the Subduer﴾ may be part of the estimated saying issued from Allah the Exalted, such that an interrogative issues from that side and its answer also issues from it. Because the interrogative is used for affirmation or arousing eagerness, it is fitting that the one who asks should also give the answer. A parallel is His saying: ﴿About what are they asking one another? About the great news﴾ [al-Naba': 1–2].

It is also permissible that it be the *maqul* of another omitted saying, meaning: the ones being questioned will say, "to Allah, the One, the Subduer," acknowledging this. The estimated reading is: the ones who emerge will say "to Allah, the One, the Subduer," and so it is an interjected clause (*mu'taridah*).

The mention of the two attributes (*al-Wahid al-Qahhar*) without others of the Most Beautiful Names is because their meanings have a greater relevance to His saying ﴿Whose is the dominion today?﴾, since the signs of Allah's oneness and His subjugation of all tyrants and oppressors are seen on that day.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 40, verse 17:

﴿Today every soul will be recompensed for what it has earned. There is no injustice today. Indeed, Allah is swift in reckoning.﴾

There is no doubt that these three sentences are connected to the speech issuing from Allah, the Exalted, whether the two preceding sentences together form one statement or the second of them is a statement of the people of the gathering (al-mahshar).

The arrangement of these five sentences is as follows: when it was established that sovereignty belongs to Allah alone on that day, by means of the two preceding sentences together, the effects of exercising that sovereignty were enumerated. These are: judging the servants according to the results of their deeds; that this judgment is just, with no admixture of injustice; and that it is swift and does not delay, because Allah is not preoccupied by anything that would divert Him from establishing the truth, nor does He need to deliberate and reflect on the ways of His judgment. It is upon these results that the order of ﴿Today every soul will be recompensed for what it has earned﴾ then ﴿there is no injustice today﴾, then ﴿Indeed, Allah is swift in reckoning﴾ came.

As for the positions (mawaqi') of these three sentences: the sentence (﴿Today every soul will be recompensed﴾) etc. stands in the position of explanation (bayan) of what is contained, in general terms, in the sentence (﴿Whose is the sovereignty today?﴾ [Ghafir: 16]) and its answer. The sentence ﴿there is no injustice today﴾ stands in the position of a substitute of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal) for the sentence ﴿Today every soul will be recompensed for what it has earned﴾, meaning: a just recompense in which there is no injustice, i.e., there is not even the slightest admixture of injustice in it, as required by the occurrence of the indefinite noun after the negating particle la which denotes the genus.

The definiteness of (al-yawm) in his saying ﴿Today every soul will be recompensed﴾ and his saying ﴿there is no injustice today﴾ is similar to the definiteness in ﴿Whose is the sovereignty today?﴾ [Ghafir: 16]. The sentence ﴿Indeed, Allah is swift in reckoning﴾ stands in the position of giving the reason (ta'lil) for the occurrence of the recompense on that day and for the negation of injustice from that recompense. Its being placed after those two sentences indicates that it is the reason for both of them. Thus the emphatic particle (inna) stands in the position of the causal fa' (fa' al-sababiyyah), as is the case with (inna) when it comes in a context other than the rejection of denial. The swiftness of reckoning requires the swiftness of judgment, and the swiftness of judgment requires that the judge be filled with knowledge of the truth, and [requires] the determination of each doer's recompense according to his deed without hesitation or investigation, because the Judge is the Knower of the unseen. Thus his saying (﴿swift in reckoning﴾) is the reason for everything that preceded it in this purpose. The meaning is that Allah reckons with them swiftly because He is swift in reckoning.

Al-hisab (reckoning) is the verbal noun of hasaba ghayrahu, when one computes for him what is required by his preparation. Its benefit varies: sometimes the reckoning is for the purpose of bringing together things so that nothing of them is lost; sometimes it is for the purpose of holding to account the one who must be held to account concerning them; and sometimes it is for the purpose of recompensing each thing among them with justice. This last is what is meant here, and for its sake the Day of Recompense is called the Day of Reckoning. It is also what is meant in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Their reckoning is only upon my Lord﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 113]. The letter ba' in his saying (bima kasabat) denotes causation, i.e., they are recompensed because of what they earned, meaning a recompense commensurate with what they earned, i.e., what they did.

In the verse there is an allusion that delaying the judgment in accordance with the truth, after it has become clear to the judge without any excuse, is a form of injustice. For if the right is the right of the servants, then delaying the ruling for the holder of the right leaves his right in the hand of another, and in it is the obstruction of his benefiting from his right for a period of time, and that is injustice. Perhaps the holder of the right is in need of hastening his right for a benefit that is being withheld or to repel a harm that is crouching, and perhaps he may die during the period of delay of his right so that he does not benefit from it, or perhaps the thing adjudged is destroyed by an accident or by intent so that its owner does not reach it afterward.

And if the right is the right of Allah, delaying the judgment concerning it amounts to acknowledging the denier.

In Sahih al-Bukhari: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ appointed Abu Musa over Yemen, then sent Mu'adh ibn Jabal after him. When Mu'adh arrived at Abu Musa, Abu Musa threw a cushion to him and said to him: 'Come down.' And behold, there was a man bound in chains with Abu Musa. Mu'adh said: 'What is this?' He said: 'He was a Jew, then he embraced Islam, then he reverted to Judaism.' Mu'adh said: 'I will not sit until he is killed, the judgment of Allah and His Messenger,' three times. So Abu Musa ordered him, and he was killed."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 40, verse 18:

﴿And warn them of the Imminent Day, when the hearts will be choking up to the throats, [they] suppressing [their grief]. The wrongdoers will have no intimate friend nor any intercessor who will be obeyed.﴾

The most apparent view is that His saying "And warn them" and what follows it is a parenthetical clause (i'tirad) placed between the sentence "Indeed, Allah is swift in reckoning" and the sentence "He knows the treachery of the eyes" [40:19], according to the two positions discussed below regarding the placement of the sentence "He knows the treachery of the eyes" [40:19]. The waw is then parenthetical (i'tiradiyyah). The connection is that mentioning the reckoning requires a reminder to prepare for the Day of Reckoning, which is the Day of the Imminent Day.

The Day of the Imminent (Yawm al-Azifah) is the Day of Resurrection. The original form of "al-Azifah" is a feminine active participle derived from the verb azifa al-amr, meaning "the matter drew near." Thus "al-Azifah" is an adjective for a omitted noun, whose implied form is "the Imminent Hour" or "the Imminent Resurrection," like "al-Sakhkhah." Accordingly, the construct "Day" (yawm) with "al-Azifah" is a true (haqiqiyyah) construct. The discussion of the transitive use of "warning" to a day was already mentioned in His saying: ﴿that He may warn of the Day of Meeting﴾ [40:15].

"Idh" is a substitute (badal) for "yawm." It is a noun of time in the accusative as an object, and it is annexed to the clause "the hearts are at the throats."

The "al-" in "al-qulub" and "al-hanajir" is a replacement (iwad) for the annexed pronoun. Its original form is: "when their hearts are at their throats." Through "al-," the definiteness of annexation was replaced with the definiteness of reference (ta'rif al-'ahd). This is the view of the grammarians of Kufa, whereas the Basrans estimate: "when the hearts of them and the throats of them..." The meaning is: when the hearts of those you warn, meaning the polytheists, [will be in this state]; as for the hearts of the righteous on that day, they will be tranquil.

Al-qulub (the hearts): the cone-shaped pieces of flesh that move in continuous motion as long as the body is alive, pumping the blood to the arteries by which the body lives.

Al-hanajir: the plural of hanjarah, with a fatha on the ha and a fatha on the jim, which is the windpipe (al-hulqum). The meaning of "the hearts are at the throats" is that the hearts' movement becomes intensely agitated from extreme anguish at what their owners witness of the terrors' lightning, until the hearts exceed their places, rising to the throats, as He, exalted, said regarding the Day of the Confederates: ﴿and when the eyes swerved and the hearts reached the throats﴾ [33:10].

Kazhim: an active participle from kazama kuzuman, meaning when his breath is held in (with a fatha on the fa). The meaning of "kazhimin" is still, unable to utter speech. According to this interpretation, no object is estimated for "kazhimin," since it is treated as an intransitive verb. It is also said: kazama kazman, when something blocks the course of water, a door, or a road, so he is kazim. According to this, the object is estimated. The estimate is "kazhimina-ha," that is, "suppressing their throats," for fear that their hearts will come out of them from the intensity of the agitation.

"Kazhimin" is in the accusative as a circumstantial (hal) from the pronoun of the absent in His saying "warn them," with the circumstance being a determined circumstance (hal muqaddarah). It is also permissible for it to be a circumstance of "the hearts," by way of rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli), by attributing the state of suppression to the hearts, whereas the ones suppressing are the owners of the hearts, as in His saying, exalted: ﴿So woe to them for what their hands have written﴾ [2:79], whereas the writers are themselves with their hands.

The sentence ﴿The wrongdoers will have no intimate friend nor any intercessor who will be obeyed﴾ is in the place of a substitution of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal) from the sentence ﴿the hearts are at the throats﴾, because that state requires that they look longingly toward the intercession of those they had taken as associates, so that they might intercede for them with Allah, but they will find neither friend nor intercessor. Al-hamim: the lover who is compassionate.

The definiteness in "al-zalimin" is for comprehensiveness (istighraq), to include every wrongdoer, meaning every polytheist. It thus includes the wrongdoers who were warned and those who passed away like them. Therefore, it functions as a concluding appendix (tadhyil). For this reason, the mention of "the wrongdoers" is not an explicit noun in a place where a pronoun would be expected (al-izhar fi maqam al-idmar).

The description of "intercessor" by the clause "who will be obeyed" is a revealing description (wasf kashif), since it is not that they have intercessors whose intercession is not obeyed, due to the evident lack of benefit in that. Rather, since it is the custom of one who seeks intercession to trust that the one interceded with will obey him, [the description clarifies this].

"Intercessor" is followed by the description "who will be obeyed" because the two are customarily linked. It is thus a case of negating an attribute that necessarily belongs to the described entity. The intended meaning is the negation of the described entity through a form of allusive metonymy (kinayah talmihiyyah), as in the line of Ibn Ahmar:

*And you will not see the lizard burrowing into its hole there*

That is, there is no lizard there to burrow, and this conveys the same meaning as emphasis (ta'kid).

The meaning is that if the intercessor is not obeyed, he is not an intercessor. And no one dares to intercede with Him except with His permission, so none intercedes with Him except one who is obeyed.

[Page 114]

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 40, verse 19:**

﴿He knows the treachery of the eyes and what the breasts conceal.﴾

It is permissible for the clause (﴿He knows the treachery of the eyes﴾) to be a predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'), a pronoun referring to the Name of Majesty (Allah) in His saying ﴿Indeed Allah is swift in reckoning﴾ (Ghafir: 17), in the manner already established before it in His saying (﴿Exalted in degrees﴾ (Ghafir: 15)). The whole of the apparent and the implied is a resumptive clause (istinaf) for emphasis in warning, because when they are reminded that Allah knows the hidden matters, the warning becomes far-reaching and demands caution against every belief or action that the Messenger (ﷺ) forbade them from. Thus, after He has made them despair of supposing that they could conceal anything of their intentions or the slightest movements of their deeds from their Lord.

It is also permissible for it to be a second predicate (khabar) of the subject of ʾinna in His saying ﴿Indeed Allah is swift in reckoning﴾ (Ghafir: 17), and what lies between them is a parenthetical clause (i'tiraḍ), as has passed, under both interpretations.

[Page 116]

The phrase (﴿treachery of the eyes﴾) is a verbal noun (maṣdar) added to its agent. So al-khā'inah is a verbal noun on the pattern of the active participle, like al-'āfiyah for al-mu'āfāh (well-being), al-'āqibah (the outcome), and al-kādhibah in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿There is no denying of its occurrence﴾ (al-Waqi'ah: 2). It is also permissible to keep (khā'inah) in its apparent form as an active participle, in which case it is an adjective of an omitted noun indicated by (al-a'yun, "the eyes"), meaning: He knows the treacherous glance of the eyes.

The true meaning of treachery (khiyanah) is the act of one who has been entrusted with something by acting contrary to the purpose for which it was entrusted, without the knowledge of the one who entrusted it. Among this is breaking a covenant without announcing its cancellation. The meaning of (﴿treachery of the eyes﴾) is the treachery of the glance, that is, the furtive looking at something in the presence of someone who does not like to be looked at in that way. So the addition of (khā'inah) to (al-a'yun) is an addition of a thing to its instrument, like the saying "he struck with the sword."

What is meant by (﴿treachery of the eyes﴾) is the glance intended to signal to the one looked at something that would displease the one present, whether by mockery or by incitement.

The use of treachery (khiyanah) to describe this glance is an implicit metaphor (isti'arah makniyyah). It likens the companion to an ally, in that when he sits with you or you sit with him, it is as though he has made a pact with you for safety. Do you not see that sitting together is preceded by the greeting, which is in origin a declaration of peace? So when you look at someone other than the two of you with a hidden glance, signalling what would not please the companion, whether mockery or incitement, it is as though you have broken the covenant that was established between you. Thus applying the term treachery to that is an expression of severe condemnation. The closeness of the comparison varies in proportion to how grave the harm and the consequences of the glance are. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "It is not befitting for a prophet that he should have the treachery of the eyes," meaning that it should not proceed from him.

And (﴿what the breasts conceal﴾) refers to the intentions and resolves that their owner harbours within himself. The breast (ṣadr) is used figuratively for what the principal organs contain, according to the usage of the lexicographers.

[Page 117]

"Allah judges with truth, while those you call upon besides Him judge nothing. Indeed, Allah is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing."

The apparent expectation was that the clause (﴿He judges with truth﴾) would be joined by the conjunction *wa* (and) to the clause (﴿He knows the treachery of the eyes﴾ [Ghafir: 19]), so that it would say: "and He judges with truth." But it departs from that because of what the proper name (*ism 'alam*, a proper noun) of Allah conveys, by way of indication, of the attributes of perfection implied by the One so named, among them justice in judgment. Its parallel, where a noun is used in place of a pronoun, is His saying: ﴿Do they not see that We come to the land, reducing it from its borders? And Allah judges; there is no repeller of His judgment﴾ [al-Ra'd: 41]. Also, by placing the subject before the verbal predicate, the meaning is strengthened. Among its examples is His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve spend their wealth to avert [people] from the way of Allah. They will spend it; then it will become a regret for them; then they will be overcome. And those who disbelieve will be gathered to Hell﴾ [al-Anfal: 36]. The relative pronoun was repeated, and a pronoun referring to ﴿those who disbelieve﴾ was not used, in order to convey that placing the noun before the verb strengthens the ruling.

This sentence completes the purpose for which the sentence ﴿He knows the treachery of the eyes﴾ [Ghafir: 19] was brought, as mentioned earlier, and both look back to His saying: ﴿The wrongdoers will have no intimate friend nor any intercessor﴾ [Ghafir: 18], meaning that this is part of judging with truth.

As for the sentence ﴿those you call upon besides Him judge nothing﴾, it looks back to the sentence ﴿The wrongdoers will have no intimate friend nor any intercessor﴾ [Ghafir: 18]. So, after intercession was negated of their idols, judgment in anything, whether with truth or with falsehood, was also negated of them, and this is a demonstration of their impotence.

Do not suppose that the sentence ﴿those you call upon besides Him judge nothing﴾ was brought as an addition to ﴿Allah judges with truth﴾, so that the two sentences together convey restriction of judgment with truth to Allah the Exalted, a restriction by reversal (*qasr qalb*), meaning excluding the idols. Restriction is conveyed by the joining of two sentences in the verse of al-Samaw'al or 'Abd al-Malik al-Harithi:

*Our souls flow along the edges of the swords,*
*and they do not flow except on the edges of the swords.*

Because what is negated of their gods is more general than what is affirmed for Allah, and since this is not of the kind that contradicts the form of restriction, the placement of the subject before the predicate suffices to convey it, by taking it to mean exclusivity in ﴿Allah judges with truth﴾. Thus the purpose of ﴿those you call upon besides Him judge nothing﴾ is to remind [the audience] of the impotence of those they call upon, and that they are not fit for divinity. This is a method of affirming an attribute of a subject and then following it with the affirmation of its opposite in something considered equivalent to it, as in the words of Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt:

*Those are the noble deeds, not two bowls of milk*
*mixed with water, which afterward became urine.*

Otherwise, there would be no suitable connection in the coordination of his saying "not two bowls of milk."

The word *du'a'* (calling upon) may mean calling out (*nida'*) or it may mean worship, as mentioned just before.

The sentence ﴿Indeed Allah is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾ confirms the sentences from ﴿He knows the treachery of the eyes and what the breasts conceal﴾ [Ghafir: 19] up to His saying ﴿judge nothing﴾.

The placement of the separating pronoun (*damir al-fasl*, a pronoun placed between subject and predicate to indicate restriction) conveys restriction, and it hints that their gods do not hear or see, so how could they ascribe divinity to them? Affirming intensified hearing and seeing for Allah the Exalted confirms the meaning of ﴿He judges with truth﴾, because the One who knows everything has wisdom that is not directed toward falsehood, and His judgments do not err by stumbling into falsehood. Emphasizing the sentence with the particle of emphasis (*inna*) establishes the restriction. Al-Taftazani mentioned in his commentary on *al-Miftah*, in the discussion of the separating pronoun, that restriction is emphatic.

[Page 118]

Nafi' and Hisham, on the authority of Ibn 'Amir, read *tad'ūna* with the *ta'* of address, as a shift (*iltifat*, change of grammatical person) from the third person to the second person, to strike the ears of the polytheists with it. The majority read it with the *ya'* of the third person, following the apparent sense.

[Page 119]

﴿Have they not traveled through the land and seen what was the end of those who came before them? They were greater than them in strength and in their traces upon the earth, but God seized them for their sins, and they had no protector from God.﴾ ﴿That is because their messengers used to come to them with clear proofs, but they disbelieved, so God seized them. Indeed, He is Strong, severe in punishment.﴾

This is a shift from warning them of the punishment of the Hereafter because of their disbelief to admonishing them and warning them lest the punishment of the Hereafter befall them as it befell nations like them.

The conjunction *wa* (و) joins the sentence ﴿Have they not traveled through the land﴾ to the sentence ﴿And warn them of the Day of the Approaching [Calamity]﴾ (Ghafir: 18), and so on.

The interrogation is a *taqrir* (affirmative interrogation, a question that seeks acknowledgment of a known fact), in line with what is common in such interrogations that enter upon a negation in the past with the particle *lam* (لم). The affirmation is directed at the Quraysh who traveled and observed the remains of the nations whom God destroyed as a consequence of their denial of their messengers. They witnessed this during their two journeys, the journey of winter and the journey of summer. What they witnessed was related by those who gathered in their assemblies and sittings, so it became known to all. On this basis, the verb affirmed is attributed to the plural pronoun in the sentence as a whole.

The present-tense verb after *lam* (لم), and the present-tense verb in its answer, are both converted to the past by means of *lam* (لم).

A similar verse has been mentioned at the end of Surah Fatir and in Surah al-Rum.

The separate pronoun in the phrase ﴿they were﴾ (كانوا هم) is a *damir al-fasl* (separating pronoun), referring back to the wrongdoers, who are the disbelievers of Quraysh intended by the phrase ﴿and warn them﴾. The separating pronoun serves merely to emphasize and strengthen the judgment. It is not meant to restrict the predicate to the subject, that is, to restrict superiority in strength to the pronoun ﴿they﴾ (كانوا), since restriction has no meaning here, as was previously explained in the verse ﴿Indeed, I am God﴾ (Ta-Ha: 14) in Surah Ta-Ha. This is the criterion for distinguishing the separating pronoun that conveys restriction from the one that conveys mere emphasis. Al-Qazwini's abridgment of the *Miftah* (Miftah al-'Ulum by al-Sakkaki) restricts the separating pronoun's function to exclusivity, which is a shortcoming that he followed from the text of the *Miftah*. Sa'd al-Din (al-Taftazani) pointed this out in his commentary on the *Talkhis*.

The intended meaning of strength (*quwwah*) is moral strength, namely, the large number of the community and the abundance of means of self-sufficiency from others, as God says: ﴿As for 'Ad, they were arrogant upon the earth without right and said, "Who is stronger than us in strength?" Did they not see that God, who created them, is stronger than them in strength?﴾ (Fussilat: 15).

The sentence ﴿they were greater than them﴾ and so on is a resumptive sentence of explanatory type (*istinaf bayani*), explaining the general statement in the phrase ﴿what was the end of those who came before them﴾, because the lesson is conveyed by the consequent introduced after it with the phrase ﴿God seized them for their sins﴾.

The Majority read ﴿than them﴾ (منهم) with the third-person pronoun. Ibn 'Amir read it as ﴿than you﴾ (منكم) with the second-person plural pronoun, and it is written thus in the Mushaf of Syria. This reading follows the rhetorical device of *iltifat* (a shift in grammatical person).

*Al-athar* (الآثار) is the plural of *athar* (أثر), which is a thing or a form left by the action of something else, like the trace of a walker in sand. God says: ﴿So I took a handful from the trace of the Messenger﴾ (Ta-Ha: 96). Like the vegetation that follows rain, as in God's words: ﴿So look at the traces of God's mercy, how He brings the earth to life after its death﴾ (al-Rum: 50). The word *athar* is also used metaphorically for what comes after something, as in God's words: ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief over their traces﴾ (al-Kahf: 6).

The intended meaning of "the earth" is the land of their nation.

The *fa'* (ف) in ﴿so God seized them﴾ (فأخذهم الله) indicates that the seizing is a consequence of their being greater in strength than the Quraysh, because "strength" here is intended as a metaphor for turning away from the truth and aversion to the call. The implied meaning is: "They turned away, or disbelieved, so God seized them."

*Al-akhdh* (الأخذ), "seizing," means annihilation and destruction. Punishment is expressed by the word "seizing" metonymically, or the word "seizing" is used metaphorically for punishment.

*Al-dhunub* (الذنوب) is the plural of *dhanb* (ذنب), which means disobedience. What is intended by it is associating partners with God and denying the messengers. That entails many sins, and their explanation will follow in God's words: ﴿That is because their messengers used to come to them with clear proofs﴾.

The meaning of ﴿they had no protector from God﴾ is that they had no protection from His punishment and His power over them. *Al-waqi* (الواقي) is the one who defends and supports.

The first *min* (من) is connected to *waqin* (واق), and the prepositional phrase is placed first for emphasis on what it governs. The second *min* (من) is extra, for emphasizing the negation introduced by the particle *ma* (ما). The demonstrative ﴿that﴾ refers to what was mentioned, namely God's seizing them for their sins.

The *ba'* (ب) indicates causation, meaning that the seizing was because their messengers came to them with clear proofs and they disbelieved in them. This is a detailed explanation of the general statement in the phrase ﴿so God seized them for their sins﴾. The clause after *anna* (أن), the one opened with the letter *alif*, is in the position of a verbal noun. The implied meaning is: "That is because the coming of the messengers to them was established, and so was their disbelief in them."

The present tense in the phrase ﴿their messengers used to come to them﴾ (تأتيهم) conveys the renewal of coming again and again to all those nations together, meaning that each nation had a messenger sent to it. The plural pronoun in ﴿come to them﴾ and ﴿their messengers﴾ and the plural of "messengers" in ﴿their messengers﴾ are a plural-to-plural correspondence. So the meaning is that every nation among them had a messenger come to it. The present tense is not used in the phrase ﴿so they disbelieved﴾ (فكفروا) because the disbelief of those nations was one thing, namely associating partners with God and denying the messengers.

The phrase ﴿so God seized them﴾ is repeated after its counterpart had preceded in the phrase ﴿so God seized them for their sins﴾ and so on, as an elaboration (*itnab*) to affirm God's seizing them for their disbelief in their messengers, and as an intimidation to those who warn them, lest they be equal to them in their end just as they were equal to them in its causes.

The sentence ﴿Indeed, He is Strong, severe in punishment﴾ is a reason and an explanation of God's seizing them, its manner, and the swiftness of His seizing, which is derived from the *fa'* of immediate consequence. The Strong is not overcome by anything, so He does not frustrate His will nor delay. The phrase ﴿severe in punishment﴾ explains that seizing, in the manner of His words: ﴿So We seized them with the seizing of the Mighty, the Omnipotent﴾ (al-Qamar: 42).

[Page 119]

﴿Have they not traveled through the land and seen what was the end of those who came before them? They were greater than them in strength and in their traces upon the earth, but God seized them for their sins, and they had no protector from God.﴾ ﴿That is because their messengers used to come to them with clear proofs, but they disbelieved, so God seized them. Indeed, He is Strong, severe in punishment.﴾

This is a shift from warning them of the punishment of the Hereafter because of their disbelief to admonishing them and warning them lest the punishment of the Hereafter befall them as it befell nations like them.

The conjunction *wa* (و) joins the sentence ﴿Have they not traveled through the land﴾ to the sentence ﴿And warn them of the Day of the Approaching [Calamity]﴾ (Ghafir: 18), and so on.

The interrogation is a *taqrir* (affirmative interrogation, a question that seeks acknowledgment of a known fact), in line with what is common in such interrogations that enter upon a negation in the past with the particle *lam* (لم). The affirmation is directed at the Quraysh who traveled and observed the remains of the nations whom God destroyed as a consequence of their denial of their messengers. They witnessed this during their two journeys, the journey of winter and the journey of summer. What they witnessed was related by those who gathered in their assemblies and sittings, so it became known to all. On this basis, the verb affirmed is attributed to the plural pronoun in the sentence as a whole.

The present-tense verb after *lam* (لم), and the present-tense verb in its answer, are both converted to the past by means of *lam* (لم).

A similar verse has been mentioned at the end of Surah Fatir and in Surah al-Rum.

The separate pronoun in the phrase ﴿they were﴾ (كانوا هم) is a *damir al-fasl* (separating pronoun), referring back to the wrongdoers, who are the disbelievers of Quraysh intended by the phrase ﴿and warn them﴾. The separating pronoun serves merely to emphasize and strengthen the judgment. It is not meant to restrict the predicate to the subject, that is, to restrict superiority in strength to the pronoun ﴿they﴾ (كانوا), since restriction has no meaning here, as was previously explained in the verse ﴿Indeed, I am God﴾ (Ta-Ha: 14) in Surah Ta-Ha. This is the criterion for distinguishing the separating pronoun that conveys restriction from the one that conveys mere emphasis. Al-Qazwini's abridgment of the *Miftah* (Miftah al-'Ulum by al-Sakkaki) restricts the separating pronoun's function to exclusivity, which is a shortcoming that he followed from the text of the *Miftah*. Sa'd al-Din (al-Taftazani) pointed this out in his commentary on the *Talkhis*.

The intended meaning of strength (*quwwah*) is moral strength, namely, the large number of the community and the abundance of means of self-sufficiency from others, as God says: ﴿As for 'Ad, they were arrogant upon the earth without right and said, "Who is stronger than us in strength?" Did they not see that God, who created them, is stronger than them in strength?﴾ (Fussilat: 15).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 40, verse 23–24:

Page 122
﴿And We certainly sent Musa with Our signs and a clear authority﴾ ﴿to Pharaoh, Haman and Qarun, but they said, "A sorcerer, a liar."﴾.

This is the mention of another group of nations, which the Arabs did not witness the traces of, namely the people of Pharaoh, the Copts of Egypt. The like of this verse has already occurred at the end of Surah Hud. The name Haman has already been mentioned, and it is the title of Pharaoh's minister, in Surah al-Qasas.

In this story, beyond what was summarized of the stories of other nations, there are two lessons: a lesson in the scheming and obstinacy of the deniers and their subsequent destruction, and a lesson in the patience and steadfastness of the believers and their subsequent victory. In both lessons there is both a warning and a promise.

The phrase ﴿they said, "A sorcerer, a liar."﴾ is a parenthetical clause between the phrase ﴿And We certainly sent Musa﴾ and the phrase ﴿So when the truth came to them﴾.

Qarun was from the Children of Israel and denied Musa; his mention has already occurred in the stories. It has been said that he was attached to Pharaoh and served him, but this is far-fetched, because he was among those who went out with Musa. That is, those people joined in branding their messenger as a liar and a sorcerer, just as Quraysh did.

Page 122
﴿And We certainly sent Musa with Our signs and a clear authority﴾ ﴿to Pharaoh, Haman and Qarun, but they said, "A sorcerer, a liar."﴾.

In both lessons there is both a warning and a promise.
