Qarun was from the Children of Israel and denied Musa; his mention has already occurred in the stories. It has been said that he was attached to Pharaoh and served him, but this is far-fetched, because he was among those who went out with Musa. That is, those people joined in branding their messenger as a liar and a sorcerer, just as Quraysh did.

﴿So when he brought them the truth from Us, they said, "Kill the sons of those who believe with him, and spare their women. But the scheming of the disbelievers is nothing but misguidance."﴾

That is, they first accused him of being a sorcerer and a liar, imagining that they could overwhelm him with the stone of stoning (*ḥajar al-iḥjām*). But when he persisted in his call and brought them the truth, meaning that he showed them the clear and manifest signs, the phrase "brought them" is used for the manifestation of the truth, as in His saying: ﴿The truth has come and falsehood has vanished﴾ [al-Isra': 81].

The phrase ﴿from Us﴾ describes the truth, to indicate that it is a truth that breaks customary norms, which could only come through God's subjugation of things and His support, and these are the nine signs of his prophethood.

The reason ﴿So when he brought them the truth from Us﴾ comes after His saying ﴿We sent Moses with Our signs﴾ [Ghafir: 23], despite the two clauses having the same meaning, is that the meaning of "brought them" is equivalent to the meaning of "sent," and the meaning of "with the truth" is equivalent to the meaning of ﴿with Our signs and a clear authority﴾ [Ghafir: 23]. The first serves to honour the message of Moses and the greatness of his stand before the greatest kings of the earth at that time. As for His saying ﴿So when he brought them the truth﴾, it explains his call to them and what resulted from it. The sense of the sentence is: We sent Moses with Our signs to Pharaoh, and when he brought them the truth. Thus this composition adopts the method of elaboration (*iṭnāb*) for honouring and ennobling.

The clause ﴿They said, "A sorcerer and a liar"﴾ [Ghafir: 24] is a parenthetical clause (*i'tirāḍ*). By their saying ﴿"Kill the sons of those who believe with him"﴾ they intended to terrify his followers so that they would abandon him, and he would find no helpers, and the Children of Israel would remain in servitude to the Egyptians.

The pronoun in ﴿brought them﴾ may be taken to refer to something not mentioned explicitly, since it is a plural pronoun indicated by the context. They are the members of Pharaoh's council, whom the council of a king does not lack in such momentous events, as in His saying: ﴿Pharaoh said, "O chiefs, I know of no god for you other than me. So kindle for me, O Haman, upon the clay..."﴾ [al-Qasas: 38], and the verse continues. It does not refer to Pharaoh, Haman and Qarun, because Qarun was not with Pharaoh when Moses called him, and he was not among those who denied Moses at the time of Moses's presence before Pharaoh. Rather, he rebelled after the Children of Israel left Egypt, and his rebellion reached the point of disbelief, as was mentioned in his story in Surat al-Qasas.

The pronoun in their saying ﴿"Kill"﴾ is addressed to Pharaoh with the address of honour, like ﴿"My Lord, send me back"﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 99].

The speakers were left unidentified because the purpose of the speech is not tied to knowing them. So the verb ﴿they said﴾ is like the passive form, or like "a speaker said," because the intended point is what follows: ﴿But the scheming of the disbelievers is nothing but misguidance﴾, which is the place of lesson for the Quraysh, that the scheming of their like was doomed, and so too would be their scheming.

This killing is different from the killing that Pharaoh carried out, during whose time Moses was born.

This opinion was called a scheme (*kayd*) because they consulted about it among themselves without Moses and those who believed with him knowing of it, and they concealed it and did not declare it. Then what befell them of the calamities, mentioned in His saying in Surat al-A'raf, ﴿We seized the people of Pharaoh with years of drought﴾ [al-A'raf: 130] and the verse continues, and then in His saying ﴿So We sent upon them the flood and the locusts﴾ [al-A'raf: 133] and the verse continues, occupied them from carrying it out.

The word *ḍalāl* (misguidance) means loss and perishing, as in His saying: ﴿They said, "When we have been lost in the earth, shall we indeed be in a new creation?"﴾ [al-Sajdah: 10]. That is, this scheme that they devised has been checked by God, so they found no way to carry it out.

"And Pharaoh said: 'Leave me to kill Moses, and let him call upon his Lord. Indeed, I fear that he will change your religion or that he will cause corruption to appear in the land.'"

The conjunction (wa, "and") in "wa-qala" indicates that he said this statement in another situation, and it was not a reply to their saying "Kill the sons of those who believe with him" (Ghafir: 25). This style also hints that Pharaoh did not act upon the suggestion of those who said "Kill the sons of those who believe with him" (Ghafir: 25), and that he remained silent, neither supporting nor rejecting them in response. Then he judged that the more fitting course was to kill Moses rather than kill those who believed with him, because killing him would more effectively cut off their trial.

The meaning of "dhurūnī" (leave me) is to inform them of his resolve, by way of showing his inclination toward it and awaiting their agreement to it, in a manner that portrays his own state and the state of those he addresses as that of someone who wants to do something but is being prevented from it. Because of his desire for it, he says to the one who holds him back: "Leave me to do such-and-such," for this construction is one used when addressing someone who objects, or one who agrees, and similar. Ṭarafah said:

"If you cannot repel my appointed death, then leave me to hasten toward it with what my hand possesses."

Then this expression came to be used to express desire even when there was no opponent or obstacle. This is a common usage in this and in its synonyms, such as "da'nī" and "khallanī" (leave me, let me alone), as in the words of God Most High: ﴿Leave me with the one whom I created alone﴾ (al-Muddaththir: 11), and His words: ﴿Leave me with the deniers﴾ (al-Muzzammil: 11), and the verse of Abu Qasim al-Suhayli:

Page 125

"Leave me upon the judgment of passion, that I may humble myself, so that perhaps the beloved will soften toward me and submit."

This implies, as a metonymy, the gravity of that act and the difficulty of accomplishing it, because such a thing is of the kind that a consultant restrains his consultee from undertaking. For this reason he follows it with "and let him call upon his Lord," because Moses had warned them of God's punishment and challenged them with the nine signs.

The imperative lam in "wa-liyad'u rabbahu" is used to express indifference and disregard.

The clause "Indeed, I fear that he will change your religion" is an explanation of the resolve to kill Moses.

"Fear" is used here in the sense of apprehension, meaning: I strongly suspect that he will change your religion.

The "min" which the verb "akhāfu" normally takes was omitted, because it fell between it and "an."

"Tabdīl" means replacing a thing with another. Pharaoh perceived this from Moses' denial of Pharaoh's claim that he was a god to his people, for changing the roots (of belief) entails changing all the branches of the Sharia.

The possessive in his words "your religion" implies an insinuation that they are more entitled to defend the religion, even though it was also his own religion; but in consulting them he stripped himself of any consideration of his own personal interest, as they themselves said: ﴿Will you leave Moses and his people to cause corruption in the land and abandon you and your gods?﴾ (al-A'raf: 127). All of this is incitement and urging.

"The land" refers to what was known to them, namely the kingdom of Pharaoh.

The meaning of Moses causing corruption to appear, in their view, is that he would be the cause of its appearing through his call to change what they held of religion and customs. "Appearing" (izhār) was used for spreading and dissemination, by way of metaphor.

His arrogance and lack of reflection on matters led him to suppose that whatever opposed their religion would count as corruption, since they had no argument for their religion other than habit and immediate benefit.

Nāfi', Ibn Kathīr, Ibn 'Āmir, Abu 'Amr and Abu Ja'far read "wa-an" with the conjunction waw (and). Others read "aw an" with "aw" (or), which indicates alternation, meaning that Moses' endeavor cannot be free of one of these two outcomes.

Nāfi', Abu 'Amr, Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Āṣim, and Abu Ja'far read "yuẓhira" with a dammah on the yā' and "al-fasād" in the accusative, meaning: he changes, and will be a cause of the appearance of corruption. Ibn Kathīr, Ibn 'Āmir, Ḥamzah, al-Kisā'ī, Ḥafs on the authority of 'Āṣim, Ya'qūb and Khalaf read it with a fatḥah on the yā' and "al-fasādu" in the nominative, meaning that corruption appears because of the emergence of Moses' followers, or by another person emboldening himself to make a claim like his, such that the sanctity of the state would vanish; for the nature of people who live in fear is that their cowardice turns into courage when they see the success of one who dared to undertake the very act they wish to emulate.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 40, verse 27:

﴿And Moses said: "Indeed, I have sought refuge in my Lord and your Lord from every arrogant one who does not believe in the Day of Reckoning."﴾

This is a report of words that Moses spoke, without doubt, outside the presence of Pharaoh, because Moses was not among the council (mala' al-isti'shara) of Pharaoh when he said to his people ﴿Leave me to kill Moses﴾ [Ghafir: 26]. Rather, when Moses learned of what Pharaoh had said before his chiefs, Moses said to his people ﴿Indeed, I have sought refuge in my Lord and your Lord﴾. For this reason, the verb of his speech is reported with the conjunction "wa" (and), because that speech did not occur in a dialogue with Pharaoh's statement, unlike the reported speeches in Surat al-Shu'ara' from his saying ﴿He said: "Did we not raise you among us as a child?"﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 18] to his saying ﴿He said: "Then bring it, if you are of the truthful."﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 31].

His saying ﴿I have sought refuge in my Lord and your Lord from every arrogant one﴾ is an address to his people from the Children of Israel, to reassure them and to calm their anxiety for him from Pharaoh's violence.

The meaning is: I have prepared the means to repel Pharaoh's violence, by seeking refuge in God from every arrogant one who does not believe in the Day of Reckoning, and at the forefront of these arrogant ones is Pharaoh.

The meaning of this is: Moses knew that he would encounter rebellious, arrogant people who would hate what God had sent him with. So he called upon his Lord, and he knew that God had guaranteed him protection and had sufficed him against the harm of every opponent. This is what is reported in Surat Ta-Ha: ﴿They said: "Our Lord, indeed we fear that he will hasten against us or that he will transgress."﴾ [Ta-Ha: 45] ﴿He said: "Do not fear. Indeed, I am with you both; I hear and I see."﴾ [Ta-Ha: 46]

Moses then informed his people that his Lord was his protector, so that they would trust in God, just as the station of the Prophet (ﷺ) was at the beginning of the mission, when his companions would guard him at night. When the verse of His Exalted saying was revealed ﴿So declare what you are commanded and turn away from the polytheists﴾ [al-Hijr: 94] ﴿Indeed, We have sufficed you against the mockers﴾ [al-Hijr: 95], and so on, he commanded his companions to abandon guarding him.

The emphasis of the statement with the particle (inna) is directed at its necessary implication, which is that God guaranteed him safety. He stressed this because some of his people, or most of them, were treated as those who doubt it, given what he saw of their anxiety for him.

Al-'awdh (seeking refuge): resorting to a place by which the one seeking refuge protects himself, so that it repels from him whoever intends harm to him. One says: "he took refuge in the mountain" and "he took refuge in the army." God the Exalted said ﴿So seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan﴾ [al-Nahl: 98].

He referred to the Majesty by the attribute of Lord, idafa (annexed) to the pronoun of the speaker, because in the attribute "Lord" there is an allusion to directing the seeking of refuge toward Him, since the servant seeks refuge with his master.

The addition of the description "Lord of those addressed" is to allude to the fact that they should not panic at Pharaoh's hostility toward them, and that they should seek refuge in God from everything that terrifies them.

The description ﴿who does not believe in the Day of Reckoning﴾ was made to suffice in place of the description of disbelief or association (shirk), because it includes association and more, for when arrogance and denial of recompense are combined in a person, his concern for the consequences of his deeds diminishes, and so the causes of harshness and audacity toward people are fully present in him.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 40, verse 28:**

﴿And a believing man from the family of Pharaoh, who concealed his faith, said: "Would you kill a man for saying, 'My Lord is Allah,' when he has brought you clear evidences from your Lord? And if he is a liar, upon him is his lying; but if he is truthful, some of what he promises you will befall you. Indeed, Allah does not guide one who is a transgressor and a liar."﴾.

The conjunction ('atf) introducing this man's words implies that he said this statement outside of a council of consultation (majlis shura) of Pharaoh. For if his statement had been in the manner of a dialogue with Pharaoh in a session of Pharaoh's consultation, or if he had answered with it Pharaoh's words ﴿Leave me to kill Moses﴾, then the report of his words would have come without a conjunction, in the manner of dialogues.

What appears is that Allah inspired this man to speak his statement, as an inspiration, and this was the first manifestation of Allah's fulfilling Moses's seeking refuge in Allah. When Pharaoh's threat to kill Moses (peace be upon him) became widely known, this man came to Pharaoh as an advisor, and Pharaoh did not accuse him, because he was one of his family.

His address with the words "Would you kill" is directed to Pharaoh, because Pharaoh is the one to whom the killing is attributed, as he is the one who ordered it. It also serves to report Pharaoh's speech following the speech of the believer of Pharaoh's family, without a conjunction with "wa" (and), in His saying ﴿Pharaoh said: "I show you only what I see."﴾ [Ghafir: 29].

His description as "from the family of Pharaoh" is explicit that he was of the Copts, and was not from the Children of Israel, contrary to some exegetes. Do you not see His saying, exalted is He, after it: ﴿O my people, yours is the kingdom today, dominant in the land, but who will help us against the might of Allah if it comes to us?﴾ [Ghafir: 29]? For the Children of Israel did not have a kingdom there.

The more apparent view is that he was a relative of Pharaoh and one of his close associates, according to what the word "Al" (family) requires of that, whether literally or figuratively.

The meaning is that he was a believer in Allah and a believer in the truthfulness of Moses, and his faith was only because he was a righteous man who was guided to the Oneness of Allah (tawhid), either by reflecting upon the evidences, so he affirmed Moses when he heard his call, just as Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) was guided to affirm the Prophet (ﷺ) at the moment he heard his call, and he said to him, "You have spoken truly."

His concealing of faith was continuous and ongoing, a precaution (taqiyya, dissimulation for protection) against Pharaoh and his people, since he knew that displaying his faith would harm him and would not benefit anyone else, just as Socrates used to conceal his faith in Allah in the land of the Greeks, for fear that they would kill him in defense of their gods.

By his saying "Would you kill a man" to the end, he intended to strive to protect Moses from being killed, by opening the door of argument concerning his affair, so as to create doubt in Pharaoh regarding his denial of Moses. This man was not the man mentioned in Surah al-Qasas in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And there came a man from the farthest part of the city, running﴾ [al-Qasas: 20], for that story took place shortly before Moses's departure from Egypt, whereas this story is at the beginning of his entry into Egypt.

There he was not described as a believer, nor as being from the family of Pharaoh; rather he was from the Children of Israel, as is explicit in the Book of Exodus. The apparent view is that the man mentioned here was a righteous man, who reflected upon the evidences of Oneness, and faith did not settle firmly in his heart in its proper form until he heard the call of Moses. Allah appoints for His righteous servants protectors at times of hardship.

It is said that this man's name was Habib al-Najjar, and it is said Sim'an. It has already been mentioned in Surah Ya-Sin that Habib al-Najjar was one of the messengers of 'Isa (peace be upon him).

The story of this believing man from the family of Pharaoh is not explicitly mentioned in the Torah, but it is mentioned in summary in the seventh paragraph of the tenth chapter, where it says: "The servants of Pharaoh said to him, 'How long will this man be a snare to us? Let the men go to serve the LORD their God.'"

The interrogative in "Would you kill" is an interrogative of denunciation, meaning: it is disgraceful for you to kill a soul, because he says, "My Lord is Allah," that is, he did not compel you to believe in him, but he has said to you a statement; so accept it or reject it. This is the meaning of His saying ﴿that he says, "My Lord is Allah"﴾, and it is the meaning by which it is possible to reconcile this with the fact that this man was concealing his faith.

The phrase "that he says" (an yaqula) is in the genitive by the implied causal lam (the lam of cause), since it is often omitted together with "an".

The mention of the name of Allah is because it is the name that Moses mentioned, and it was not among the names of the gods of the Copts.

As for His saying ﴿And he has certainly brought you clear evidences from your Lord﴾, it is an ascent in argument, after he had become familiar in addressing his people with a speech directed at them. He ascended to an explicit affirmation of Moses's truthfulness, on the ground that he has brought clear proofs, that is, evidences clearly demonstrating his truthfulness, and to an explicit statement that the one whom Allah named in His saying ﴿that he says, "My Lord is Allah"﴾ is the Lord of the addressees, so he said "from your Lord."

Thus the clause ﴿and he has certainly brought you clear evidences from your Lord﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to "a man," and the preposition "bi" in "bi-al-bayyinat" is for accompaniment.

His saying ﴿And if he is a liar, upon him is his lying﴾ is a reversion to a kind of creating the appearance of doubt about Moses's truthfulness, so that his speech includes two possibilities of affirmation and denial that he alternates in his speech, so that it is not held against him that he is affirming Moses. Rather, it gives them the impression that he is in a state of reflection and contemplation, in order to lead Pharaoh and his chiefs to the evidences of Moses's truthfulness in a manner that does not arouse their aversion. Thus the clause is coordinated with the clause ﴿and he has certainly brought you clear evidences﴾, and so it is a circumstantial clause.

He placed the possibility of his lying before the possibility of his truthfulness, in addition to distancing himself from their suspicion that he was supporting Moses, so he wished to appear as one concerned with the affairs of his people from the outset.

The meaning of ﴿And if he is a liar, upon him is his lying﴾ is an invitation to them to reflect: that is, look at his signs and do not hasten to kill him or to follow him. If it becomes clear to you that he is lying in what he challenged you with and what he warned you of in terms of calamities, and none of that occurs, then it will not harm you at all, and his lie will return upon him, by his being branded a liar. And if it becomes clear to you that he is truthful, then some of what he has threatened you with will befall you, that is, its harbingers will strike you, so that you will know his truthfulness and follow him. This is the reason for the expression "some" (ba'd) rather than saying, "what he promises you will befall you." The intended meaning of "promise" here is the promise of evil, which is called a threat (wa'id). That is: if you continue in obstinacy, then all that he has threatened you with will befall you, by way of greater emphasis.

The station of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq resembled the station of the believer from Pharaoh's family, when he believed in the Prophet (ﷺ) upon hearing his call, though he was not from his family. And on the day that 'Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt came to the Prophet (ﷺ) while the Prophet (ﷺ) was in the courtyard of the Ka'bah, strangling him with his garment, Abu Bakr came and seized the shoulder of 'Uqba and pushed him away, and said: ﴿Would you kill a man for saying, "My Lord is Allah," when he has brought you clear evidences from your Lord?﴾ 'Ali ibn Abi Talib said: "By Allah, the day of Abu Bakr was better than the believer of Pharaoh's family. The believer of Pharaoh's family was a man who concealed his faith, whereas Abu Bakr displayed his faith and spent his wealth and his blood." And I say: Abu Bakr was stronger in certainty than the believer of Pharaoh's family, because the believer of Pharaoh's family concealed his faith, while Abu Bakr displayed his faith.

The clause ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide one who is a transgressor and a liar﴾ may be from the speech of the believer of Pharaoh's family. The purpose of it is to give the reason for his saying ﴿And if he is a liar, upon him is his lying; but if he is truthful, some of what he promises you will befall you﴾; that is, because Allah does not let him persist in his lying. So if he is lying against Allah, his affair will not remain long before being exposed, or Allah will destroy him, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if he had fabricated against Us some sayings﴾ [al-Haqqah: 44], ﴿We would have seized him by the right hand﴾ [al-Haqqah: 45], ﴿then We would have cut from him the aorta﴾ [al-Haqqah: 46]. For Allah does not give respite to one who lies against Him. Also, if he has come to you with extraordinary events that break customary patterns, then his truthfulness has become clear, because Allah does not break the customary pattern after the challenge of one who challenges by it, except to make it a sign that he has been sent by Him, since the affirmation of a liar is impossible for Allah, exalted is He.

The meaning of ﴿some of what he promises you﴾ is: some of what he has threatened you with occurring in this world or in the Hereafter. How much more so when the clear evidence itself was calamities that befell them, such as the flood, the locusts, and the rest of the nine signs.

"Al-musrif" (the transgressor) is one who exceeds what is known in something. The intended meaning here is one who transgresses in lying, because the greatest of lies is to lie against Allah. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against Allah or says, "It has been revealed to me," when nothing has been revealed to him﴾ [al-An'am: 93].

Since the intended meaning is transgression in lying, it is determined that His saying "a liar" (kadhdhab) is an explicative apposition (atf bayan) and not a second predicate, since there is no transgression here other than the transgression of lying. In this there is an acknowledgment by this believer of Allah, whom Pharaoh had denied, that he had cast him among them.

It is also possible that the clause ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide﴾ to its end is a parenthetical clause placed between the two statements of the believer of Pharaoh's family, not part of the report of his speech, but rather a statement from Allah in His Qur'an, intended to commend this believing man, since Allah guided him to the truth, and that he is pious and truthful. Thus the negation of guidance from the transgressing liar is a metonymy (kinaya) for the piety and truthfulness of this man, because he spoke from guidance, and Allah does not grant guidance to one who is a transgressor and a liar.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 40, verse 29:

﴿O my people, the kingdom is yours today, dominant in the land. But who will help us against the might of Allah should it come upon us?﴾

When he (the believing man) perceived that his argument had taken hold among them and had entered their souls, he felt secure from their harm, and he seized the opportunity of their hearts being softened. So he spoke to them plainly about his purpose in believing in Musa, following the custom of orators and of people of disputation: after establishing the premises and proofs, they rush at the intended goal. Thus he admonished them with this admonition.

He included his people in the address and called them, in order to draw them to support him before Fir'awn, so that Fir'awn would find no alternative but to yield to their agreement and united stance. Also, making his people partners in the admonition is more fitting within the category of sincere counsel (nasihah). He began by advising Fir'awn, since he is the one who holds command and prohibition, and then he turned to advising those present from his people, warning them of calamities that would befall them as a consequence of obeying Fir'awn's order to kill Musa, for that concerns them just as it concerns Fir'awn. This ordering in giving counsel is like the ordering in the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "And for the leaders of the Muslims and their common folk."

It is not hidden what is in their being addressed with the title "his people" (qawmuhu) from the drawing of attention to his counsel and the softening of their hearts toward his words.

The beginning of the admonition with his words, ﴿The kingdom is yours today, dominant in the land﴾, is a reminder of Allah's blessing upon them and a preparation for frightening them of Allah's wrath. The meaning is: do not let your greatness and your kingdom deceive you, for both are exposed to decline if Allah becomes angry with you.

The intended aim is to frighten Fir'awn about the loss of his kingdom, but he made the kingdom belong to his people in order to avoid confronting Fir'awn directly with the prospect of the loss of his kingdom.

"Al-ard" (the land) here means the land of Egypt, that is, your rule is effective in this region.

He built upon this preparation: ﴿But who will help us against the might of Allah should it come upon us?﴾ The "man" (man) is an interrogative of denial concerning any helper, so the meaning is: there is no help for us against the might of Allah.

He included himself with his people in "will help us" (yansuruna) and "should it come upon us" (ja'anā), to show them that he refuses for his people what he refuses for himself, and that if the calamity strikes, it does not strike some of them without others.

The meaning of "dominant" (zahirin) is victorious, and it has been mentioned previously. That is: if you are capable of killing Musa, then Allah is capable of destroying you.

Al-ba's: strength to overcome an opponent and an obstinate one; it is the strength to inflict harm.

* * *

﴿Fir'awn said: I show you only what I see, and I guide you only to the path of right conduct.﴾

Fir'awn perceived that he was the one alluded to in the believing man's address to his people, so he interrupted his speech and explained the reason for his resolve to kill Musa, peace be upon him: that he presented this to them only because he sees no benefit except in killing Musa, and he does not regard anything else as correct, and he considers that to be the path of right conduct. It seems he wanted not to leave any entry for the counsel of their believing man into the souls of his council, for fear that they would be influenced by his advice and not assist Fir'awn in killing Musa.

Because Fir'awn's speech came as an interruption of the believer's speech, the verb of Fir'awn's saying came disconnected, not conjoined, and this is the manner of recounting exchanges and dialogue.

The meaning of "﴿mā urīkum﴾" (I show you): I do not make you see except what I see for myself; that is, I do not advise you to believe except what I believe, so "seeing" is cognitive, meaning: I advise only what is my conviction.

"Al-sabil" (the path) is used metaphorically for the action, and its being attributed to "al-rashad" (right conduct) is an indicator (qarinah): that is, I guide you and advise you only toward an action containing right conduct. It seems he is implying that the speech of their believer is foolishness of opinion. The meaning derived from the second clause is other than the meaning derived from the first clause, as is clear, and as the requirement of the conjunction (ʿatf) indicates.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 40, verses 30–31:

﴿And he who believed said, "O my people, indeed I fear for you a day like the day of the factions,﴾ ﴿like the custom of the people of Noah, and 'Ad, and Thamud, and those after them. And Allah does not desire injustice for the servants."﴾

When this was a completion of the speech of the one who believed, and there was no digression into the exchange with Pharaoh over his saying ﴿I show you only what I see﴾ [Ghafir: 29], and so on, and the one who believed had placed Pharaoh's speech in between,

[p. 134]

and he continued, completing his statement, he joined the phrase of his saying with the conjunction "wa" (and), so that his speech would connect to the speech before it, and lest it be imagined that he intended by it a reply to Pharaoh; rather, he intended to complete his address. He referred to him as "the one who believed" because he had become known by the content of the relative clause after what had preceded. Repeating the address "O my people" is an emphasis on what he intended by the first address, as already discussed.

The fear and what has its meaning are construed to take the object of fear directly, and, for the one feared for, with the preposition ʿalā (on/for). Labid said, lamenting his brother Arbad:

*I fear for Arbad the calamities of death, and I do not fear for him the winds and the rain.*

The phrase ﴿a day of the factions﴾ is meant as a genus, not a specific day, as shown by its being an annexation to a plural whose times are far apart. So the sense is: "like the days of the factions." The singular "day" (yawm) is for brevity, like *baṭn* (belly) in the verse of the poet, which is one of the examples of Sibawayh in the section on the adjective resembling the active participle:

*Eat from part of your bellies, you will be chaste, for your time is a lean time.*

By "the days of the factions" is meant the days of their destruction, and the Arabs apply "day" to the day of the victor and the day of the vanquished.

"Factions" (al-aḥzāb) means the nations, because each nation is a faction (ḥizb): its members share one condition and support one another; for this reason a nation is called a faction. This was discussed previously at His saying ﴿every faction, with what they have, rejoicing﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 53], in Surat al-Mu'minun.

The *da'b* (custom, practice) is the habit and the action that its doer persists in: he continues with it and repeats it. This was discussed earlier at His saying ﴿like the custom of the people of Pharaoh﴾ [Al 'Imran: 11], at the beginning of Al 'Imran.

﴿Like the custom of the people of Noah﴾ is in the accusative as an apposition (ʿatf al-bayān) to "like the day of the factions." Since it is an explanation of it, what each is annexed to must necessarily be identical, so "the factions" and "the custom" come to have one meaning. This is only completed by postulating a shared elided noun annexed to both. So the sense is: "like the day of the requital of the factions, like the day of the requital of the custom of the people of Noah, 'Ad and Thamud," that is, the requital of their deeds. Their custom in which they shared was associating partners with Allah.

[p. 135]

This implies that the Copts had knowledge of what befell the people of Noah, 'Ad and Thamud. As for the people of Noah, their flood was well known; and as for 'Ad and Thamud, because their lands were near the Egyptian lands, and it was a great event that could not be hidden from their neighbours.

The clause ﴿And Allah does not desire injustice for the servants﴾ is a parenthetical clause, and the "wa" is parenthetical; it is an interjection between his two conjoined statements. That is: "I fear for you a just requital from Allah, which is the requital of associating partners."

Injustice (ẓulm) is applied to association with partners ("Indeed, association is a great injustice" [Luqman: 13]), and it is applied to dealing unjustly. His saying ﴿And Allah does not desire injustice for the servants﴾ combines the negation of injustice in both its senses, following the method of using a homonym (mushtarak) in both its meanings.

Likewise the verb "desire" (yurīd) is used in the sense of will, as in ﴿Allah does not desire to place upon you any hardship﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6], and it is used in the sense of love, as in ﴿I do not desire any provision from them﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 57]. When the verb of desire falls within the scope of negation, it implies the general negation of desire in both its senses, following the method of using a homonym in both its meanings. So Allah, exalted is He, does not love the occurrence of injustice from His servants, and does not will to wrong His servants. The first of the two meanings of desire and of injustice is more relevant to the context of warning, and the second meaning follows the first, because it indicates that Allah, exalted is He, does not abandon the punishment of the people of association, since He is just. The threat of punishment for association and injustice is among the strongest means of making people refrain from them, and the truthfulness of the threat is among what completes this, together with it being required by wisdom to establish justice.

The fronting of the name of Allah before the verbal predicate serves to restrict the predicated meaning to the subject (qaṣr). Since the predicate falls within a negative context, the meaning is: the restriction of the negation of desiring injustice to Allah, exalted is He, is a restriction by reversal (qaṣr qalb): that is, Allah does not desire injustice for the servants, but others desire it for them, namely the leaders of association and its imams, who call them to it and claim that Allah commanded them with it. He, exalted is He, said ﴿And when they commit an immorality, they say, "We found our fathers doing it, and Allah commanded us with it." Say: "Indeed Allah does not command immorality."﴾ [al-A'raf: 28].

This is according to the first meaning of injustice. As for the second meaning, the sense is: Allah does not desire that

[p. 136]

He wrong His servants, but they wrong themselves by following their imams without insight, as in His saying ﴿Indeed Allah does not wrong people at all, but people wrong themselves﴾ [Yunus: 44], and by their wronging their callers and imams, as He, exalted is He, said ﴿and they increased them only in ruin﴾ [Hud: 101]. Thus the fronting of the subject before the verbal predicate in a negative context in this verse does not depart from its usual use in conveying the restriction of the predicate to the subject, so reflect on it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 40, verses 32–33:

﴿And O my people, indeed I fear for you the Day of Calling Out (yawm al-tanad),﴾ ﴿the Day you will turn back fleeing; for you there will be no protector from Allah. And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide.﴾

He followed his warning of them with the punishment of this world, whose example befell the people of Nuh, 'Ad, Thamud, and those after them, by warning them and cautioning them of the punishment of the Hereafter, joining this sentence to the sentence about the punishment of this world by conjunction.

He inserted, between the conjunctive particle and what it conjoins, the calling out to his people for the purpose mentioned just before.

And ﴿yawm al-tanad﴾ is the Day of Reckoning and Gathering. It was named "the Day of Calling Out" (yawm al-tanad) because people call out to one another on that day: some seeking intercession, some pleading humbly, some greeting and congratulating, some reproaching, some making excuses, some ordering, and some announcing their obedience. Allah the Exalted said, regarding the day when He calls to them, ﴿Those are called from a far place﴾ [Fussilat: 44]; ﴿And the companions of Paradise will call out to the companions of the Fire﴾ [al-A'raf: 44]; ﴿And the companions of the Fire will call out to the companions of Paradise﴾ [al-A'raf: 50]; ﴿The Day We will call every people with their leader﴾ [al-Isra': 71]; ﴿There they will call for destruction﴾ [al-Furqan: 13]; ﴿The Day the caller calls to a terrible thing﴾ [al-Qamar: 6], and similar to that.

Among the elegance of eloquence is the mention of this description of the Day in this context, to remind them that he, in his station among them, calls to them with "O my people," advising them and desiring their deliverance from every frightening call on the Day of Resurrection, and preparing them for every joyful call in it.

The majority of readers recited ﴿yawm al-tanad﴾ without a yā' in both pause and continuation. It is not nunated (tanwin), but it was treated as if it were nunated, for the purpose of observing the rhyme (fawasil), like the saying of the ninth of the women in the Hadith of Umm Zar': "My husband is tall of pillars (rafi' al-'imad), long of sword-belt (tawil al-nijad), abundant in ashes (kathir al-ramad), near the house to the fire (qarib al-bayt min al-nad)." She deleted the yā' from the word al-nad, although it is definite.

Ibn Kathir recited ﴿yawm al-tanadi﴾ with the yā' retained, according to the original form, considering that the rhyme is His saying ﴿fa-ma lahu min hadin﴾.

﴿Yawm tuwallun﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿yawm al-tanad﴾. The clause ﴿ma lakum min Allahi min 'asim﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause. The meaning: in a state where turning away will not benefit you.

Al-'asim means the one who prevents and protects. ﴿Min Allah﴾ is connected to ﴿'asim﴾, and the ﴿min﴾ connected to it is for origin (ibtida'); you say: "He protected him from the oppressor," meaning he placed him in a protection originating from the oppressor. The verb ('asama) is understood to include the sense of rescuing and snatching away, and the meaning of ﴿min Allah﴾ is from His punishment and His retribution, because prevention relates to meanings, not to essences.

The ﴿min﴾ entering upon ﴿'asim﴾ is superfluous, for emphasizing the negation.

The discussion of the transitive use of the verb ﴿akhafu 'alaykum mithla yawm al-ahzab﴾ [Ghafir: 30] has sufficed from repeating it here.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 40, verses 32–33:

﴿And O my people, indeed I fear for you the Day of Calling Out (yawm al-tanad),﴾ ﴿the Day you will turn back fleeing; for you there will be no protector from Allah. And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide.﴾

He followed his warning of them with the punishment of this world, whose example befell the people of Nuh, 'Ad, Thamud, and those after them, by warning them and cautioning them of the punishment of the Hereafter, joining this sentence to the sentence about the punishment of this world by conjunction.

He inserted, between the conjunctive particle and what it conjoins, the calling out to his people for the purpose mentioned just before.

And ﴿yawm al-tanad﴾ is the Day of Reckoning and Gathering. It was named "the Day of Calling Out" (yawm al-tanad) because people call out to one another on that day: some seeking intercession, some pleading humbly, some greeting and congratulating, some reproaching, some making excuses, some ordering, and some announcing their obedience. Allah the Exalted said, regarding the day when He calls to them, ﴿Those are called from a far place﴾ [Fussilat: 44]; ﴿And the companions of Paradise will call out to the companions of the Fire﴾ [al-A'raf: 44]; ﴿And the companions of the Fire will call out to the companions of Paradise﴾ [al-A'raf: 50]; ﴿The Day We will call every people with their leader﴾ [al-Isra': 71]; ﴿There they will call for destruction﴾ [al-Furqan: 13]; ﴿The Day the caller calls to a terrible thing﴾ [al-Qamar: 6], and similar to that.

Among the elegance of eloquence is the mention of this description of the Day in this context, to remind them that he, in his station among them, calls to them with "O my people," advising them and desiring their deliverance from every frightening call on the Day of Resurrection, and preparing them for every joyful call in it.

The majority of readers recited ﴿yawm al-tanad﴾ without a yā' in both pause and continuation. It is not nunated (tanwin), but it was treated as if it were nunated, for the purpose of observing the rhyme (fawasil), like the saying of the ninth of the women in the Hadith of Umm Zar': "My husband is tall of pillars (rafi' al-'imad), long of sword-belt (tawil al-nijad), abundant in ashes (kathir al-ramad), near the house to the fire (qarib al-bayt min al-nad)." She deleted the yā' from the word al-nad, although it is definite.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 40, verses 34–35 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Joseph came to you before with clear proofs, but you remained in doubt about what he brought, until when he died you said: "God will never send a messenger after him."﴾

He perceived in them little benefit from advising them, and that they were determined to deny Moses. So he advanced in his admonition to rebuke them for what had passed, and to remind them that they were descendants of a people who denied Joseph when he came to them with clear proofs. Denying those who guide to the truth was a well-known trait (shanshana) among their forefathers, so it became a settled disposition (sajiyya) in them.

The emphasis of the report with qad (قَدْ) and the oath-lam (لامُ القِسْمِ) is to confirm it, because they were liable to deny it given how long ago it was.

The word "came" (جاءَكم) in His saying is used metaphorically (mustaʿār) for occurrence and manifestation, and the bāʾ (بِ) indicates accompaniment (mulābasa). The meaning is: Joseph had clearly appeared to you with proofs. It does not follow that the showing of the proofs must have accompanied a call to a sharia (sharīʿa, religious law). When he displayed the proofs and they recognised his rank, it was incumbent upon them, by the judgement of sound reason, to examine his signs and seek the way of guidance and salvation. God did not command Joseph to call Pharaoh and his people, for a wisdom that may have been waiting for the appropriate time and condition that God had reserved for Moses, peace be upon him.

"The clear proofs" (al-bayyināt) are the manifest evidences showing that he was chosen by God to guide to good. Thus it was incumbent on every rational person to follow his path, trace his traces, and seek from him what lies beyond this material world. This is based on the principle that knowledge of God's oneness (tawḥīd) is obligatory in the times of the intervals between prophets (al-fatarāt, the periods without a prophet), either by reason, or by what had been transmitted among humanity from the teachings of earlier messengers, according to the disagreement among the theologians (al-mutakallimūn, scholastic theologians).

The "clear proofs" are also his informing them of what was hidden from them about their own circumstances through revelation, in the interpretation of dreams; likewise the sign of his infallibility (ʿiṣma), in which he stood alone among them, and to which the wife of the Governor and a witness of her household testified, until the king said: ﴿Bring him to me, I will take him for my own service﴾ [Joseph: 54]. So the evidences of Joseph's prophethood were clear, but they did not draw from them any reasoning by which they might follow his path toward the good of their afterlife. They were eager to benefit from him in managing their worldly affairs, so they entrusted him with the treasuries of their wealth and the administration of their kingdom. The king said to him: ﴿Today you are with us established and trusted﴾ [Joseph: 54].

It did not occur to them to seek guidance from him in their religious conduct.

If you say: since they did not turn to seek guidance from Joseph in the affairs of their religion, and their concern with managing the world distracted them from managing the religion, why did Joseph not call them to belief in the truth, and instead limited himself to asking the king: ﴿Set me over the treasuries of the land; indeed I am a keeper, knowing﴾ [Joseph: 55]?

I say: because God did not command him to call to guidance except when he was asked for it, for a wisdom, as you have known just now. So God established him in the station of a mufti (muftī, one who gives religious rulings) and a guide for whoever sought guidance, not in the station of a muhtasib (muḥtasib, one who enjoins good and forbids wrong in public) who changes what is evil. And: ﴿God knows best where to place His message﴾ [al-Anʿām: 124]. When God established him thus, and Joseph knew from the king's words ﴿Today you are with us established and trusted﴾ [Joseph: 54] that the king wanted only the management of his kingdom and his wealth, he did not ask him for more than he could fulfil for him in that. As for the obligation on them to seek knowledge and guidance from him, that was a right incumbent upon them. So the meaning of ﴿you remained in doubt about what he brought﴾ is a censure of their forefathers for their scant concern in searching for the highest perfection, which is the perfection of the soul through following the upright religion. That is: your forefathers continued to feel that Joseph was upon a great matter of guidance, unfamiliar to them, and they rushed to him in their important affairs, yet their souls were not resolved to ask him for guidance in matters of religion. So they were in a state of doubt about his matter; that is, the outcome of what they reached concerning him was that they were in doubt about what would reveal to them their duty towards him. Thus Joseph's lifetime among them passed while they were in doubt about the matter.

So the blame is directed at them for their negligence in seeking what would save them after death. He, exalted, said: ﴿Whoever desires the hasty life, We hasten for him therein what We will﴾ [al-Isrāʾ: 18], and the verses that follow.

The "until" (ḥattā, حَتّى) indicates a limit, and its limit is the content of the clause that follows it, which is the clause "when he died" (idhā halaka, إذا هَلَكَ). Here "idhā" is a noun denoting a past time, governed in the genitive by ḥattā, and it is not an adverb of time. That is: until the time of Joseph's death, you said: "God will never send a messenger after him." That is, your forefathers said at the time of Joseph's death: "God will never in the future send a messenger after Joseph, ever." They meant: we were hesitant to believe in Joseph, so now we are relieved of the hesitation, for no one will come after him claiming a message from God. This was a statement made by them according to the custom of the obstinate and those who oppose the people of reform and virtue: they acknowledge the merit of such people only after their death, out of regret for the good they had been calling them to and missed.

In it there is a kind of exaggeration of his perfection in his era, as one says: "the seal of the verifiers," "the remnant of the righteous," or "one whom time does not bring the like of." The sum of it is that they were in doubt about the sending of a single messenger, and that they were certain that whoever claims a message after him is a liar; therefore they denied Moses.

This saying of theirs does not imply that they believed he was a messenger, since they were in doubt about that. Rather, they intended by it to cut off this possibility in the future and to remove the doubt from their souls. The apparent meaning of this verse is that Joseph was a messenger, based on the apparent sense of His saying: ﴿you said: God will never send a messenger after him﴾, that "messenger" (rasūlan, رَسُولًا) is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) from the pronoun in "after him" (min baʿdihi, مِن بَعْدِهِ). The more correct reading is that the word "messenger" (rasūlan) is the object (maf'ūl) of "will send" (yabʿathu, يَبْعَثَ), and it does not require describing Joseph by it. For there is no report counting him among the messengers, nor that he called to a religion in Egypt. And how could that be, when God says: ﴿He could not have taken his brother under the king's law, except that God willed﴾ [Joseph: 76]? And there is no doubt that he was a prophet, and when he found an opening for guidance he made it manifest, as in His saying: ﴿O my two fellow prisoners, are separate lords better, or God, the One, the Subduer?﴾ [Joseph: 39], ﴿What you worship besides Him are only names you have named, you and your fathers, for which God has sent down no authority﴾ [Joseph: 40], and His saying: ﴿I have forsaken the religion of a people who do not believe in God and who are disbelievers in the Hereafter﴾ [Joseph: 37], ﴿and I follow the religion of my fathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob; it was not for us to associate anything with God﴾ [Joseph: 38].

The verb "came" (jāʾakum, جاءَكم) is transitive to the pronoun of the addressees, and "you remained" (fa-mā ziltum, فَما زِلْتُمْ) and "you said" (qultum, قُلْتُمْ) are also attributed to their pronoun, though they were not present at that time. This is deliberate, to place the burden of their forefathers' conduct upon them, and to record against them that denying those who advise and the confusion of their minds in benefiting from the evidences of truthfulness were inherited from their forefathers in their natural disposition, and became established in their souls, so that it passed to them generation after generation. This is as was mentioned in the address to the Children of Israel in Surat al-Baqara: ﴿And when We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh﴾ [al-Baqara: 49], and similar.

﴿Thus God leads astray whoever is an extravagant doubter. Those who dispute concerning the signs of God without any authority that has come to them, it is greatly hateful in the sight of God and in the sight of those who believe. Thus God seals every heart of a proud, tyrannical person.﴾

Most of the commentators took these sentences as a continuation of the speech of the believer. Some of them took part of it as the speech of the believer and part as a statement from God, the Exalted. This arises from allowing that His saying ﴿Those who dispute﴾ etc. may be an apposition (badal) or a new subject (mubtadaʾ). Some of them remained silent about this, limiting themselves to explaining the meaning without addressing how it connects to what precedes it.

What appears is that His saying ﴿Thus God leads astray whoever is an extravagant doubter﴾ up to His saying "tyrannical" is entirely a statement from God, the Exalted, interposed between the speech of the believer and the speech of Pharaoh. This is one of the Islamic meanings, intended as a lesson from the state of those who denied Moses, as an allusion to the idolaters of Quraysh. That is: just as God led astray the people of Pharaoh, God leads astray extravagant doubters like you, so your recompense is the same. This view is supported by His saying at the end of it: ﴿and in the sight of those who believe﴾, for the believer of Pharaoh's household had no other believer in Moses and Aaron with him. This is of the type of recalling a thing by its opposite. What adds further certainty to this is that the description ﴿those who dispute concerning the signs of God﴾ is repeated four times from the beginning of the surah; then it occurs here in the middle, in His saying: ﴿Indeed those who dispute concerning the signs of God without any authority that has come to them, there is in their breasts only pride, which they will never attain﴾ [Ghāfir: 56], and then it occurs as a conclusion in His saying: ﴿Have you not seen those who dispute concerning the signs of God, how they are turned away?﴾ [Ghāfir: 69].

The demonstrative in His saying "thus" (kadhālika, كَذَلِكَ) refers to the straying derived from His saying "God leads astray" (yuḍillu Allāhu, يُضِلُّ اللَّهُ). That is: like that straying, God leads astray the extravagant doubters. That is, the straying of the polytheists in denying Muhammad (ﷺ) is like the straying of the people of Pharaoh in denying Moses, peace be upon him.

The address through the kāf (ك) attached to the demonstrative is an address to the Muslims.

The "extravagant" (musrif, مُسْرِفٌ) is one who goes to excess in an act in which there is no good. The "doubter" (murtāb, مُرْتابٌ) is one who has intense doubt (rayb), that is, uncertainty.

Attributing the leading astray to God is like attributing to Him the negation of guidance in His saying: ﴿God does not guide one who is an extravagant liar﴾ [Ghāfir: 28], which was mentioned just now.

His saying ﴿Those who dispute concerning the signs of God﴾ may be a subject (mubtadaʾ) whose predicate is ﴿it is greatly hateful﴾ (kabura maqtan, كَبُرَ مَقْتًا). It may also be an apposition (badal) from "whoever" (man, مَن) in His saying ﴿whoever is an extravagant doubter﴾. In that case it clarifies that the referent of "whoever" is a group and not a single person. So in ﴿whoever is an extravagant doubter﴾ the wording of "whoever" (man) is observed, and the predicate is given in the singular; while in the apposition the meaning of "whoever" is observed, so a relative pronoun in the plural (alladhīna) is substituted for it. The relative "those who" (alladhīna, الَّذِينَ) is used to identify the polytheists. God the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed those who distort Our signs are not hidden from Us﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 40], and He said in this surah: ﴿None dispute the signs of God except those who disbelieve, so let not their going about in the lands deceive you﴾ [Ghāfir: 4].

The choice of the present tense in "they dispute" (yujādilūna, يُجادِلُونَ) serves to convey that their disputing is renewed and repeated, and that they do not cease from it. This is explicit in condemning them, and an implicit disparagement of their disputing, which necessitated their straying.

In the relative form there is an indication of the cause of their being led astray: that is, the reason for the creation of straying in their hearts is extravagance in falsehood and the repetition of their disputing, intending falsehood.

Disputation (mujādala, الْمُجادَلَة) is the repetition of argument to establish the claim of the disputant and to refute the claim of the one who opposes him. God said: ﴿and argue with them in the best manner﴾ [al-Naḥl: 125]. Among the disputing concerning the signs of God is contesting to refute their indication, and among it is stubborn obstinacy about them, as they said: ﴿Our hearts are in coverings against what you call us to, and in our ears is deafness, and between us and you is a veil﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 5]; and among it is refusing to listen to them, as ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy ibn Salūl said at the time of the openness of his disbelief toward the Prophet (ﷺ): "The Prophet (ﷺ) came to a gathering in which Ibn Salūl was, and he recited the Qur'an to them. ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salūl said: 'I do not understand what you say, O man, and do not trouble us with it in our gathering. Sit in your saddle-place; whoever comes to you, recite to him.'"

The phrase "without any authority" (bi-ghayri sulṭānin, بِغَيْرِ سُلْطانٍ) is connected to "they dispute" (yujādilūna). The bāʾ (بِ) indicates instrumentality (istiʿāna), and "authority" (sulṭān, السُّلْطانِ) means proof. The meaning is that they dispute with what is not a proof, but with obstinacy and mockery.

"That has come to them" (atāhum, أتاهم) is a description of "authority" (sulṭān), and the "coming" (itiyān, الإتْيانُ) is used metaphorically for manifestation and occurrence.

The occurrence of the proof is its being believed and its appearing to the intellect. That is, they dispute with a dispute that is not of the kind stirred up by reason and intellectual reflection, but is deception and silencing.

The clause ﴿it is greatly hateful in the sight of God﴾ (kabura maqtan ʿinda Allāh, كَبُرَ مَقْتًا عِنْدَ اللَّهِ) is the predicate of "indeed" (inna, إنَّ), in the form of giving information through a performative (al-ikhbār bil-inshāʾ), since it is a performative expression of condemnation of their disputing, intended to silence the truth. That is: their disputing is greatly hateful in the sight of God. So the subject of "is great" (kabura) is a pronoun referring to the disputing derived from "they dispute", in the manner of His saying ﴿Be just, that is nearer to piety﴾ [al-Māʾida: 8].

"Hatred" (maqtan, مَقْتًا) is a specifier (tamyīz) of the greatness, and it is a specifier of relation transferred from the agent. The estimated meaning is: the hatefulness of their disputing is great.

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary on verses 34–35 of Surah Ghafir (40), part 2 of 2:

The verb (kabura) here is treated as belonging to the verbs of censure, like (sa'a, "how evil"), because the pattern (fa'ula) with a damma on the ayn comes to mean (ni'ma and bi'sa, "what an excellent" and "what an evil"). Even if the damma on its ayn were original, the purpose of this is an express declaration of reprehensibility, after it had been understood from the relative clause that their disputation was the cause of their being led astray with that firm misguidance. Thus, through this resumptive statement, the atrocity of their disputation was established by both means: implication (kinaya) and explicit statement (tasrih).

Al-kibr: here used metaphorically for intensity; that is, He abhorred their disputation with intense abhorrence.

Al-maqt: intense hatred. It is a kinaya for the intensity of the punishment from Allah for it. That it is maqt "with Allah" is a denunciation of it and an expression of its atrocity.

As for the conjunction of ﴿and with those who believe﴾, I have not seen, among the many tafsir works before me, anyone who addressed the benefit of the conjunction of ﴿and with those who believe﴾ except al-Mahá'imi in Tabsirat al-Rahman, when he said: "﴿Greatly hateful in the sight of Allah﴾, and this necessitates misguidance, and what shows that it is greatly hateful is that it is with those who believe, meaning the loci in which the manifestation of the truth appears." End of quote. The words of al-Mahá'imi are a fine expression, meaning that the fact that it is hateful in the sight of Allah does not become known to people except through report; so the report is reinforced by observation, for those who believe, despite their small number on that day, openly display their hatred of the disputation of the polytheists.

In my view, what is more evident than this is that Allah intended to honour the believers, not to persuade the polytheists, for they do not heed the hatred of the believers, nor do they accept the hatred of Allah towards them. So the purpose is praise of the believers for hating falsehood, as He said: ﴿And the believing men and believing women are allies of one another; they enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong﴾ [al-Tawba: 71], together with an indication of exalting their rank by joining their being "with" to Allah's being "with," in the manner of His saying ﴿Allah bears witness that there is no deity except Him, and the angels and those of knowledge﴾ [Al 'Imran: 18], His saying ﴿O Prophet, sufficient for you is Allah and whoever follows you of the believers﴾ [al-Anfal: 64], His saying ﴿It is He who supported you with His help and with the believers﴾ [al-Anfal: 62], and like the words of the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning the account of the wolf's speech, when some of those present marvelled and he said: "I believe in that, and Abu Bakr," though Abu Bakr was not in the gathering.

In attributing the aversion to disputing about the signs of Allah without authority to the believers there is an instruction to the believers to turn away from disputing with the polytheists, in the manner of what is in His saying ﴿And when they hear vain talk, they turn away from it﴾ [al-Qasas: 55], His saying ﴿And when the ignorant address them, they say, "Peace"﴾ [al-Furqan: 63], and His saying ﴿And when they pass by vain talk, they pass by with dignity﴾ [al-Furqan: 72].

The discussion of ﴿Thus Allah seals upon every heart of a proud, tyrannical one﴾ is like the discussion of ﴿Thus Allah leaves astray whoever is excessive and doubting﴾.

Al-tabʿ (ṭabʿ): the sealing, and it was discussed in His saying ﴿Allah has sealed over their hearts﴾ [al-Baqara: 7] in Surat al-Baqara.

The sealing, the ṭabʿ, and the akinna (coverings): the creation of misguidance in the heart, that is, the self (nafs).

Al-mutakabbir: one who possesses pride to an intensive degree, and for this reason the form of effort (taka"ulluf) was borrowed.

Page 145

Al-jabbar: an intensive pattern from al-jabr, which is compulsion. So al-jabbar is one who compels people to do what they do not like, owing to his oppression.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿upon every heart of a proud one﴾ with the heart (qalb) in the genitive construction with (mutakabbir). Abu 'Amr alone, and Ibn Dhakwan from 'Amir, read (qalb) with tanwin, so that (mutakabbir) and (jabbar) are adjectives of (qalb). The attribution of pride and compulsion to the heart is a rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli). What is meant is describing its possessor, as in His saying ﴿for he is sinful, his heart﴾ [al-Baqara: 283], because it is the cause of sin, as one says: "my eye saw and my ear heard."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 40, verses 34–35 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Joseph came to you before with clear proofs, but you remained in doubt about what he brought, until when he died you said: "God will never send a messenger after him."﴾

He perceived in them little benefit from advising them, and that they were determined to deny Moses. So he advanced in his admonition to rebuke them for what had passed, and to remind them that they were descendants of a people who denied Joseph when he came to them with clear proofs. Denying those who guide to the truth was a well-known trait (shanshana) among their forefathers, so it became a settled disposition (sajiyya) in them.

The emphasis of the report with qad (قَدْ) and the oath-lam (لامُ القِسْمِ) is to confirm it, because they were liable to deny it given how long ago it was.

The word "came" (جاءَكم) in His saying is used metaphorically (mustaʿār) for occurrence and manifestation, and the bāʾ (بِ) indicates accompaniment (mulābasa). The meaning is: Joseph had clearly appeared to you with proofs. It does not follow that the showing of the proofs must have accompanied a call to a sharia (sharīʿa, religious law). When he displayed the proofs and they recognised his rank, it was incumbent upon them, by the judgement of sound reason, to examine his signs and seek the way of guidance and salvation. God did not command Joseph to call Pharaoh and his people, for a wisdom that may have been waiting for the appropriate time and condition that God had reserved for Moses, peace be upon him.

"The clear proofs" (al-bayyināt) are the manifest evidences showing that he was chosen by God to guide to good. Thus it was incumbent on every rational person to follow his path, trace his traces, and seek from him what lies beyond this material world. This is based on the principle that knowledge of God's oneness (tawḥīd) is obligatory in the times of the intervals between prophets (al-fatarāt, the periods without a prophet), either by reason, or by what had been transmitted among humanity from the teachings of earlier messengers, according to the disagreement among the theologians (al-mutakallimūn, scholastic theologians).

The "clear proofs" are also his informing them of what was hidden from them about their own circumstances through revelation, in the interpretation of dreams; likewise the sign of his infallibility (ʿiṣma), in which he stood alone among them, and to which the wife of the Governor and a witness of her household testified, until the king said: ﴿Bring him to me, I will take him for my own service﴾ [Joseph: 54]. So the evidences of Joseph's prophethood were clear, but they did not draw from them any reasoning by which they might follow his path toward the good of their afterlife. They were eager to benefit from him in managing their worldly affairs, so they entrusted him with the treasuries of their wealth and the administration of their kingdom. The king said to him: ﴿Today you are with us established and trusted﴾ [Joseph: 54].

It did not occur to them to seek guidance from him in their religious conduct.

If you say: since they did not turn to seek guidance from Joseph in the affairs of their religion, and their concern with managing the world distracted them from managing the religion, why did Joseph not call them to belief in the truth, and instead limited himself to asking the king: ﴿Set me over the treasuries of the land; indeed I am a keeper, knowing﴾ [Joseph: 55]?

I say: because God did not command him to call to guidance except when he was asked for it, for a wisdom, as you have known just now. So God established him in the station of a mufti (muftī, one who gives religious rulings) and a guide for whoever sought guidance, not in the station of a muhtasib (muḥtasib, one who enjoins good and forbids wrong in public) who changes what is evil. And: ﴿God knows best where to place His message﴾ [al-Anʿām: 124]. When God established him thus, and Joseph knew from the king's words ﴿Today you are with us established and trusted﴾ [Joseph: 54] that the king wanted only the management of his kingdom and his wealth, he did not ask him for more than he could fulfil for him in that. As for the obligation on them to seek knowledge and guidance from him, that was a right incumbent upon them. So the meaning of ﴿you remained in doubt about what he brought﴾ is a censure of their forefathers for their scant concern in searching for the highest perfection, which is the perfection of the soul through following the upright religion. That is: your forefathers continued to feel that Joseph was upon a great matter of guidance, unfamiliar to them, and they rushed to him in their important affairs, yet their souls were not resolved to ask him for guidance in matters of religion. So they were in a state of doubt about his matter; that is, the outcome of what they reached concerning him was that they were in doubt about what would reveal to them their duty towards him. Thus Joseph's lifetime among them passed while they were in doubt about the matter.

So the blame is directed at them for their negligence in seeking what would save them after death. He, exalted, said: ﴿Whoever desires the hasty life, We hasten for him therein what We will﴾ [al-Isrāʾ: 18], and the verses that follow.

The "until" (ḥattā, حَتّى) indicates a limit, and its limit is the content of the clause that follows it, which is the clause "when he died" (idhā halaka, إذا هَلَكَ). Here "idhā" is a noun denoting a past time, governed in the genitive by ḥattā, and it is not an adverb of time. That is: until the time of Joseph's death, you said: "God will never send a messenger after him." That is, your forefathers said at the time of Joseph's death: "God will never in the future send a messenger after Joseph, ever." They meant: we were hesitant to believe in Joseph, so now we are relieved of the hesitation, for no one will come after him claiming a message from God. This was a statement made by them according to the custom of the obstinate and those who oppose the people of reform and virtue: they acknowledge the merit of such people only after their death, out of regret for the good they had been calling them to and missed.

In it there is a kind of exaggeration of his perfection in his era, as one says: "the seal of the verifiers," "the remnant of the righteous," or "one whom time does not bring the like of." The sum of it is that they were in doubt about the sending of a single messenger, and that they were certain that whoever claims a message after him is a liar; therefore they denied Moses.

This saying of theirs does not imply that they believed he was a messenger, since they were in doubt about that. Rather, they intended by it to cut off this possibility in the future and to remove the doubt from their souls. The apparent meaning of this verse is that Joseph was a messenger, based on the apparent sense of His saying: ﴿you said: God will never send a messenger after him﴾, that "messenger" (rasūlan, رَسُولًا) is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) from the pronoun in "after him" (min baʿdihi, مِن بَعْدِهِ). The more correct reading is that the word "messenger" (rasūlan) is the object (maf'ūl) of "will send" (yabʿathu, يَبْعَثَ), and it does not require describing Joseph by it. For there is no report counting him among the messengers, nor that he called to a religion in Egypt. And how could that be, when God says: ﴿He could not have taken his brother under the king's law, except that God willed﴾ [Joseph: 76]? And there is no doubt that he was a prophet, and when he found an opening for guidance he made it manifest, as in His saying: ﴿O my two fellow prisoners, are separate lords better, or God, the One, the Subduer?﴾ [Joseph: 39], ﴿What you worship besides Him are only names you have named, you and your fathers, for which God has sent down no authority﴾ [Joseph: 40], and His saying: ﴿I have forsaken the religion of a people who do not believe in God and who are disbelievers in the Hereafter﴾ [Joseph: 37], ﴿and I follow the religion of my fathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob; it was not for us to associate anything with God﴾ [Joseph: 38].

The verb "came" (jāʾakum, جاءَكم) is transitive to the pronoun of the addressees, and "you remained" (fa-mā ziltum, فَما زِلْتُمْ) and "you said" (qultum, قُلْتُمْ) are also attributed to their pronoun, though they were not present at that time. This is deliberate, to place the burden of their forefathers' conduct upon them, and to record against them that denying those who advise and the confusion of their minds in benefiting from the evidences of truthfulness were inherited from their forefathers in their natural disposition, and became established in their souls, so that it passed to them generation after generation. This is as was mentioned in the address to the Children of Israel in Surat al-Baqara: ﴿And when We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh﴾ [al-Baqara: 49], and similar.

﴿Thus God leads astray whoever is an extravagant doubter. Those who dispute concerning the signs of God without any authority that has come to them, it is greatly hateful in the sight of God and in the sight of those who believe. Thus God seals every heart of a proud, tyrannical person.﴾

Most of the commentators took these sentences as a continuation of the speech of the believer. Some of them took part of it as the speech of the believer and part as a statement from God, the Exalted. This arises from allowing that His saying ﴿Those who dispute﴾ etc. may be an apposition (badal) or a new subject (mubtadaʾ). Some of them remained silent about this, limiting themselves to explaining the meaning without addressing how it connects to what precedes it.

What appears is that His saying ﴿Thus God leads astray whoever is an extravagant doubter﴾ up to His saying "tyrannical" is entirely a statement from God, the Exalted, interposed between the speech of the believer and the speech of Pharaoh. This is one of the Islamic meanings, intended as a lesson from the state of those who denied Moses, as an allusion to the idolaters of Quraysh. That is: just as God led astray the people of Pharaoh, God leads astray extravagant doubters like you, so your recompense is the same. This view is supported by His saying at the end of it: ﴿and in the sight of those who believe﴾, for the believer of Pharaoh's household had no other believer in Moses and Aaron with him. This is of the type of recalling a thing by its opposite. What adds further certainty to this is that the description ﴿those who dispute concerning the signs of God﴾ is repeated four times from the beginning of the surah; then it occurs here in the middle, in His saying: ﴿Indeed those who dispute concerning the signs of God without any authority that has come to them, there is in their breasts only pride, which they will never attain﴾ [Ghāfir: 56], and then it occurs as a conclusion in His saying: ﴿Have you not seen those who dispute concerning the signs of God, how they are turned away?﴾ [Ghāfir: 69].

The demonstrative in His saying "thus" (kadhālika, كَذَلِكَ) refers to the straying derived from His saying "God leads astray" (yuḍillu Allāhu, يُضِلُّ اللَّهُ). That is: like that straying, God leads astray the extravagant doubters. That is, the straying of the polytheists in denying Muhammad (ﷺ) is like the straying of the people of Pharaoh in denying Moses, peace be upon him.

The address through the kāf (ك) attached to the demonstrative is an address to the Muslims.

The "extravagant" (musrif, مُسْرِفٌ) is one who goes to excess in an act in which there is no good. The "doubter" (murtāb, مُرْتابٌ) is one who has intense doubt (rayb), that is, uncertainty.

Attributing the leading astray to God is like attributing to Him the negation of guidance in His saying: ﴿God does not guide one who is an extravagant liar﴾ [Ghāfir: 28], which was mentioned just now.

His saying ﴿Those who dispute concerning the signs of God﴾ may be a subject (mubtadaʾ) whose predicate is ﴿it is greatly hateful﴾ (kabura maqtan, كَبُرَ مَقْتًا). It may also be an apposition (badal) from "whoever" (man, مَن) in His saying ﴿whoever is an extravagant doubter﴾. In that case it clarifies that the referent of "whoever" is a group and not a single person. So in ﴿whoever is an extravagant doubter﴾ the wording of "whoever" (man) is observed, and the predicate is given in the singular; while in the apposition the meaning of "whoever" is observed, so a relative pronoun in the plural (alladhīna) is substituted for it. The relative "those who" (alladhīna, الَّذِينَ) is used to identify the polytheists. God the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed those who distort Our signs are not hidden from Us﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 40], and He said in this surah: ﴿None dispute the signs of God except those who disbelieve, so let not their going about in the lands deceive you﴾ [Ghāfir: 4].

The choice of the present tense in "they dispute" (yujādilūna, يُجادِلُونَ) serves to convey that their disputing is renewed and repeated, and that they do not cease from it. This is explicit in condemning them, and an implicit disparagement of their disputing, which necessitated their straying.

In the relative form there is an indication of the cause of their being led astray: that is, the reason for the creation of straying in their hearts is extravagance in falsehood and the repetition of their disputing, intending falsehood.

Disputation (mujādala, الْمُجادَلَة) is the repetition of argument to establish the claim of the disputant and to refute the claim of the one who opposes him. God said: ﴿and argue with them in the best manner﴾ [al-Naḥl: 125]. Among the disputing concerning the signs of God is contesting to refute their indication, and among it is stubborn obstinacy about them, as they said: ﴿Our hearts are in coverings against what you call us to, and in our ears is deafness, and between us and you is a veil﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 5]; and among it is refusing to listen to them, as ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy ibn Salūl said at the time of the openness of his disbelief toward the Prophet (ﷺ): "The Prophet (ﷺ) came to a gathering in which Ibn Salūl was, and he recited the Qur'an to them. ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salūl said: 'I do not understand what you say, O man, and do not trouble us with it in our gathering. Sit in your saddle-place; whoever comes to you, recite to him.'"

The phrase "without any authority" (bi-ghayri sulṭānin, بِغَيْرِ سُلْطانٍ) is connected to "they dispute" (yujādilūna). The bāʾ (بِ) indicates instrumentality (istiʿāna), and "authority" (sulṭān, السُّلْطانِ) means proof. The meaning is that they dispute with what is not a proof, but with obstinacy and mockery.

"That has come to them" (atāhum, أتاهم) is a description of "authority" (sulṭān), and the "coming" (itiyān, الإتْيانُ) is used metaphorically for manifestation and occurrence.

The occurrence of the proof is its being believed and its appearing to the intellect. That is, they dispute with a dispute that is not of the kind stirred up by reason and intellectual reflection, but is deception and silencing.

The clause ﴿it is greatly hateful in the sight of God﴾ (kabura maqtan ʿinda Allāh, كَبُرَ مَقْتًا عِنْدَ اللَّهِ) is the predicate of "indeed" (inna, إنَّ), in the form of giving information through a performative (al-ikhbār bil-inshāʾ), since it is a performative expression of condemnation of their disputing, intended to silence the truth. That is: their disputing is greatly hateful in the sight of God. So the subject of "is great" (kabura) is a pronoun referring to the disputing derived from "they dispute", in the manner of His saying ﴿Be just, that is nearer to piety﴾ [al-Māʾida: 8].

"Hatred" (maqtan, مَقْتًا) is a specifier (tamyīz) of the greatness, and it is a specifier of relation transferred from the agent. The estimated meaning is: the hatefulness of their disputing is great.

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary on verses 34–35 of Surah Ghafir (40), part 2 of 2:

The verb (kabura) here is treated as belonging to the verbs of censure, like (sa'a, "how evil"), because the pattern (fa'ula) with a damma on the ayn comes to mean (ni'ma and bi'sa, "what an excellent" and "what an evil"). Even if the damma on its ayn were original, the purpose of this is an express declaration of reprehensibility, after it had been understood from the relative clause that their disputation was the cause of their being led astray with that firm misguidance. Thus, through this resumptive statement, the atrocity of their disputation was established by both means: implication (kinaya) and explicit statement (tasrih).

Al-kibr: here used metaphorically for intensity; that is, He abhorred their disputation with intense abhorrence.

Al-maqt: intense hatred. It is a kinaya for the intensity of the punishment from Allah for it. That it is maqt "with Allah" is a denunciation of it and an expression of its atrocity.
