As for the conjunction of ﴿and with those who believe﴾, I have not seen, among the many tafsir works before me, anyone who addressed the benefit of the conjunction of ﴿and with those who believe﴾ except al-Mahá'imi in Tabsirat al-Rahman, when he said: "﴿Greatly hateful in the sight of Allah﴾, and this necessitates misguidance, and what shows that it is greatly hateful is that it is with those who believe, meaning the loci in which the manifestation of the truth appears." End of quote. The words of al-Mahá'imi are a fine expression, meaning that the fact that it is hateful in the sight of Allah does not become known to people except through report; so the report is reinforced by observation, for those who believe, despite their small number on that day, openly display their hatred of the disputation of the polytheists.

In my view, what is more evident than this is that Allah intended to honour the believers, not to persuade the polytheists, for they do not heed the hatred of the believers, nor do they accept the hatred of Allah towards them. So the purpose is praise of the believers for hating falsehood, as He said: ﴿And the believing men and believing women are allies of one another; they enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong﴾ [al-Tawba: 71], together with an indication of exalting their rank by joining their being "with" to Allah's being "with," in the manner of His saying ﴿Allah bears witness that there is no deity except Him, and the angels and those of knowledge﴾ [Al 'Imran: 18], His saying ﴿O Prophet, sufficient for you is Allah and whoever follows you of the believers﴾ [al-Anfal: 64], His saying ﴿It is He who supported you with His help and with the believers﴾ [al-Anfal: 62], and like the words of the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning the account of the wolf's speech, when some of those present marvelled and he said: "I believe in that, and Abu Bakr," though Abu Bakr was not in the gathering.

In attributing the aversion to disputing about the signs of Allah without authority to the believers there is an instruction to the believers to turn away from disputing with the polytheists, in the manner of what is in His saying ﴿And when they hear vain talk, they turn away from it﴾ [al-Qasas: 55], His saying ﴿And when the ignorant address them, they say, "Peace"﴾ [al-Furqan: 63], and His saying ﴿And when they pass by vain talk, they pass by with dignity﴾ [al-Furqan: 72].

The discussion of ﴿Thus Allah seals upon every heart of a proud, tyrannical one﴾ is like the discussion of ﴿Thus Allah leaves astray whoever is excessive and doubting﴾.

Al-tabʿ (ṭabʿ): the sealing, and it was discussed in His saying ﴿Allah has sealed over their hearts﴾ [al-Baqara: 7] in Surat al-Baqara.

The sealing, the ṭabʿ, and the akinna (coverings): the creation of misguidance in the heart, that is, the self (nafs).

Al-mutakabbir: one who possesses pride to an intensive degree, and for this reason the form of effort (taka"ulluf) was borrowed.

Al-jabbar: an intensive pattern from al-jabr, which is compulsion. So al-jabbar is one who compels people to do what they do not like, owing to his oppression.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿upon every heart of a proud one﴾ with the heart (qalb) in the genitive construction with (mutakabbir). Abu 'Amr alone, and Ibn Dhakwan from 'Amir, read (qalb) with tanwin, so that (mutakabbir) and (jabbar) are adjectives of (qalb). The attribution of pride and compulsion to the heart is a rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli). What is meant is describing its possessor, as in His saying ﴿for he is sinful, his heart﴾ [al-Baqara: 283], because it is the cause of sin, as one says: "my eye saw and my ear heard."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 40, verse 36:

﴿Pharaoh said, "O Haman, build me a tower so that I may reach the means, the means of the heavens, and look upon the God of Moses. Indeed, I think he is a liar."﴾ [Ghafir: 37].

This is another statement of Pharaoh's, made in a different assembly from the one in which Moses argued with him. For this reason, he introduces it with the conjunction "wa" (and), as we noted regarding the earlier statements listed just before it, and as we noted in Surat al-Qasas. The discussion there already covered, in full, the meaning of this verse according to its apparent sense, and the mention of Haman and the tower was also made there.

Here, however, another interpretation has occurred to me, which is closer to being the intended meaning of the verse. It agrees with what we mentioned there in its aim but differs in its implication. It is that Pharaoh ordered the building of a tower not for the purpose of ascending to the heavens, but so that he could seclude himself in spiritual exercise (riyada) in order to draw revelation from the Lord whom Moses claimed had revealed to him, when he said: ﴿Indeed, it has been revealed to us that the punishment is upon him who denies and turns away﴾ [Ta-Ha: 48]. Retreating to a place isolated from people was a symbol of the priestly practice of seeking inspiration (al-istihya' al-kahnuti) among them. Pharaoh considered himself fit for this, because he claimed to be the son of the gods and the protector of the priests and temples. What occupied him, however, was managing the affairs of the kingdom, so he left the matters of religion to the priests in their temples. In this critical, argumentative situation, he wished to take charge of this matter himself, so that his word would be decisive in denying the existence of any other god, in order to mislead the common folk of his nation. This is because he intended to prepare the ground for announcing the denial of a god other than their gods, so he wanted to take charge of the means of denial himself, just as the Jews had prayer niches (mihrab) for seclusion in worship, as was mentioned earlier in the words of God, Exalted: ﴿So he came out to his people from the prayer niche﴾ [Maryam: 11], and His words: ﴿Whenever Zechariah entered upon her in the prayer niche﴾ [Al 'Imran: 37]. Likewise, the Christian monks took cells (sawami') on the tops of mountains for seclusion in worship. Their existence among these nations indicates that they existed among the nations contemporary with them and those that preceded them.

Al-asbab (the means) is the plural of sabab, and a sabab is that which conveys one to a distant place. So the word sabab is applied to a road, and it is applied to a rope, because people used to reach the tops of palm trees by means of it. What is meant here is the paths of the heavens, as in the verse of Zuhayr:

"Whoever fears the causes of death will be overtaken by them, even if he climbs the causes of the sky by a ladder."

The phrase (asbab al-samawat) is in the accusative as an appositive (badal mutabiq) of His words (al-asbab). This style, of generality followed by detail, was used to arouse curiosity about what is meant by "the means," in order to magnify their importance and the importance of his action, since it is a wondrous matter, and to present it to a soul eager to know it, which is the soul of Haman.

Al-ittila' with the shadda on the ta' is an intensive form of al-tuluw (rising), and al-tuluw means appearing. Most often it is appearing from an elevated place, and whether this is intended or not is known by the transitive particle used with the verb. If it is governed by the preposition "ala," it means appearing from a height. If it is governed by "ila," it means appearing in a general sense.

The majority of readers recite "fa-attali'u" with a damma, as a consequence of (ablugh), as though it were said: "I will reach, then I will look." Hafs from 'Asim recites it with a fatha, as a response to the optative (jawab al-tarajji), treating the expression of hope as the expression of wish (tamanni), although this is not well known. The Basran grammarians deny it, as though it were said: "When I reach, I will look." There may be a subtle point here, which is the metaphorical use of the particle of hope to mean wish, by way of metonymic metaphor (isti'ara taba'iyya), indicating how far away what he hoped for was. The accusative of the verb following it serves as an indication of this metaphor.

Between (ila) and (ilah) there is an imperfect paronomasia (jinas naqis) by a single letter, as occurs twice in the verse of Abu Tammam:

"They extend from hands that grip, grips that hold, while they attack with swords that sever, cutting blades."

The clause ﴿And indeed I think he is a liar﴾ [Ghafir: 37] is a parenthetical insertion (mu'taridah) to forestall the thought that Haman and his people might have that Moses' call had weakened his conviction in his religion and his gods, and that he intended to inquire as a reflective investigator into the proofs of knowledge. So he assured them that he intended by this only to deny what Moses claimed, by the evidence of the senses.

The emphatic particle "inna" reinforced with the lam of commencement (lam al-ibtida') was used to clear himself of the accusation that his minister made against him of shaking his belief in his religion. The meaning is: "I do this so that the lie of Moses may become manifest."

The word "zann" (thought) is used here in the sense of certainty and conviction, and for this reason God named this resolve of his a scheme, in His words: ﴿And the scheme of Pharaoh is nothing but in ruin﴾ [Ghafir: 37].

صفحة ١٤٧ (page 147)

**[Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah Ghafir (40), verse 37]**

﴿And thus was made attractive to Pharaoh the evil of his deeds, and he was averted from the way; and the plot of Pharaoh was nothing but in ruin.﴾

The clause ﴿And thus was made attractive to Pharaoh﴾ is coordinated (*'atf*) with the clause ﴿And Pharaoh said﴾ [Ghafir: 26], to explain the state of his belief and his action after the state of his speech was explained. The meaning is that he uttered a statement arising from misguided belief and inciting corrupt deeds. For this reason, the whole state of Pharaoh is considered, and this clause is not separated from the preceding one, since it was not intended to begin another narrative. This is among what they call the *tawassut* (intermediate position) between the two perfect forms of connection and disconnection (*kamal al-ittisal wa al-infisal*) in the chapter on *fasl* and *wasl* (disjunction and conjunction) in the science of *ma'ani* (rhetoric).

Its opening with ﴿Thus﴾ is like the opening of God's words ﴿And thus We made you a justly balanced community﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143] in Surah al-Baqarah. That is, *like that adornment*, that is, like the deeds of Pharaoh: the evil of his deeds was made attractive to him, with emphasis on the fact that the adornment of his deeds for him reached such strength within its category that no likeness exists to which it can be compared. Whoever wishes to liken it should liken it to itself.

The verb *zuyyina* (was made attractive) is in the passive voice, because the aim is to identify the object of the adornment, not its agent. That is, the adornment of the evil of his deeds occurred within himself, so he took falsehood to be truth and error to be guidance.

The majority of reciters (*al-Jumhur*) read *wa Sadda* with a fatha on the *sad*, which may be considered intransitive, whose present tense is *yasidd* with a kasra on the *sad*, or transitive, whose present tense is *yasuddu* with a damma on the *sad*. That is: he turned away from the way and prevented his people from following the way. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and 'Asim read it with a damma on the *sad*. The discussion of it is the same as the discussion of ﴿The evil of his deeds was made attractive to Pharaoh﴾.

The definiteness of *al-sabil* (the way) is for a known reference, that is, the way of God, or the way of good, or the way of guidance. It may also be that the definiteness indicates perfection within the category, that is, averting from the complete and righteous way.

The clause ﴿And the plot of Pharaoh was nothing but in ruin﴾ is coordinated with the clause ﴿And thus was made attractive to Pharaoh the evil of his deeds﴾. What is meant by his plot is what he commanded regarding the building of the tower and its purpose. It was called a plot because it is an action whose apparent meaning is not what is intended; rather, what is intended is to lead his people to the illusion that Moses, peace be upon him, was a liar.

*Al-tabab* means loss and destruction, and from it comes God's words ﴿Perish the hands of Abu Lahab, and perish﴾ [al-Masad: 1]. The particle of location (*harf al-zarfiyyah*, here *fi*) is a subordinate metaphor (*isti'arah tab'iyyah*) for the meaning of intense involvement, as if it were said: "And the plot of Pharaoh was nothing but in severe ruin." The exception (*al-istithna'*) is from unstated conditions (*ahwal muqaddarah*).

This is a restriction by reversal (*qasr qalb*), placing his people, in their fixation on the benefits of life, in the position of one who thinks these are everlasting benefits.

**[Page 150]**

The *man* in his words, ﴿Whoever does an evil deed﴾, is conditional. The meaning of "except its like" is equivalence in the attribute indicated by the noun "evil deed", which is an evil recompense. That is, one is not recompensed for an evil deed with a good recompense. That is, they should not hope that they may do evil deeds and be recompensed for them with good. In the Sahih of al-Bukhari, it is narrated from Wahb ibn Munabbih, who used to give much admonition to people, that it was said to him, "Your admonition makes people despair." He said, "Am I able to make people despair, when God says, ﴿O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of God﴾ [al-Zumar: 53]? But you love to be given good news of Paradise while holding to the faults of your deeds."

It seems that the Believer restricted the recompense to deeds because they were negligent about deeds, and the most they cared about was holding a good belief about the gods. For this reason, on the walls of Egyptian temples there is found the depiction of judgment in the form of placing the heart of the deceased in the scale, so that his recompense would be according to what his heart's balance reveals.

For this reason you see that the Believer of the family of Pharaoh did not neglect to mention faith after giving great attention to presenting deeds. You see him saying, ﴿Whoever does righteousness, male or female, while being a believer﴾ [al-Nahl: 97]. Faith is the foundation of the structure of salvation. For this reason, disbelief is the foundation of everlasting misery. Every evil deed, its evil and corruption are partial and come to an end, so its punishment was not everlasting. As for disbelief, it is a lasting evil that stays with its owner, because its seat is his heart and belief, and it is constant with him. Therefore its punishment is everlasting, because wisdom requires correspondence between causes and their effects. His words, ﴿Then he will not be recompensed except with its like﴾ indicate that the recompense for disbelief is everlasting misery, because it is like disbelief in being constant with the disbeliever if he dies in disbelief.

With this explanation, we have refuted the view of the Mu'tazila (a theological school) and the Khawarij (a sectarian group) that the grave sinner is equal to the unbeliever in eternal abiding in punishment. This view leads to diminishing the value of faith, and the proofs of the Law, which reach the level of certainty, reject that.

A parallel to this meaning is His words, Exalted is He, ﴿Freeing a slave﴾ [al-Balad: 13], ﴿or feeding on a day of hunger﴾ [al-Balad: 14], ﴿an orphan near of relation﴾ [al-Balad: 15], ﴿or a poor man in misery﴾ [al-Balad: 16], ﴿then he was among those who believed﴾ [al-Balad: 17].

His arrangement of entry into Paradise upon doing righteous deeds means: whoever does righteous deeds and does not do an evil deed, as indicated by its contrast with his words, ﴿Whoever does an evil deed, he will not be recompensed except with its like﴾. For when a believer mixes righteous and evil deeds, there is settlement (*muqassa*), and its explanation is in the details of the Law.

**[Page 151]**

His words, ﴿without account﴾, are a metonymy (*kinaya*) for abundance and plenty of provision, as was mentioned earlier at His words, Exalted is He, ﴿God provides for whom He wills without account﴾ [Al 'Imran: 37], in Surat Al 'Imran.

The *man* in his words, ﴿And whoever does righteous deeds﴾ and so on, is conditional, and its response is ﴿then those will enter Paradise﴾.

The demonstrative noun was used to alert that the one indicated deserves what will be mentioned after the demonstrative, because of the qualities mentioned before the demonstrative, namely doing righteous deeds together with faith. This is in addition to deriving that from its being conditioned upon the conditional sentence. The preposing of the subject over the verbal predicate in the response clause is to convey restriction. The meaning is: if you die in polytheism and in evil deeds, you will not enter it.

His words, ﴿male or female﴾, explain the indefiniteness in *man* regarding the possibility of generality. The phrase ﴿male or female﴾ is meant to cover people in general, by mentioning their two categories, as an explicit indication of the intended generality. It is not meant to convey equality of females with males in recompense for deeds, since that has no relevance in this context. It also contains an implicit reproach to Pharaoh and his close associates, that they will not escape the recompense.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿yadkhulūna al-Janna﴾ with a fatha on the *ya'*. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read it with a damma on the *ya'* and a fatha on the *kha'*. The meaning is one.

[Page 152]

**(Verses 41–43)**

﴿And, O my people, what is [the matter] with me that I call you to salvation, while you call me to the Fire?﴾ ﴿You call me to disbelieve in God and to associate with Him that of which I have no knowledge, while I call you to the Mighty, the Forgiving.﴾ ﴿Undoubtedly, what you call me to has no call [answered] in this world or in the Hereafter, and our return is to God, and the transgressors are the companions of the Fire.﴾

He repeated his address to them, and the report of it was joined by the conjunctive "wa" (and) to indicate that his address included what, in their language, requires that the speech has passed from one purpose to another, and that he would bring in what differs from the beginning of his speech, a difference like that between two conjoined elements in the Arabic language. He would also advance, by leading them step by step along the path of inference, toward the intended aim after the premises. Thus he moved here to rebuke them for something that had come from them toward him: they had followed his admonition with a call on him to abandon it and to hold to their religion. This matter is implicit within the narrative, indicated by the report of his rebuke of them. It is the speech of one who has despaired of their responding to his words, in His saying (in the surah): ﴿So you will remember what I say to you﴾ [Ghafir: 44], and of one who expects their harm, in His saying: ﴿And I entrust my affair to God﴾ [Ghafir: 44], and in His saying, at the end of the narrative: ﴿So God protected him from the evils of what they plotted﴾ [Ghafir: 45].

He here declared and made clear that he had never ceased calling them to follow what Moses had brought, and that in following him lies salvation from the punishment of the Hereafter. Therefore he calls them to salvation in its true sense. The application of "salvation" to what he calls them to is not a figurative usage of the kind called *majaz mursal* (a figure of speech by relation, not by resemblance). Rather, he calls them to the true reality of salvation by means of intermediaries.

The interrogative in ﴿What is [the matter] with me that I call you to salvation﴾ is an interrogative of wonder (*istifham ta'ajjubi*), given its restriction by the circumstantial clause, which is ﴿while you call me to the Fire﴾. So the clause ﴿while you call me to the Fire﴾ stands in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*), with an implied subject, meaning: "while you, [in fact,] call me to the Fire." It is not a coordinate clause, because the basic usage of "*ma li af'alu*" (what is [the matter] with me that I do such-and-such) and "*ma li la af'alu*" (what is [the matter] with me that I do not do such-and-such) and the like is that it is an interrogation about an act or a state that is established for the one indicated by the preposition *li* (to/for), which is the *lam al-ikhtisas* (the lam of specification, i.e., of particular attribution). The meaning of the *lam al-ikhtisas* gives its complement a state, hidden in its cause, which is attached to the complement of the *lam*. Examples are His saying: ﴿What is [the matter] with you, when it is said to you: "Go forth in the way of God," that you cling heavily to the earth?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 38], and ﴿What is [the matter] with me that I do not see the hoopoe?﴾ [al-Naml: 20], and your saying to one who detains you: "What is [the matter] with you?" So the clause that follows the interrogative noun and its predicate is a verbal clause.

The construction "*ma li*" (what is [the matter] with me) and the like is like the construction "*hal laka*" (would you?/do you wish?) and the like, in His saying: ﴿So say: "Would you like to purify yourself?"﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 18], and in the verse of Ka'b ibn Zuhayr:

*Ala balligha 'anni Bujayran risalatan*
*Fa-hal laka fima qultu waykaha hal laka*

[Ah, convey from me a message to Bujayr,
So would you, regarding what I said — woe to you — would you?]

When the context indicates that the true interrogative is not intended, that [interrogation] is directed toward wonder at the state, or toward disapproval, or the like. So the meaning here is that of wonder, that is, that he wonders at their calling him to their religion, given what they had seen of his eagerness to advise them and to call them to salvation, and of the proofs that he had brought them for the soundness of his call and the falsity of their call.

The clause ﴿You call me to disbelieve in God﴾ is an explanation of the clause ﴿while you call me to the Fire﴾, because the call to the Fire is a general and strange matter, so he clarified it by explaining that they were calling him to engage in the causes that bring the punishment of the Fire. The meaning: "You call me to disbelief in God and to associating with Him, in divinity, that of which I have no knowledge."

The meaning of ﴿that of which I have no knowledge﴾ is: "of which I have no knowledge of its validity or of its existence." The statement is a *kinaya* (metonymy) for his knowing that they are not gods, through the method of negating the necessary consequence in order to negate what it necessarily implies.

It is conjoined to this by ﴿while I call you to the Mighty, the Forgiving﴾, so it is an explanation of the general clause ﴿I call you to salvation﴾. The bringing forward of the first-person pronoun in ﴿while I call you﴾ serves to strengthen the assertion, by placing the subject before its verbal predicate.

**(Verses 41–43)**

He would also advance, by leading them step by step along the path of inference, toward the intended aim after the premises. Thus he moved here to rebuke them for something that had come from them toward him: they had followed his admonition with a call on him to abandon it and to hold to their religion. This matter is implicit within the narrative, indicated by the report of his rebuke of them. It is the speech of one who has despaired of their responding to his words, in His saying (in the surah): ﴿So you will remember what I say to you﴾ [Ghafir: 44], and of one who expects their harm, in His saying: ﴿And I entrust my affair to God﴾ [Ghafir: 44], and in His saying, at the end of the narrative: ﴿So God protected him from the evils of what they plotted﴾ [Ghafir: 45].

Its meaning of establishment derives from the fact that what does not cease is lasting, and all of this returns to the meaning of *haqqa* (it is true/established). They also say *la dha jaram*, *la an dha jaram*, *la 'an dha jaram*, and *la jar* without the *mim*, as an apocopation for lightening.

The more evident view is that *jaram* is a noun, not a verb, because if it were a verb it would be past by its form, and then the entry of *la* upon it would be among the features of verbal usage in supplication.

The most common usage is that after it comes *anna* (that) with a shadda and fatha, and then the preposition *fi* (in) is implicitly assumed with it, its deletion being obligatory in most cases. The estimate is: "There is no doubt that what you call me to has no call [answered]."

The explanation of the meaning of *la jaram*, and that *jaram* is a verb or a noun, has already been given at His saying ﴿Undoubtedly they in the Hereafter are the greatest losers﴾ [Hud: 22] in the surah of Hud.

The referent of *ma* (what) is the idols, and the pronoun referring to them is repeated in the singular in His saying ﴿has no [call]﴾, out of consideration for the singular form of the word *ma*.

His saying ﴿Undoubtedly, what you call me to﴾ up to ﴿the companions of the Fire﴾ stands in the position of a causal justification for the two clauses ﴿What is [the matter] with me that I call you to salvation, while you call me to the Fire﴾, because when it is established that there is no call [answered] for the idols in this world, by the evidence of observation, nor in the Hereafter, by the indication of implication, then it is established that they do not save their followers in this world, and their calling or their supplicating does not benefit them. And it is then established that the one hoped for in bestowing favour in this world and the Hereafter is the Lord to whom He calls them. This is a persuasive argument, not a decisive one against the one who disputes the divinity of the Lord of this believer. But he intended to persuade them and to have them retain his argument

[Page 153]

for soon it would become manifest to them that the Lord of Moses has a call [answered] in this world, being confident that they would see Moses' victory over Pharaoh, and would see Pharaoh turned away from killing Moses after his resolve to do so. Then they would know that the One to whom Moses called is the One who disposes of affairs in this world, and therefore they would know that He disposes of affairs in the Hereafter.

The meaning of ﴿has no call [answered]﴾ is the negation that calling upon Him, by worship or by seeking refuge, would be beneficial. It is not the negation of the occurrence of a call, because its occurrence is observed. This is of the type of the saying: "There is no prayer for one who does not recite the Opening of the Book" (the Fatiha). And their saying: "That is not a thing," meaning, not a beneficial thing. By this you know that "*da'wa*" (call) is a verbal noun carrying the meaning of an implicit agent, i.e., "there is no call of a caller," and that the pronoun in "*lahu*" (for it) refers to the relative pronoun *ma*, meaning that it does not possess the call of those who call, i.e., it does not possess the answering of them.

Joined to this clause is the clause ﴿and our return is to God﴾, as a conjunction of the necessary consequence to its necessitating premise. For when it becomes clear that the Lord of Moses, who is named "God," is the One who has the call [answered], it becomes clear that the return, that is, the destination, is to God: in this world by seeking refuge and seeking victory, and in the Hereafter by judgment and recompense.

Had the content of this clause been conjoined by the particle *fa* (then), which indicates derivation, it would have been appropriate for it. But he deviated from that to conjoining it by *wa* (and), out of concern for its matter, so that it would have an independent indication in itself, without the hearer being obliged to investigate what it is connected to. This is because a thing derived from another thing is considered subordinate to it, just as the usulis (jurists of legal theory) said that the answer to a questioner, if not independent in itself, follows the generality of the question.

Similarly, the clause ﴿and the transgressors are the companions of the Fire﴾ [stands in relation] to the derivation of its content from the content of the clause ﴿and our return is to God﴾, because if the destination is to Him, then judgment and recompense are among those who arrive at Him, the rewarded and the punished. So it is necessary that the punished are those who disbelieve in God.

Therefore *al-israf* (transgression) here means excessive disbelief. It also includes what has been said: that what is meant here is the shedding of blood without right, in order to turn Pharaoh away from killing Moses, peace be upon him. But the correct view is that it covers all who commit crimes and sins. The definite article in it is the definite article of genus, which implies totality, and it is an oblique reference to those he is addressing, since they are transgressors in every case: they are transgressors in the excess of their disbelief in the Lord to whom Moses called, and transgressors in what follows from that of disobedience and crimes. So the pronoun of separation in His saying ﴿they are the companions of the Fire﴾ conveys a restriction of an assertive kind, because they are the ones most thoroughly in companionship with the Fire, by reason of eternal abiding, unlike the disobedient believers. This is to bring the speech of the believer into agreement with the reality, since he is presumed to be a prophet or one inspired; otherwise the context is one of distinguishing the state of the believers from the state of the polytheists, and not one of detailing the degrees of recompense in the Hereafter.

This statement is a disengagement from his people and an ending of his address to them. Perhaps he sensed from their demeanour, or from their interrupting his speech with expressions of denial, that they would not be affected by his words. So he challenged them: if they turn away from accepting his counsel, they will regret it when they see the punishment, either in this world, as his words ﴿Indeed I fear for you the day of calling out﴾ [Ghafir: 32] imply. Thus the particle "fa" (so) is a consequence of the sentence ﴿What is [the matter] with me, that I call you to salvation while you call me to the Fire?﴾ [Ghafir: 41].

The verb (sa-tadhkurūna, "you will remember") derives from *al-dhikr* (remembrance), with a *dhāl* that takes a damma, which is the opposite of forgetfulness. That is, "you will remember in your minds": what I am saying to you now will come before the eyes of your insight on the day it is realised. He likened turning away to forgetting, and alluded to forgetting by one of its concomitants in the intellect, namely its mutual exclusion from its opposite, remembering. This is by way of the *makniyya* (implicit metaphor, where the comparison is hidden and only one of its features is named), and in its accompanying indication there is a *isti'āra tab'iyya* (verbal metaphor, a metaphor in the verb).

The meaning is: a punishment will befall you that will remind you of what I am saying; it will surely befall you.

The sentence ﴿And I commit my affair to God﴾ is conjoined to the sentence ﴿What is [the matter] with me, that I call you to salvation while you call me to the Fire?﴾ [Ghafir: 41]. Its purpose is a form of taking justice against them for the evil they have shown towards him. The meaning is: I leave my affair and your affair with me to God, and He will repay every doer for what he has done. This is the speech of one who is fair, so by "my affair" (*amrī*) is meant my concern and my matter.

The meaning of taking justice is supported by his following it with the words ﴿Indeed God is All-Seeing of the servants﴾, giving as the reason for committing his affair with them to God that God has knowledge of the circumstances of all the servants. So the generality of "the servants" includes him and includes his opponents.

In *al-Kashshaf* it says: "His saying ﴿And I commit my affair to God﴾ is because they had threatened him." End of quote. He means that this contains an indication of that, with the help of what follows it.

*Al-'ibād* (the servants) means the people; the term "servants" is applied to them as a collective. I have not seen "*'abd*" (servant) applied to a single human being, nor "*'abīd*" (slaves) applied to people.

*Al-baṣīr* means the one who is informed, to whom no matter is hidden. The particle *bāʾ* here is for transitivity, as in His saying ﴿So she saw him from afar﴾ [al-Qasas: 11]. When they want to make the verb of seeing transitive without the particle, they say *ubṣiruhu*.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 40, verses 45–46:

﴿So Allah protected him from the evils of what they schemed, and there befell the family of Pharaoh the worst of punishment.﴾ ﴿The Fire; they are exposed to it morning and evening, and on the day the Hour arises: "Admit the family of Pharaoh into the most severe punishment!"﴾

The clause ﴿So Allah protected him﴾ is a consequence that indicates they had concealed a scheme against him. Calling it a scheme (makr) indicates that they did not make him aware of it, and that Allah took responsibility for his protection because he had entrusted his affair to Him.

The meaning is: Allah delivered him. It is possible that he was saved along with Moses and the Children of Israel and went out with them, and it is possible that he fled with Pharaoh and they did not find him.

The particle (ma) is verbal-masdariyyah (a kind of maṣdariyyah, turning the following into a verbal noun). The meaning is: "the evils of their scheming." The construction of "evils" (sayyi'at) with "scheming" (makr) is an explanative genitive (idafah bayaniyyah), and here it has the force of attributing a quality to the thing it qualifies, since scheming is evil. He used the plural "evils" in view of the multiplicity of the kinds of scheming they devised by night (bayyatu-hu).

Haqa (ḥāqa) means: it encompassed. The "punishment" (al-'adhab) here is drowning. The definite article is for a known reference, because it is well known and familiar.

Mention of it has preceded in the surahs revealed before this surah.

The suitability of the verb ḥāqa for that punishment is that it is among the things that truly encompass. Drowning is "the worst of punishment" because the drowning person is tormented by the restraint of breath for a period while he floats on the water and sinks into it, the terror of the waves frightens him, and he is certain of destruction; then he becomes prey to fish, while alive and dead, and that is pain in life and disgrace after death, by which they are mentioned among people.

His saying ﴿The Fire; they are exposed to it morning and evening﴾ may be a clause in apposition (badal) to the clause ﴿there befell the family of Pharaoh the worst of punishment﴾. In that case, "the Fire" is the subject (mubtada') and the clause ﴿they are exposed to it﴾ is its predicate (khabar), and the whole clause of subject and predicate is a comprehensive apposition (badal ishtimal) for the clause ﴿there befell the family of Pharaoh the worst of punishment﴾, because when "the worst of punishment" is intended to mean drowning, it includes their death, and their death includes their being exposed to the Fire morning and evening. So what is mentioned is two punishments: the punishment of this world, which is drowning and what accompanies it of punishment before the punishment of the Day of Resurrection.

It is also possible that "the Fire" is a single appositive (badal mufrad) for "the worst of punishment," a full apposition (badal mutabaqah), and the clause ﴿they are exposed to it﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from "the Fire." In that case, what is mentioned in the verse is one punishment, and the punishment of drowning is not mentioned.

On both interpretations, what is mentioned in the verse is a punishment before the punishment of the Day of Resurrection, and that is what is mentioned after it with His saying ﴿and on the day the Hour arises: "Admit the family of Pharaoh into the most severe punishment!"﴾

The basic meaning of 'arḍ (exposure) is: showing something to one who sees it, for encouragement or warning. It transitively takes the thing displayed directly, and the one for whose sake it is displayed with the particle "ʿalā" (upon/before). This requires that the one presented before must be a rational being, or one treated as rational. This usage may be reversed for the purpose of emphasis, as in the Arabs' saying "I presented the she-camel to the watering-trough" (ʿaraḍtu al-nāqata ʿalā al-ḥawḍ), whereas its proper form is "I presented the watering-trough to the she-camel." This is the usage in this verse, and in His saying in Surat al-Aḥqāf ﴿And on the day those who disbelieved are exposed to the Fire﴾ [al-Aḥqāf: 20]. The scholars of rhetoric (ʿulamāʾ al-maʿānī) counted inversion (qalb) among the types of speech deviating from the apparent requirement, and they exemplified it with the Arabs' saying "I presented the she-camel to the watering-trough." They differed on counting it among the elegant figures of eloquent speech: Abu ʿUbayda, al-Fārisī and al-Sakkākī counted it among them, while the majority did not accept it. Al-Qazwīnī said: if it includes a subtle consideration, it is accepted; otherwise it is rejected.

In my view, both usages are according to the apparent requirement, and ʿarḍ has become frequent in the sense of passing before, without intent of encouragement, as one says: "the army was reviewed (ʿuriḍa) before its commander," and "the commander reviewed it (istaʿraḍahu)." Perhaps its origin is a metaphor that became equal to the literal sense, so there is no inversion in the two verses, nor in the Arabs' saying "I presented the she-camel to the watering-trough," there is no inversion. It is said: "the sons of so-and-so were exposed to the sword" (ʿuriḍa banū fulān ʿalā al-sayf), when they were killed by it. In al-Kashshāf, the verse of al-Aḥqāf is explained according to their saying: "he was exposed to the sword" (ʿuriḍa ʿalā al-sayf).

The meaning of their exposure to the Fire is that their spirits witness the places prepared for them in Hell. This is what the hadith of ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar in the Ṣaḥīḥ clarifies. He said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When one of you dies, his seat is shown to him morning and evening: if he is among the people of Paradise, then [it is shown as] of the people of Paradise; and if he is among the people of the Fire, then [it is shown as] of the people of the Fire. It is said: 'This is your seat, until Allah resurrects you on the Day of Resurrection.'"

His saying ﴿morning and evening﴾ is a metonymy (kināyah) for continuity, because time is never free of these two periods.

His saying ﴿and on the day the Hour arises: "Admit the family of Pharaoh into the most severe punishment!"﴾ is a mention of the punishment of the everlasting Hereafter. That is, it is said: "Admit the family of Pharaoh into the most severe punishment." It is known from the punishment of the family of Pharaoh that Pharaoh is included in that punishment by the indication of implication (dalālat al-fahwā).

Nafi', Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Hafs, Abu Ja'far and Ya'qub read ﴿adkhilū﴾ with a hamzat qat' (cut hamza) and kasrah on the kha'. The rest read it with a hamzat wasl (connecting hamza) and ḍammah on the kha', meaning that the address is directed to the family of Pharaoh, and that "the family of Pharaoh" is a vocative (munādā) with the particle of address omitted.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (*al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir*) on Surah 40, verses 47–48:

﴿And when they dispute in the Fire, the weak will say to those who were arrogant, "Indeed, we were your followers, so will you relieve us of a portion of the Fire?"﴾ ﴿Those who were arrogant will say, "Indeed, we are all in it. Indeed, Allah has already judged between the servants."﴾

It is permissible for *idh* (إذْ, "when") to be governed by a suppressed *udhkur* (اذْكُرْ, "remember"), so that it is coordinated (*'atf*) with the clause ﴿And warn them of the Day of the Approaching﴾ [Ghafir: 18]. The pronoun would then refer to ﴿those who dispute concerning the signs of Allah without authority﴾ [Ghafir: 56]. What lies between this and that is an interjection (*i'tiraD*) and a digression (*istitrad*), because the purpose of the passage is to admonish the polytheists with the examples of the earlier disbelieving nations. When that was complete, the discourse returned to them. This indicates explicit threat (*wa'id*) to the polytheists after the parables had been struck for them, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And for the disbelievers are similar things﴾ [Muhammad: 10]. The admonition of the polytheists in this manner recurs in the Qur'an, such as His saying: ﴿When those who were followed disassociate themselves from those who followed﴾ [al-Baqarah: 166], the verse in Surah al-Baqarah, and His saying: ﴿Their first will say to their last, "Our Lord, these misled us, so give them a double punishment of the Fire"﴾ [al-A'raf: 38], the verse in Surah al-A'raf.

It is also permissible that ﴿and when they dispute﴾ is coordinated with the clause ﴿And on the Day the Hour is established: "Admit the family of Pharaoh into the most severe punishment"﴾ [Ghafir: 46], because *idh* and *yawma* (يَوْمَ, "the day") are both adverbs of time with the meaning of *hina* (حِينَ, "when"). The meaning would then be: "And when the Hour is established, it will be said: 'Admit the family of Pharaoh into the most severe punishment,' and when the people of the Fire dispute, and the weak say..." etc.

He associated ﴿the weak will say﴾ with the particle *fa* (فَ, "then/so") to indicate that this speech arises from their disputing in the Fire, while also indicating that this is in the sense of what is related to *idh*. This is one of the usages of *fa* which the grammarians call *za'ida* (زَائِدَة, "superfluous"). Among those who affirmed its superfluity were a group including al-Akhfash, al-Farra', al-A'lam and Ibn Burhan, and it is transmitted from their Basran companions. The pronoun in *yatahajjun* (يَتَحاجُّونَ, "they dispute") on this reading refers to the family of Pharaoh, because this is contradicted by His saying: ﴿And those in the Fire will say to the keepers of Hell, "Call upon your Lord"﴾ [Ghafir: 49], and His saying: ﴿Did there not come to you your messengers with clear proofs?﴾ [Ghafir: 50]. Yet only one messenger came to the family of Pharaoh, Musa (عَلَيْهِ السَّلامُ). Therefore the pronoun of *yatahajjun* refers to something known from the context, namely the people of the Fire.

*Tahajj* (التَّحَاجُّ, "mutual disputing") is arguing from two or more sides, that is, each party establishing its proof. It implies that there is disagreement between the disputants, since a proof (*hujjah*) is the confirmation of a claim to remove doubt about its validity.

The weak (*al-du'afa'*, الضُّعَفَاءُ) are the common people who have no authority over the affairs of the community. Those who were arrogant (*alladhina istakbaru*, الَّذِينَ اسْتَكْبَرُوا) are the leaders of the people, that is, those who were extremely proud. The *sin* and *ta'* in *istakbaru* are for emphasis (*mubalagha*, "intensification").

The weak's saying this to the great may be understood literally, since it arises from their habit of turning to them for their needs while they were in the world, so they assumed that the great would manage their affairs in that place. For this reason, those who were arrogant replied with what indicates that they are today equal in helplessness and lack of resource, saying: ﴿Indeed, we are all in it﴾, meaning: if we could relieve you, we would have relieved ourselves.

The placement of their saying ﴿Indeed, we were your followers﴾ before the request for lightening the punishment is a preface to the request, aimed at directing and justifying it, and reminding them of the allegiance that existed between them in the world. Allah inspires them with this speech so that the arrogant's inability to benefit their followers is exposed, as a humiliation for them in recompense for the self-importance with which they used to magnify themselves in the world.

It is also possible that the weak's saying is not used in its literal sense of urging lightening of the punishment, but is used for rebuke, meaning: "You used to call us to the religion of polytheism, and the outcome of that was that we came to be in this punishment. So are you able to repel it from us?"

The emphasis of ﴿Indeed, we were your followers﴾ with *inna* (إنَّ, "indeed") is for attention to the information, not to refute a denial.

*Tabi'* (التَّبَعُ, "followers") is a noun for one who follows another; it is used for both singular and plural, and it is like *khadam* (خَدَمٌ, "servants") and *hashram* (حَشَمٌ, "retinue"), because its origin is a verbal noun (*masdar*), so it is equal for singular and plural. It was said: *tabi'* is a plural that does not apply to the singular, so it is then one of the rare plurals.

The interrogative in His saying ﴿so will you relieve us﴾ is used for urging and reproach for their abandoning them and not caring for the punishment they are in.

The nominal sentence, which indicates permanence, is used: meaning, "Is it part of your nature that you relieve us?"

*Mughnun* (مُغْنُونَ, "relieving") is an active participle (*ism fa'il*, اسْمُ فَاعِلٍ) from *aghna* (أغْنى), with *ghana'* (غَناءً) meaning benefit and sufficiency.

*Nasib* (النَّصِيبُ, "portion") is the share or portion of something. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿For men is a share of what the parents and close relatives leave﴾ [al-Nisa': 7], up to His saying ﴿an obligatory share﴾ [al-Nisa': 7].

*Mughnun* has been understood to include the meaning of *dafi'un* (دَافِعُونَ, "repelling") and *radduna* (رَادُّونَ, "returning"), so it takes an object, namely *nasiban*, meaning a part of the heat of the Fire, of indeterminate quantity in its intensity. *Min al-nar* (مِنَ النَّارِ, "from the Fire") is an explanation of *nasiban*, like His saying: ﴿Will you relieve us of any of the punishment of Allah?﴾ [Ibrahim: 21]. They are content with whatever lightens the severity of the Fire's heat for them, and they do not hope to leave it.

It is also permissible that *mughnun* retains its own meaning without inclusion, and *nasiban* is in the accusative as an absolute object (*maf'ul mutlaq*, المَفْعُولُ المُطْلَقُ) of *mughnun*, the estimate being *ghanna'an nasiban*, meaning "any relief at all, even if little." *Min al-nar* is then related to *mughnun*, like His saying: ﴿And I will not avail you anything against Allah﴾ [Yusuf: 67].

It is also permissible that *nasib* means a part of the periods of the punishment, in which case there is an elision of a modifying noun, its estimate being: "a portion of the duration of the Fire."

Since the reply of those who were arrogant to those who were oppressed proceeds in the manner of conversation, the verb *qala* (قَالَ, "he said") was stripped of a conjunction, following the manner of conversation, as has been mentioned more than once.

The meaning of their saying ﴿Indeed, we are all in it﴾ is: we and you are equal in being in the Fire, so how do you hope that we could repel from you any part of the punishment?

On the reading that the saying of the weak, ﴿Indeed, we were your followers﴾ to its end, is a rebuke and blame directed at their leaders, the saying of the leaders ﴿Indeed, we are all in it﴾ is an acknowledgment of error, meaning: "Leave off your blame and rebuke of us, for it is enough that we are with you in the Fire." The emphasis of the speech with *inna* is for attention to establishing it, or because it treats those who demanded from them relief from the Fire's punishment, while seeing that they are in the same punishment, as if they were thought not to be in the Fire. In this treatment there is a kind of rebuke: "Do you not see us in the Fire just like you? So how can we relieve you?"

*Kullun* (كُلٌّ, "all") is nominative as the subject (*mubtada'*, مُبْتَدَأٌ), and its predicate is *fiha* (فِيها, "in it"). The sentence formed by the subject and predicate is the predicate (*khabar*, خَبَرٌ) of *inna*. The tanwin of *kullun* is the tanwin of compensation (*tanwin 'iwad*, تَنْوِينُ عِوَضٍ) for the omitted genitive complement, since the estimate is: "Indeed, all of us are in it."

The clause ﴿Indeed, Allah has already judged between the servants﴾ functions as a substitute of inclusion (*badal al-ishtimal*, بَدَلُ الِاشْتِمالِ) for the clause ﴿Indeed, we are all in it﴾. Both clauses are a reply to them that despairs them of obtaining any relief.

The meaning is: we are equal in the punishment, and this is the judgment of Allah, so there is no hope of escape from His judgment, for each party has been recompensed according to what it deserves.

The generality in this second clause of the judgment's relation to the servants makes this substitute function as a tadhyil (التَّذْيِيلُ, "concluding generalization"), meaning: Allah has judged among all the servants by the recompense of their deeds, and our share of that judgment was this punishment.

Thus the word *bayna* (بَيْنَ, "between") here is used in its literal meaning, the middle place. That is, His judgment and decree took place in their assembly, which was attended by the one judged against, the one judged for, and the one who was not subject to judgment because he is among the people of honour in Paradise. Therefore *bayna* here does not have the same function as *bayna* in His saying: ﴿So judge between them by what Allah has revealed﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 48], for there it is used figuratively to mean distinguishing between the righteous and the wrongdoer.

In this verse there is a lesson for the leaders and commanders of nations, that they should beware of casting themselves into the pits of loss, thereby leading those who follow them into those pits. If their advancing and gambling with themselves and their nations was with knowledge of its consequences, they deserve blame and disgrace in this world and doubled punishment in the Hereafter, since it is not right for them to incite peoples who entrusted their affairs to their leaders out of good opinion of them, that they should betray the trust placed in them, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And they will surely carry their burdens and burdens along with their burdens﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 13]. And if their thrusting themselves into the narrows of leadership was out of ignorance of the consequences of their deficiency and failure, then they are to be blamed for not making sure of their competence to manage the community, so that they stumble with it blindly until they slip with it and fall with it from distant heights, becoming dust and meeting a blazing Hell in the Hereafter.

**[Page 160]**

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (*al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir*) on Surah 40, verses 47–48:

﴿And when they dispute in the Fire, the weak will say to those who were arrogant, "Indeed, we were your followers, so will you relieve us of a portion of the Fire?"﴾ ﴿Those who were arrogant will say, "Indeed, we are all in it. Indeed, Allah has already judged between the servants."﴾

It is permissible for *idh* (إذْ, "when") to be governed by a suppressed *udhkur* (اذْكُرْ, "remember"), so that it is coordinated (*'atf*) with the clause ﴿And warn them of the Day of the Approaching﴾ [Ghafir: 18]. The pronoun would then refer to ﴿those who dispute concerning the signs of Allah without authority﴾ [Ghafir: 56]. What lies between this and that is an interjection (*i'tiraD*) and a digression (*istitrad*), because the purpose of the passage is to admonish the polytheists with the examples of the earlier disbelieving nations. When that was complete, the discourse returned to them. This indicates explicit threat (*wa'id*) to the polytheists after the parables had been struck for them, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And for the disbelievers are similar things﴾ [Muhammad: 10]. The admonition of the polytheists in this manner recurs in the Qur'an, such as His saying: ﴿When those who were followed disassociate themselves from those who followed﴾ [al-Baqarah: 166], the verse in Surah al-Baqarah, and His saying: ﴿Their first will say to their last, "Our Lord, these misled us, so give them a double punishment of the Fire"﴾ [al-A'raf: 38], the verse in Surah al-A'raf.

It is also permissible that ﴿and when they dispute﴾ is coordinated with the clause ﴿And on the Day the Hour is established: "Admit the family of Pharaoh into the most severe punishment"﴾ [Ghafir: 46], because *idh* and *yawma* (يَوْمَ, "the day") are both adverbs of time with the meaning of *hina* (حِينَ, "when"). The meaning would then be: "And when the Hour is established, it will be said: 'Admit the family of Pharaoh into the most severe punishment,' and when the people of the Fire dispute, and the weak say..." etc.

He associated ﴿the weak will say﴾ with the particle *fa* (فَ, "then/so") to indicate that this speech arises from their disputing in the Fire, while also indicating that this is in the sense of what is related to *idh*. This is one of the usages of *fa* which the grammarians call *za'ida* (زَائِدَة, "superfluous"). Among those who affirmed its superfluity were a group including al-Akhfash, al-Farra', al-A'lam and Ibn Burhan, and it is transmitted from their Basran companions. The pronoun in *yatahajjun* (يَتَحاجُّونَ, "they dispute") on this reading refers to the family of Pharaoh, because this is contradicted by His saying: ﴿And those in the Fire will say to the keepers of Hell, "Call upon your Lord"﴾ [Ghafir: 49], and His saying: ﴿Did there not come to you your messengers with clear proofs?﴾ [Ghafir: 50]. Yet only one messenger came to the family of Pharaoh, Musa (عَلَيْهِ السَّلامُ). Therefore the pronoun of *yatahajjun* refers to something known from the context, namely the people of the Fire.

*Tahajj* (التَّحَاجُّ, "mutual disputing") is arguing from two or more sides, that is, each party establishing its proof. It implies that there is disagreement between the disputants, since a proof (*hujjah*) is the confirmation of a claim to remove doubt about its validity.

The weak (*al-du'afa'*, الضُّعَفَاءُ) are the common people who have no authority over the affairs of the community. Those who were arrogant (*alladhina istakbaru*, الَّذِينَ اسْتَكْبَرُوا) are the leaders of the people, that is, those who were extremely proud. The *sin* and *ta'* in *istakbaru* are for emphasis (*mubalagha*, "intensification").

The weak's saying this to the great may be understood literally, since it arises from their habit of turning to them for their needs while they were in the world, so they assumed that the great would manage their affairs in that place. For this reason, those who were arrogant replied with what indicates that they are today equal in helplessness and lack of resource, saying: ﴿Indeed, we are all in it﴾, meaning: if we could relieve you, we would have relieved ourselves.

The placement of their saying ﴿Indeed, we were your followers﴾ before the request for lightening the punishment is a preface to the request, aimed at directing and justifying it, and reminding them of the allegiance that existed between them in the world. Allah inspires them with this speech so that the arrogant's inability to benefit their followers is exposed, as a humiliation for them in recompense for the self-importance with which they used to magnify themselves in the world.

It is also possible that the weak's saying is not used in its literal sense of urging lightening of the punishment, but is used for rebuke, meaning: "You used to call us to the religion of polytheism, and the outcome of that was that we came to be in this punishment. So are you able to repel it from us?"

The emphasis of ﴿Indeed, we were your followers﴾ with *inna* (إنَّ, "indeed") is for attention to the information, not to refute a denial.

*Tabi'* (التَّبَعُ, "followers") is a noun for one who follows another; it is used for both singular and plural, and it is like *khadam* (خَدَمٌ, "servants") and *hashram* (حَشَمٌ, "retinue"), because its origin is a verbal noun (*masdar*), so it is equal for singular and plural. It was said: *tabi'* is a plural that does not apply to the singular, so it is then one of the rare plurals.

The interrogative in His saying ﴿so will you relieve us﴾ is used for urging and reproach for their abandoning them and not caring for the punishment they are in.

[Page 164]

When they found no opening for lightening the punishment on the side of their leaders, and their leaders disowned that, or admitted their error and their having led their people and themselves into ruin, they all colluded in trying to seek a lightening of the punishment through a supplication to the guardians of Hell. Therefore the speech is attributed to "those who are in the Fire," meaning all of them, both the weak and those who were arrogant.

*Khazanah* is the plural of *khazin*, which is one who guards what is kept in a place, whether wealth or goods. The guardians of Hell (*khazanat Jahannam*) are the angels entrusted with what it contains of fire, its fuel, and those being punished in it, and they are charged with managing what the abode of punishment and its people contain. For this reason they are called "guardians of the Fire," because guarding does not pertain to the Fire itself but to what it contains. Thus the mention here of "Jahannam" is not a case of putting the apparent noun in place of the pronoun, since it would not be proper to attach "guardians" to "the Fire." Had the word "Jahannam" been mentioned previously, he would have said "its guardians," as in His words in Surat al-Mulk: ﴿And for those who disbelieved in their Lord is the punishment of Hell, and it is an evil destination﴾ [al-Mulk: 6] up to His words ﴿Its guardians will ask them﴾ [al-Mulk: 8], for the pronoun refers to *Jahannam*, not to *al-Nar*.

In *al-Kashshaf* it is said that it is the placing of the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun, for the sake of inspiring awe through the word "Jahannam." The approach we have followed is clearer.

In attaching "Rabb" (Lord) to the pronoun of the addressees there is a kind of encouragement to supplicate, meaning: because you are closer to His answering you.

Since they thought the guardians more likely to be answered, they asked for a lightening of the punishment for one day out of the periods of punishment, and that is more beneficial to them than lightening the intensity of the Fire, which they asked of their arrogant leaders.

*Yukhaffif* is in the jussive after the imperative of supplication. Perhaps it is by implying the imperative *lam* because of its frequent use. Some grammarians make it jussive as an answer to the imperative, to establish causation. In this case there is an indication that those in the Fire were certain that if the guardians of Hell supplicated to God, He would respond to them. This jussive is common after an imperative of speech or what has its meaning, for this reason, and its proper form is the nominative or the explicit *lam* of command. The discussion of it was given earlier at His words ﴿Say to My servants who have believed: they should establish prayer﴾ [Ibrahim: 31] in Surat Ibrahim.

*Yukhaffif* is construed with the sense of *yanquss* (diminish), so *yawman* is in the accusative, or it is by assuming an omitted genitive, meaning "the punishment of a day," that is, the quantity of a day. *Yawman* is in the accusative as the direct object of *yukhaffif*.

[Page 165]

The "day" is a metaphor for a small amount, meaning: lighten it for us even for a short time.

And ﴿from the punishment﴾ is an explanation of *yawman*, since by it is meant a quantity, so it needed explanation in the manner of a specification. It is also permissible for it to be connected to *yukhaffif*.

The guardians of Hell's reply to them is in the form of a rhetorical interrogation (*istifham taqriri*), whose purpose is to make manifest the evil of their own conduct, since they did not follow the messengers until they fell into this punishment, and to make them regret what they had squandered in their worldly life of the means of salvation from punishment. It is a comprehensive statement that contains rebuke, reproach, regret, and an explanation of the reason for the refusal to supplicate for them, and a reminder to them that the messengers had warned them about abiding forever in punishment.

As for the *waw* in His words ﴿Did not your messengers come to you with clear proofs?﴾, the commentators did not dwell on its position. It is the *waw* of conjunction, by which the guardians of Hell joined their speech to the speech of those in the Fire, in the manner of a speaker conjoining one statement to another that came from the addressee, implying that it should be part of his speech and that he should not neglect it. This is what is called *'atf al-talqin* (the conjunction of prompting), as in His words ﴿He said: Indeed I will make you a leader for the people. He said: and from my offspring﴾ [al-Baqarah: 124]. For when the people of the Fire recall this, they will know the soundness of the guardians of Hell's disavowal of intercession for them. The branching of "so supplicate" upon this is evident under both interpretations.

The interrogative hamzah is placed before its original position under both interpretations, because it must head its clause.

The clause ﴿And the supplication of the disbelievers is only in error﴾ may be part of the guardians' speech, as a concluding remark that makes clear that their saying "so supplicate" is used to draw attention to error, meaning: your supplication did not benefit you, because the supplication of the disbelievers is in error. The *waw* is parenthetical. It may also be part of God's speech, as a concluding and parenthetical remark.

*Al-bayyinat* means the clear proofs and the explicit calls to follow guidance. So they had no choice but to acknowledge the coming of the messengers to them with clear proofs, and they said: "Yes." Then the guardians of Hell replied by disowning any supplication to God on their behalf, leaving their affair to themselves, with their saying "so supplicate," as a consequence of their acknowledgment that the messengers had come to them with clear proofs.

[Page 166]

The meaning of its being a consequence of that is that it follows from it in terms of its implicit meaning, which is the disowning of supplicating on their behalf. That is: just as you turned away from the messengers, acting autonomously by your own opinions, so now take charge of your own affairs and supplicate yourselves. For whoever turns away from the coolness (of the Fire) must also bear its heat. Thus the imperative in "so supplicate" is used to express permission or equality, and in it is an indication of the error of those who asked.

The addition of the verb of existence (*kana*) in ﴿Did not your messengers come to you?﴾ serves to indicate that the coming of messengers to nations is an established and confirmed matter, since the verb of existence indicates existence in the sense of being realized. As for its indicating that the verb of coming occurred in past time, that is derived from the negating *lam* in the past.

*Al-dalal* is loss, and its original meaning is missing the way, as in His words ”﴿When we have gone astray in the earth, shall we indeed be in a new creation?﴾ [al-Sajdah: 10]“.

The meaning is: their supplication does not benefit them and is not accepted from them. Whether the statement ﴿And the supplication of the disbelievers is only in error﴾ is part of the speech of the angels or of God Most High, it necessarily implies the generality of their supplication, because the attached verbal noun is among the forms of generality. Thus it entails that the supplication of the disbelievers is not accepted in the Hereafter or in this world, since the generality of the essences entails the generality of times and places.

As for what might give the impression that the supplication of the disbelievers is answered, such as His words ﴿Say: Who rescues you from the darkness of the land and the sea, when you call upon Him humbly and secretly, saying: If He rescues us from this, we will surely be among the thankful?﴾ [al-An'am: 63] ﴿Say: God rescues you from them﴾ [al-An'am: 64], and His words ﴿They called upon God, sincere to Him in religion: If You rescue us from this, we will surely be among the thankful﴾ [Yunus: 22] ﴿But when He rescued them, behold, they transgressed upon the earth without right﴾ [Yunus: 23], it is evident that these do not indicate an answer as an honour, but rather serve to record their disbelief and denial. It may be imagined in some circumstances that a disbeliever supplicates and what he asked for occurs, but that is only because his supplication coincided with the time of the answering of another's supplication from among the righteous. And how could the supplication of a disbeliever be answered, when the Prophet ﷺ has reported the improbability of answering the supplication of a believer who eats what is unlawful and wears what is unlawful, in the hadith of Muslim from Abu Hurayrah: "The Messenger of God mentioned a man who travels far, dishevelled and dusty, who stretches out his hands to the sky, saying: O Lord, O Lord, while his food is unlawful, his drink is unlawful, and he is nourished with the unlawful. How then could he be answered?"

For this reason God did not say "when He answered their supplication," but said "when He rescued them," meaning either because He had decreed their rescue before they supplicated, or because their supplication coincided with the supplication of some believers.

It is a comprehensive statement that contains rebuke, reproach, regret, and an explanation of the reason for the refusal to supplicate for them, and a reminder to them that the messengers had warned them about abiding forever in punishment.

As for the *waw* in His words ﴿Did not your messengers come to you with clear proofs?﴾, the commentators did not dwell on its position. It is the *waw* of conjunction, by which the guardians of Hell joined their speech to the speech of those in the Fire, in the manner of a speaker conjoining one statement to another that came from the addressee, implying that it should be part of his speech and that he should not neglect it. This is what is called *'atf al-talqin* (the conjunction of prompting), as in His words ﴿He said: Indeed I will make you a leader for the people. He said: and from my offspring﴾ [al-Baqarah: 124]. For when the people of the Fire recall this, they will know the soundness of the guardians of Hell's disavowal of intercession for them. The branching of "so supplicate" upon this is evident under both interpretations.

The interrogative hamzah is placed before its original position under both interpretations, because it must head its clause.

The clause ﴿And the supplication of the disbelievers is only in error﴾ may be part of the guardians' speech, as a concluding remark that makes clear that their saying "so supplicate" is used to draw attention to error, meaning: your supplication did not benefit you, because the supplication of the disbelievers is in error. The *waw* is parenthetical. It may also be part of God's speech, as a concluding and parenthetical remark.

*Al-bayyinat* means the clear proofs and the explicit calls to follow guidance. So they had no choice but to acknowledge the coming of the messengers to them with clear proofs, and they said: "Yes." Then the guardians of Hell replied by disowning any supplication to God on their behalf, leaving their affair to themselves, with their saying "so supplicate," as a consequence of their acknowledgment that the messengers had come to them with clear proofs.

[Page 166]

The meaning of its being a consequence of that is that it follows from it in terms of its implicit meaning, which is the disowning of supplicating on their behalf. That is: just as you turned away from the messengers, acting autonomously by your own opinions, so now take charge of your own affairs and supplicate yourselves. For whoever turns away from the coolness (of the Fire) must also bear its heat. Thus the imperative in "so supplicate" is used to express permission or equality, and in it is an indication of the error of those who asked.

The addition of the verb of existence (*kana*) in ﴿Did not your messengers come to you?﴾ serves to indicate that the coming of messengers to nations is an established and confirmed matter, since the verb of existence indicates existence in the sense of being realized. As for its indicating that the verb of coming occurred in past time, that is derived from the negating *lam* in the past.

*Al-dalal* is loss, and its original meaning is missing the way, as in His words ”﴿When we have gone astray in the earth, shall we indeed be in a new creation?﴾ [al-Sajdah: 10]“.

The meaning is: their supplication does not benefit them and is not accepted from them. Whether the statement ﴿And the supplication of the disbelievers is only in error﴾ is part of the speech of the angels or of God Most High, it necessarily implies the generality of their supplication, because the attached verbal noun is among the forms of generality. Thus it entails that the supplication of the disbelievers is not accepted in the Hereafter or in this world, since the generality of the essences entails the generality of times and places.

As for what might give the impression that the supplication of the disbelievers is answered, such as His words ﴿Say: Who rescues you from the darkness of the land and the sea, when you call upon Him humbly and secretly, saying: If He rescues us from this, we will surely be among the thankful?﴾ [al-An'am: 63] ﴿Say: God rescues you from them﴾ [al-An'am: 64], and His words ﴿They called upon God, sincere to Him in religion: If You rescue us from this, we will surely be among the thankful﴾ [Yunus: 22] ﴿But when He rescued them, behold, they transgressed upon the earth without right﴾ [Yunus: 23], it is evident that these do not indicate an answer as an honour, but rather serve to record their disbelief and denial. It may be imagined in some circumstances that a disbeliever supplicates and what he asked for occurs, but that is only because his supplication coincided with the time of the answering of another's supplication from among the righteous. And how could the supplication of a disbeliever be answered, when the Prophet ﷺ has reported the improbability of answering the supplication of a believer who eats what is unlawful and wears what is unlawful, in the hadith of Muslim from Abu Hurayrah: "The Messenger of God mentioned a man who travels far, dishevelled and dusty, who stretches out his hands to the sky, saying: O Lord, O Lord, while his food is unlawful, his drink is unlawful, and he is nourished with the unlawful. How then could he be answered?"

For this reason God did not say "when He answered their supplication," but said "when He rescued them," meaning either because He had decreed their rescue before they supplicated, or because their supplication coincided with the supplication of some believers.

[Page 164]

When they found no opening for lightening the punishment on the side of their leaders, and their leaders disowned that, or admitted their error and their having led their people and themselves into ruin, they all colluded in trying to seek a lightening of the punishment through a supplication to the guardians of Hell. Therefore the speech is attributed to "those who are in the Fire," meaning all of them, both the weak and those who were arrogant.

*Khazanah* is the plural of *khazin*, which is one who guards what is kept in a place, whether wealth or goods. The guardians of Hell (*khazanat Jahannam*) are the angels entrusted with what it contains of fire, its fuel, and those being punished in it, and they are charged with managing what the abode of punishment and its people contain. For this reason they are called "guardians of the Fire," because guarding does not pertain to the Fire itself but to what it contains. Thus the mention here of "Jahannam" is not a case of putting the apparent noun in place of the pronoun, since it would not be proper to attach "guardians" to "the Fire." Had the word "Jahannam" been mentioned previously, he would have said "its guardians," as in His words in Surat al-Mulk: ﴿And for those who disbelieved in their Lord is the punishment of Hell, and it is an evil destination﴾ [al-Mulk: 6] up to His words ﴿Its guardians will ask them﴾ [al-Mulk: 8], for the pronoun refers to *Jahannam*, not to *al-Nar*.

In *al-Kashshaf* it is said that it is the placing of the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun, for the sake of inspiring awe through the word "Jahannam." The approach we have followed is clearer.

In attaching "Rabb" (Lord) to the pronoun of the addressees there is a kind of encouragement to supplicate, meaning: because you are closer to His answering you.

Since they thought the guardians more likely to be answered, they asked for a lightening of the punishment for one day out of the periods of punishment, and that is more beneficial to them than lightening the intensity of the Fire, which they asked of their arrogant leaders.

Some grammarians make it jussive as an answer to the imperative, to establish causation. In this case there is an indication that those in the Fire were certain that if the guardians of Hell supplicated to God, He would respond to them. This jussive is common after an imperative of speech or what has its meaning, for this reason, and its proper form is the nominative or the explicit *lam* of command. The discussion of it was given earlier at His words ﴿Say to My servants who have believed: they should establish prayer﴾ [Ibrahim: 31] in Surat Ibrahim.

*Yukhaffif* is construed with the sense of *yanquss* (diminish), so *yawman* is in the accusative, or it is by assuming an omitted genitive, meaning "the punishment of a day," that is, the quantity of a day. *Yawman* is in the accusative as the direct object of *yukhaffif*.

[Page 165]
