**[Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur, al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir, on Surah 40, verse 52]**

﴿Indeed, We will surely help Our messengers and those who believe, in the life of this world and on the Day when the witnesses stand.﴾ [Ghafir: 51]
﴿On the Day when their excuse will not benefit the wrongdoers, and for them is the curse, and for them is the evil abode.﴾

This is a resumed statement (isti'naf, a new sentence that is not grammatically tied to what precedes it). It draws a lesson from the earlier stories, and it is meant to console the Messenger (ﷺ) and promise him a good outcome, and to console the believers and promise them victory and a good outcome in this world and the Hereafter. This is because the discourse from the beginning of the surah had been about the disputing of the polytheists concerning the Qur'an, as in His saying: ﴿None dispute the signs of God except those who disbelieve﴾ [Ghafir: 4]. It also hinted to the Messenger (ﷺ) that their faction is bound for loss, in His saying: ﴿So do not let their movement throughout the land deceive you﴾ [Ghafir: 4]. The discourse extended into refuting the disputers and depicting their condition by the condition of their likes among the nations whose affair ended in failure and annihilation in this world, and in lasting punishment in the Hereafter. When the purpose had fulfilled what it required of extensive clarification, God made clear to His Messenger (ﷺ), after it, that He will help His messengers and those who believe in this world, as His saying at the end of the discourse indicates: ﴿So be patient; indeed, the promise of God is true﴾ [Ghafir: 55].

It is known from the verb "to help" (nasr) that there is a group who are helped, namely the messengers and the believers, in this world and the Hereafter. It is necessarily the case that the group in question is the group that opposes the messengers and the believers. So the help of the messengers and the believers against them in this world is by making them prevail over them and destroying them, and in the Hereafter by the bliss of Paradise for them and the punishment of the Fire for their enemies.

The use of the imperfect tense in His saying "lanansuru" (We will surely help) serves to evoke the amazing instances of help, some of which are described in this surah and others described in surahs revealed earlier. Otherwise, the help given to the messengers who preceded Muhammad (ﷺ) has already passed, and the help to Muhammad (ﷺ) was still awaited and not yet realized at the time this verse was revealed.

[p. 168]

The emphasis of the statement with (inna) and the making of the predicate a verbal phrase in His saying "lanansuru" takes into account the state of those being addressed indirectly, that God helps His messengers against them, namely the polytheists, because they used to deny this.

This is a promise to the believers that God will help them against whoever wrongs them in the life of this world, either by causing the wrongdoer to suffer an evil outcome, or by empowering against him someone who will take vengeance on him with something like or worse than what he inflicted upon a believer.

Al-ashhad (the witnesses) is the plural of shahid (witness). Al-qiyam means standing, that is, standing at the place of standing (the assembly). The witnesses are the messengers, the guardian angels, and the believers of this community, as His saying indicates: ﴿that you may be witnesses over mankind﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143]. That day is the Day of Gathering, and the testimony of the messengers against those who disbelieved is part of their being helped against them; likewise the testimony of the believers.

The phrase ﴿On the Day when their excuse will not benefit the wrongdoers﴾ is a substitute (badal, a phrase that replaces and explains a preceding noun) for ﴿the Day when the witnesses stand﴾ [Ghafir: 51], and it is in the accusative as a substitute for the adverbial phrase of time.

By "the wrongdoers" is meant the polytheists. Al-ma'dhira (excuse) is a verbal noun from i'tadhara (to make an excuse), and it was discussed earlier at His saying: ﴿They said, "An excuse before your Lord"﴾ [al-A'raf: 164], in Surah al-A'raf.

The apparent meaning of attributing the excuse (ma'dhira) to their pronoun is that an excuse will come from them on that day, by which they will apologize for the causes that brought upon them the punishment, such as their saying: ﴿Our Lord, these misled us﴾ [al-A'raf: 38]. This does not contradict His saying: ﴿Nor will they be permitted, so they could make an excuse﴾ [al-Mursalat: 36], which denies the excuse altogether, because that excuse is the permitted excuse, and this was mentioned earlier at His saying: ﴿So on that Day, the excuse of those who wronged will not benefit them﴾ [al-Rum: 57], in Surah al-Rum.

Nafi', 'Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read "la yanfa'u" (will not benefit) with the yā' (the masculine form), because the subject, which is "ma'dhiratuhum" (their excuse), is not truly feminine, and because of the separation between the verb and its subject by the object. The rest read it with the tā' (the feminine form), considering the feminine grammatical form of the word.

﴿And for them is the curse﴾ is coordinated (ʿatf, joined by conjunction) to the clause ﴿their excuse will not benefit the wrongdoers﴾, meaning: "and on the Day when for them is the curse."

[p. 169]

Al-la'nah (the curse) is distance and expulsion, that is, from the mercy of God. ﴿And for them is the evil abode﴾ [al-Ra'd: 25] is Jahannam (Hell). The placing of "for them" (lahum) first in these two clauses is for emphasis on taking vengeance upon them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 40, verses 53–54:

﴿And We certainly gave Moses the guidance, and We caused the Children of Israel to inherit the Book﴾ ﴿as guidance and a reminder for people of understanding﴾.

This is among the clearest examples of God's support for His messengers and those who believe in them, and it is the most fitting of examples for the victory that God decreed for the Prophet ﷺ. The victory of Moses over the people of Pharaoh caused God to bring into being a great community that had not been regarded, and it was given a great law and a great kingdom. Likewise, the victory of the Prophet ﷺ and the believers was greater than that, more complete and more noble.

The clause ﴿And We certainly gave Moses the guidance﴾ and so on is a parenthetical sentence between ﴿Indeed, We shall certainly support Our messengers﴾ [Ghafir: 51] and the consequence drawn from it in His saying ﴿So be patient; indeed, the promise of God is true﴾ [Ghafir: 55]. And what victory is greater than deliverance from slavery, from paucity and from being a follower of another nation in laws that suit the circumstances of the subordinate community, to the state of a nation that governs its own affairs, possessing a law suited to its conditions and its interests, and having dominion over other nations? This is like the Muslims with the Prophet ﷺ and after him. It also hints at a promise that the Qur'an, which the polytheists denied, remains and is inherited by the Islamic community.

The guidance that was given to Moses is what was revealed to him concerning the command to call to the true religion, namely the mission, and what was sent down to him of the law, and this is what is meant by the Book, namely the Torah. It is this which God caused the Children of Israel to inherit, that is, He made it remain among them after Moses, peace be upon him. They inherited it from him, that is, they took it from him during his lifetime, and God preserved it for them after his death. Thus the use of "inherit" is a metaphor. In this there is an indication that the Book is among the guidance that was given to Moses. God said: ﴿Indeed, We sent down the Torah, in which there is guidance and light﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 44]. So there is an elliptical omission in the speech, its implied meaning being: "And We certainly gave Moses the guidance and the Book, and We caused the Children of Israel to inherit the Book." For Moses was given guidance that the Children of Israel did not inherit, namely the mission, and he was given guidance that the Children of Israel inherited, namely the law that is in the Torah.

﴿As guidance and a reminder﴾ are two circumstantial clauses (ḥāl) referring to the Book, that is, guidance for the Children of Israel and a reminder to them. In it is knowledge of what the learners did not know, and in it is a reminder of what their people of knowledge already knew. The reminder includes the deduction (istinbāt) of rulings from the texts of the Book, and this is what is specific to the scholars among them, from their prophets, their judges and their rabbis. Thus ﴿for people of understanding﴾ is connected to "reminder."

Ulu al-Albab (people of understanding): those possessing sound intellects capable of deduction.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 40, verse 55:**

﴿So be patient. Indeed, the promise of Allah is true. And seek forgiveness for your sin, and exalt your Lord with praise in the evening and the morning.﴾

This is a consequence (tafri') of His saying ﴿Indeed, We will surely help Our messengers﴾ [Ghafir: 51]. That is, know that We will help you and those who believe, and be patient over what you face from your people, and do not weaken.

The clause ﴿Indeed, the promise of Allah is true﴾ is a causal explanation (ta'lil) for the command to be patient.

The particle inna is used here for emphasis on the predicate, and in a context like this it functions like the fa' of causation. It is as if it were said: "So the promise of Allah is true." This conveys that the emphasis serves to express concern and affirmation.

The promise of Allah is the promise of His Messenger of victory in the previous verse and in other verses.

The meaning is: do not seek to hasten the victory, for it will certainly come. This is what the Prophet (ﷺ) was given in his lifetime over the polytheists at the Battle of Badr, on the Day of the Conquest, on the Day of Hunayn, and in the other campaigns. The defeat that occurred at the Battle of Uhud was a trial and a warning of the evil outcome of failing to preserve the Messenger's (ﷺ) command that they should not leave their place. Then the final outcome was for the believers.

The command to seek forgiveness and to glorify God is connected to the command to be patient. Both fall within the context of the consequence drawn from the promise of victory, as a symbolic indication (ramz) of the fulfillment of the promise. This is because He commanded, right after it, what is among the effects of gratitude, as an indirect expression (kinaya) that the blessing of victory will certainly be attained. This is a symbolic kinaya.

The command to seek forgiveness is a command that he ask Allah, exalted is He, for the forgiveness that prophethood entails,

[p. 171]

that is, ask Allah for the continuance of protection (isma), so that forgiveness may continue. This is the station of clearing (takhliya) oneself of psychological troubles. In it there is an allusion (ta'rid) that his community is more deserving of being commanded to do this, as in His saying ﴿And it has certainly been revealed to you and to those before you: If you should associate others with Allah, your work will surely be nullified﴾ [al-Zumar: 65]. Also, the Prophet (ﷺ) is commanded to seek forgiveness as an act of worship and good manners.

He was commanded to glorify Allah, exalted is He, and to declare Him free of imperfections, in the evening and the morning, that is, at all times, but He limited it to the two ends of the times of activity.

Al-'ashiyy (the evening) is the end of the day until the beginning of the darkness of the night. For this reason the night meal is called 'asha' (supper), and the last prayer at night is called 'isha' (night prayer). Al-ibkar (the morning) is a name for the early part of the day, as al-isbah (the dawn) is a name for the morning. Al-bukra is the beginning of the day. It has already been mentioned in His saying ﴿that you glorify Him morning and evening﴾ [Maryam: 11] in surah Maryam. And al-'ashiyy was mentioned in His saying ﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord in the morning and the evening﴾ [al-An'am: 52] in surah al-An'am. This is the station of adorning oneself (tahalli) with psychological perfections, and by this gratitude is completed outwardly and inwardly.

The two commands are placed in conjunction with the command to be patient because patience here is for awaiting the promised victory. For this reason he was not commanded to be patient once the victory had come, in His saying ﴿When the help of Allah and the conquest come﴾ [al-Nasr: 1], ﴿and you see the people entering into the religion of Allah in multitudes﴾ [al-Nasr: 2], ﴿then glorify your Lord with His praise and seek His forgiveness﴾ [al-Nasr: 3]. This is because that is the station of pure gratitude, not patience.

Allah has informed His Prophet (ﷺ) that his past and future sins have been forgiven, as in the beginning of surah al-Fath. Therefore it is established that His command to him to seek forgiveness in surah Ghafir came before He informed him of that, in order to request the continuance of forgiveness. His command to him in surah al-Nasr came after He had informed him of the forgiveness of his past and future sins, to guide him to give thanks for the blessing of victory. Some of the Companions said to the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning his worship: "Allah has forgiven you your past and future sins." He said: "Should I not be a grateful servant?" He used to frequently say in his prostration: "Glory be to You, O Allah, our Lord, and praise be to You. O Allah, forgive me." After the revelation of the surah ﴿When the help of Allah comes﴾ [al-Nasr: 1], 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "He was interpreting the Qur'an."

From the context you know that the verse has no connection to the obligation of the prayer or its times. Rather, it is like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So glorify your Lord with His praise and seek His forgiveness﴾ [al-Nasr: 3] in surah al-Nasr.

[p. 172]

﴿Indeed, those who dispute concerning the signs of God without any authority having come to them, there is nothing in their breasts but greatness (kibr), which they will never attain.﴾

From the beginning of the surah up to this point, the discourse has been engaged in refuting the disputation of the polytheists concerning the signs of God, dismantling their doubts, threatening them for their disbelief, and setting forth for them examples of people of obstinacy like themselves. This begins with His saying, ﴿None dispute concerning the signs of God except those who disbelieve﴾, and His saying, ﴿Have they not travelled through the land and seen how was the end of those before them?﴾ It also mentions examples of their opposites, the believers, both those present and those who have passed, from His saying, ﴿And We sent Moses with Our signs and a clear authority﴾ [Ghafir: 23], ﴿to Pharaoh﴾ [Ghafir: 24], then His saying, ﴿And a believing man from the family of Pharaoh said﴾. It concluded all that with the promise to the Prophet ﷺ and the believers of victory, as He gave victory to the prophets before him and those who believed with them, and it commanded patience in the face of the obstinacy of his people and turning towards the worship of his Lord. Therefore the mention of those who dispute concerning the signs of God without authority, following that, falls under the well-known principle of "a thing is mentioned alongside its like" (al-mathal al-mashhur, al-shay' bi al-shay' yudhkaru).

On this occasion, the discourse moves here to disclosing what the breasts of the disputants conceal of the causes of their disputation without right, so that the Messenger ﷺ may know their inner intention, and so he does not think that they are denying him out of disparagement of him or out of permitting lies against him. Rather, what drives them to denial is arrogance (takabbur) at being followers of the Messenger ﷺ, and (their pride at being behind) those who preceded them in faith, among those whom they did not regard as worthy of notice.

This is similar to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We know that what they say grieves you, but it is not you they deny; rather the wrongdoers deny the signs of God﴾ [al-An'am: 33].

So His saying, ﴿Indeed, those who dispute concerning the signs of God…﴾ to the end of the verse, is an initial resumptive sentence (istinaf ibtida'i, a new sentence beginning a fresh statement), and it is like a repetition of the clause, ﴿those who dispute concerning the signs of God without authority having come to them﴾, which is greatly hateful in the sight of God. It is a repetition of enumeration for rebuke at the conclusion of the purpose of argument, just as the one being rebuked is halted again and again.

Those who dispute are the polytheists of Makkah, and they are the ones referred to at the beginning of the surah in His saying, ﴿None dispute concerning the signs of God except those who disbelieve, so do not let their going to and fro in the land deceive you﴾ [Ghafir: 4]. The meaning of disputation concerning the signs of God has already been explained there.

[p. 173]

His saying, ﴿without authority﴾ (bi-ghayri sultan), is connected to ﴿dispute﴾ (yujadilun). The particle bi (ب) here indicates accompaniment (lil-musahabah), i.e., they accompany it with the absence of authority, meaning without proof (hujjah). That is, they dispute with the disputation of obstinacy and usurpation.

The benefit of this qualifier is to censure their disputation. Otherwise, disputation concerning the signs of God can never be except without authority, because the signs of God do not contradict reality. This qualifier is a parallel to His saying, ﴿And who is more astray than one who follows his desire without guidance from God?﴾ Likewise, sultan (authority) is qualified by the clause ﴿having come to them﴾ to intensify the reprehensibility of their disputation, by describing it as devoid of any proof they possess. Thus they dispute with what they have no knowledge of. The beginning of this verse has a parallel in the course of the story of Moses and Pharaoh in this surah.

As for His saying, ﴿there is nothing in their breasts but kibr﴾, the particle inna is a negating particle (nafiyah), the prepositional phrase is the fronted predicate (khabar muqaddam), the exception is a restricted exception (istithna' mufarragh), kibr is the delayed subject (mubtada' mu'akhkhar), and the whole clause is a predicate of ﴿those who dispute﴾. The word "breasts" (sudur) is used figuratively for hearts by way of the relation of location ('alaqat al-hulul), and what is meant is the inner selves of them. The Arabs use "heart" (qalb) for the intellect, because the heart is what a person feels by its movement during psychological emotions such as joy and its opposite, and concern for something.

Kibr is one of the psychological emotions, and it is: a person's perception of thoughts that make him feel he is greater than others, so that he does not accept equality with them, let alone following them. It has already been discussed in the explanation of His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Except Iblis, who refused and was arrogant﴾ [al-Baqarah: 34], in Surat al-Baqarah.

The meaning is: nothing drives them to dispute concerning the signs of God except arrogance towards the one who brought them, and their disputation is not due to any evidence that has appeared to them.

By restriction (qasr), He has affirmed for them that kibr is what motivates the disputation, in order to negate that anything other than kibr is what calls them to dispute, in an emphatic manner. The restriction is an emphasis upon emphasis, since it contains an affirmation of the thing in a specific emphatic manner, and a negation of whatever else, so it contains two sentences.

The clause ﴿which they will never attain﴾ (ma hum bi-balighihi) may be a parenthetical clause (mu'taridah), and it may be in the position of a description (sifah) of ﴿kibr﴾.

[p. 174]

The real meaning of bulugh (attainment) is arrival. God says, ﴿to a land you could not reach except with great hardship to yourselves﴾ [al-Nahl: 7]. It is also used for obtaining a thing and acquiring it, as a figurative unrestricted metaphor (majaz mursal), as in His saying, ﴿and they did not reach even a tenth of what We had given them﴾. Here it is necessarily understood in its figurative sense: that is, they will never attain kibr.

Since kibr has been affirmed as established in their souls, with emphasis, by His saying, ﴿there is nothing in their breasts but kibr﴾, it is determined that the negation of their attaining kibr is directed to the states of kibr. Either it means the negation of their capacity for kibr, since they are too lowly for kibr to belong to them, as in His saying, ﴿The mightier will surely expel the meaner therefrom; but might belongs to God, His Messenger, and the believers﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 8], meaning there is no true might for them. So the meaning here is: a false greatness (kibr zayf). Or it means the negation of their obtaining any of the effects of their arrogance, such as belittling those whom they are arrogant towards, opposing them in what they call them to, let alone being included among their followers, humiliating them, and silencing their argument. So the meaning is: they will not attain their aim, which they hope for from you, which is in their souls and which their statements reveal, such as their saying, ﴿We await for him the vicissitudes of time﴾ [al-Tur: 30], and their saying, ﴿Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise during it, that perhaps you may prevail﴾ [Fussilat: 26], and similar statements of theirs that disclose their hopes.

Thus the indefinite form of kibr is for magnification, meaning a severe kibr, by the multiplicity of its kinds and its firm hold over their souls. The explicit pronoun in bi-balighihi refers to kibr by way of figurative speech, through the relation of causality or effectuality ('alaqat al-sababiyyah aw al-musabbabiyyah). The motive for this figure is the seeking of brevity, because attaching the negation of attainment to the noun of kibr itself includes all the states that kibr arouses. This is among the purposes of attributing judgments to essences (dhawat), when no indicator exists to show that a specific state is intended, as in His saying, ﴿We have distributed among them their livelihood﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 32], meaning all the states of their livelihood. So the phrase ﴿they will never attain it﴾ includes their not attaining anything that their kibr entails. They did not attain superiority over others so as to be arrogant, nor is there any hope for them in obtaining the effects of their arrogance, as He says, ﴿They have been arrogant within themselves and have transgressed with great transgression﴾ [al-Furqan: 21].

The negation that they attain their aim has been expressed in the form of a nominal sentence (jumlah ismiyyah), because it conveys the permanence and continuity of its meaning. So the meaning is: they are permanently deprived of attaining it. Thus the depiction of their condition, by affirmation and negation, contains many rhetorical peculiarities.

[p. 175]

Some exegetes (mufassirun) have taken the referent (mas-sadaq) of ﴿those who dispute concerning the signs of God﴾ here to be the Jews, and have made it equivalent in meaning to His saying, ﴿Or do they envy the people for what God has given them of His bounty?﴾ [al-Nisa': 54]. From this they have gone further to say that this verse is Medinan, appended to the Meccan surah, as was mentioned in the introduction to the exegesis of the surah. They have supported this interpretation with reports which, even if authentic, would show nothing more than the verse's suitability to be given as an example for every group that disputes concerning the signs of God without authority, with a disputation that kibr drives them to.

[* * *]

﴿So seek refuge in God; indeed He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing.﴾

When God guaranteed to His Messenger ﷺ that those who dispute with him concerning what has come to them are driven to disputation by their arrogance, which contains their scheming, and that they will not attain what they conceal, and what they will conceal, He made it a consequence (farra'a) that He commanded him to make God his refuge from them, that is, not to heed what they plot. In other words, prior to seeking refuge in God, put first...

And He omitted the object of isti'adhah (seek refuge) for the purpose of generalizing the seeking of refuge from everything that is feared.

The clause ﴿Indeed He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾ is a justification for the command to persist in seeking refuge, that is, because He is the one who has knowledge of their statements and deeds, while you do not comprehend in knowledge the turns of their cunning and scheming.

The emphasis by the particle inna, and the restriction by the separating pronoun (damir al-fasl), carry an implicit allusion (ta'rid) to the one spoken about, who are those who dispute concerning the signs of God without authority. The meaning is: He is the one capable of nullifying what they are doing, not you. So how could what they conceal against you be accomplished for them?

[Page 176]

The connection of this statement to what precedes it is that the most important of the signs of God that they disputed were the signs that affirm the Resurrection (al-ba'th). Their disputing over the affirmation of the Resurrection was their greatest doubt, which misled their own souls, and they spread it among the common people, saying: "﴿When we have become dust, shall we indeed be [raised] in a new creation?﴾" [al-Ra'd 13:5]. Because of this they used to mock the Prophet (ﷺ). ﴿And those who disbelieved said, "Shall we direct you to a man who will inform you that, when you have been totally torn apart, you will indeed be in a new creation?"﴾ [Saba' 34:7] ﴿"Has he invented a lie against God, or is there madness in him?"﴾ [Saba' 34:8]. Since they acknowledged that God is the Creator of the heavens and the earth, the proof for the Resurrection was established against them: the raising of the dead does not reach the level of the creation of the heavens and the earth in relation to the power of God, exalted is He.

The statement indicates an implied oath (qasam), because the lam is the lam of the answer to an oath, and the purpose is to emphasize the report.

The meaning of "greater" (akbar) is that it is greater, more important, and more numerous in its objects of power for the One who has power over it, who is not incapable of creating people whom He will raise for the reckoning.

By "people" in His saying "than the creation of people," what is meant is those whom God restores in their creation as He originated them the first time, and in whom He deposits their spirits as He deposited them in them the first time. The report is used in other than its literal meaning, because the fact that its creation is greater is a known matter; what is intended is to remind and draw attention to it, since they do not act according to what their knowledge of it requires.

The corrective contrast (istidrak) in His saying "but most people do not know" arises from what the emphasis by oath required, namely the clarity that the creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of people.

So the meaning is: the proof of the possibility of the Resurrection is clear, but those who deny it do not know. That is, they do not know the evidence, because they are heedless of reflecting on the proofs, satisfied with the first thoughts that appear to them, which they adopt as a creed without investigating what opposes them. When they behaved in the state of lacking knowledge, they were placed in the position of those who have no knowledge, and therefore the verb "they know" (ya'lamun) is used intransitively, with no object mentioned.

By "most people" is meant those who dispute the signs of the Resurrection, and they are the polytheists. As for those who knew this, they are the believers, and they are fewer in number.

The apparent wording of the phrase "but most people do not know" would have called for a pronoun, yet the noun "people" is made explicit so that the sentence stands on its own in conveying its meaning, and so that it is fit to circulate as a proverb. The meaning is that they denied the Resurrection because they regarded the creation of bodies as far-fetched, although in the creation of the heavens and the earth there is nothing that leaves room for such a far-fetched notion.

"Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 40, verse 58:

"﴿And the blind and the seeing are not equal, nor are those who believe and do righteous deeds, nor the evildoer. Little do you remember.﴾"

Since He had placed them in the position of those who do not know, He presented an example for them and for the believers. The likeness of those who dispute about the matter of resurrection, despite the clarity of its possibility, is the likeness of the blind man, and the likeness of the believers who affirm it is the state of the seer. The state of the believers is already known from the implied meaning of the description "most people," because the majority of those who do not know are contrasted with a minority who know.

The meaning is: those who are guided and those who are in error are not equal. The use of "the blind" and "the seeing" is therefore a metaphor for the two groups included in His words, "but most people do not know."

The negation of equality between them implies the preference of one over the other, as we have already noted in His words, "Not equal are those of the believers who sit [at home]..." in Surat an-Nisa'. It is evident that the better is the one with the better state, and that is the seer, since people do not differ that sight is more honourable than blindness in one and the same person. The negation of equality without a stated object implies generality in its objects, but this is restricted to the objects indicated by the context of the speech, which are the signs of God and the indications of His attributes. This kind of generality is called "customary generality" (al-'umum al-'urfi), and a parallel to it was mentioned earlier in Surat Fatir.

His words "and those who believe and do righteous deeds, nor the evildoer" are an additional clarification of the excellence of the people of faith, by mentioning their excellence in their deeds after mentioning their excellence in perceiving the proofs of the possibility of resurrection and similar proofs of faith.

The meaning is: those who believe and do righteous deeds are not equal to the evildoers, that is, in their deeds, as His words "and do righteous deeds, nor the evildoer" indicate. In this there is an allusion to the difference in recompense between the two groups, and this allusion is an *idmaj* (embedding) serving to draw attention to reward and punishment.

The conjunction "wa" in His words "and those who believe" is coordinating a clause upon a clause, with the implied meaning: "and those who believe are not equal."

The conjunction "wa" in His words "nor the evildoer" coordinates "the evildoer" upon "those who believe," a coordination of a singular upon a singular. The first coordination is a coordination of a plural group, like His words, "He is the First and the Last, and the Outward and the Inward."

He mentioned the blind before the seer, although sight is more honourable than blindness with respect to one and the same person, because the one likened to the seer is more honourable than the one likened to the blind, since the one likened to the seer is the believers. He mentioned the likening of the disbelievers out of regard for the fact that what is most important in the context is to explain the state of those who dispute the signs, since they are the intended audience of the admonition.

As for His words "and those who believe and do righteous deeds, nor the evildoer," He arranged the mention of the two groups in there in the reverse order of their arrangement in the likening to the blind and the seer, out of concern for the nobility of the believers.

The negating "la" was repeated after the conjunctive "wa" following a negation. The coordination alone would have sufficed without it, so its repetition serves to add emphasis to the negation of equality, and the context of rebuke calls for elaboration. For this reason, "la" in such a construction is counted as superfluous, as in *Mughni al-Labib*. The expected position would have been for "la" to come before "those who believe," but it was shifted from that to draw attention to the fact that the intent is the non-equality of the evildoer with the one who does righteous deeds, and that mentioning "those who believe" before "the evildoer" is for the sake of concern with the believers. There is no reason to deviate from this after the matter of concern for those whose likening was the very purpose of the speech has been fulfilled. Thus two kinds of emphasis arise in the speech.

Close to this is what occurs in Surat Fatir in four clauses: in two of them the side of the likening of the disbelievers is put first, and in two of them the likening of the side of the believers is put first. These are His words, "And the blind and the seeing are not equal" [Fatir: 19], "nor are the darkness and the light" [Fatir: 20], "nor the shade and the heat" [Fatir: 21], "And the living and the dead are not equal" [Fatir: 22].

("Qalilan," little) is a circumstantial accusative (hal) referring back to "most people" in His words just before it, "but most people do not know" [Ghafir: 57]. The "ma" in His words "ma yatadhakkarun" is verbal-masdar (ma masdariyya) and occupies a nominative position as the subject.

This emphasizes the meaning of His words "but most people do not know" [Ghafir: 57], because little remembrance amounts to a lack of knowledge. The "little" here is a metonymy for absence, which is a common usage, as in His words, "So little is it that they believe" [al-Baqara: 88]. It is also possible that it is in its literal meaning, and that "little" is intended as incompleteness: that is, they do not know, so when they do remember, they remember in a way that does not reach its goal, and they stop midway from delving deeply into deducing the indication from it, so it is like non-existence in that its effect is not produced by it.

Ibn Kathir's reading... [note: this sentence was not in the source; omitted]

The majority (al-Jumhur) read "yatadhakkarun" with the third-person ya' (ghayba), following the apparent sense of the speech. 'Asim, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read "tatadhakkarun" with the second-person ta' (khitab), by way of iltifat (shift of address), the address being to those who dispute the signs of God.

That the address is to the whole community, believers and polytheists alike, and that the little remembrance is the remembrance of the believers, so that it is little in comparison to the non-remembrance of the polytheists, is far from the context of rebuttal and does not fit the shift of address (iltifat)."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 40, verse 59:

﴿Indeed, the Hour is surely coming; there is no doubt about it, but most people do not believe.﴾

When proof of the resurrection (al-ba'th) was given the argumentation and reasoning it deserved, the ground was prepared for drawing out its verification, just as a conclusion is drawn out of a syllogism (qiyas). Thus it was announced that the coming of the Hour is certain, and the Hour is the hour of resurrection. In the terminology of Islam, "al-sa'ah" (the Hour) is a term that has become dominant for the hour of resurrection, so "the Hour" and "the resurrection" are synonymous in their outcome. It is as if it were said: what the disputers disputed about will surely occur, since the doubts of the astray and their deceptions have been removed from it, and it has become clear, with no doubt in it.

The emphasis of the statement with inna (indeed) and the lam of initiation (lam al-ibtida') serves to increase its certainty, and to indicate that the statement has been verified by the preceding proofs. This is because the discourse is addressed to those who denied the resurrection. For this reason, the lam of initiation was not used in His saying in Surah Ta-Ha: ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming﴾ [Ta-Ha: 15], because the address there was to Musa, peace be upon him.

The active participle (ism al-fa'il) "ati'ah" (coming) was used, which in its literal sense denotes the present, to hint that once it has been verified, it has become like a present, witnessed thing. The intended meaning is the verification of its occurrence, not merely the report of its occurrence.

The clause "there is no doubt about it" confirms the clause "indeed, the Hour is surely coming." The negation of doubt is about the Hour itself, while what is intended is the negation of doubt concerning its coming, as the word "coming" (ati'ah) indicates that.

The meaning of negating doubt about its occurrence is that its indications are so clear that the doubt of the doubters is not taken into account, because they doubted about it due to lack of reflection and contemplation. This is close to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is the Book; there is no doubt in it﴾.

The point of the contrastive particle (al-istidrak) found in His saying ﴿but most people do not believe﴾ is what the negation of doubt about its occurrence stirs up, namely that a questioner may ask: how does it negate doubt about it, when doubt exists among many people? So the istidrak with His saying ﴿but most people do not believe﴾ serves as an answer to that question.

The meaning: but most people pass by the proofs and signs while turning away from their indication, so they remain without believing in what they signify. Had they reflected and derived conclusions with their intellects, there would have appeared to them proofs after which they would believe. Therefore the attribute of faith is negated of them here.

This istidrak is a explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani). Had it not been that "lakinna" frequently occurs after the conjunctive waw, the sentence would have deserved to be separated without a conjunction; this conjunction is therefore a verbal embellishment.

And most people are the polytheists (mushrikun), and at that time they are vastly more numerous than the believers.

[Page 181]

Since disputation about the signs of Allah includes their disputation concerning the Divine Oneness, as His saying that follows indicates, ﴿Then it will be said to them, "Where is that which you used to worship, besides Allah?" They will say, "They have strayed from us. Rather, we did not used to invoke anything before."﴾ [Ghafir: 73-74]. Here He made "we did not used to invoke" the opposite of what was said to them, "Where is that which you used to worship?" [Ash-Shu'ara': 92]. The disputation also includes the occurrence of the Resurrection (al-ba'th), as indicated by His saying after this, ﴿Have you not seen those who dispute concerning the signs of Allah, how they are turned away?﴾ [Ghafir: 69], up to His saying, ﴿When the shackles are around their necks, and the chains﴾ [Ghafir: 71], and the verse. First, He followed the mention of the disputation with His saying, ﴿The creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of mankind﴾ [Ghafir: 57], which is an argument for the possibility of the Resurrection. Then He joined to it His saying, ﴿And your Lord said, "Call upon Me; I will respond to you"﴾, and the verse, as a warning against associating others with Him. Also, when the command of Allah to His Messenger (ﷺ) to invoke Allah alone was mentioned, it was a command that follows from the rebuke of the polytheists in His saying, ﴿That is because when Allah alone was invoked, you disbelieved; but when others were associated with Him, you believed﴾ [Ghafir: 12], and from His saying after that, ﴿And none is reminded except one who turns back in repentance﴾ [Ghafir: 13]. The discourse then moved on to what is more important, which is the warning to the polytheists, ﴿And warn them of the Day of the Imminent﴾ [Ghafir: 18], and so on. The themes followed one another until they fulfilled their purpose. The discourse now returns to what includes the pure worship of the believers to Allah, the Exalted, which is also connected to His saying, ﴿And the supplication of the disbelievers is not except in error﴾ [Ghafir: 50]. Since the mention of du'a (invocation/supplication) has preceded in its two meanings, the meaning of worship and the meaning of asking for what is sought, this command, which comprises both meanings, was added.

The statement introduced by the verb "qala" (said), "Your Lord said," may be taken to mean the inner speech of Allah (kalam nafsi), that is, what the will of Allah has related to in the sense of its capacity (ta'alluq salahi), so that He says it at the time of the will to bring it into existence. It may also be taken to mean the spoken word, and the use of the past tense "qala" would then be a report of statements that had already been made in verses before the revelation of this verse, such as His saying, ﴿So invoke Allah, being sincere to Him in religion﴾ [Ghafir: 14]. This is in contrast to His saying, ﴿I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 186], which was revealed after this verse. It is also possible that the past tense is used metaphorically for the present, meaning "your Lord says: Call upon Me."

The word "du'a" is used in the sense of calling out (nida'), which implies acknowledgment of the one called upon, and it is also used to mean request (talab). There has come in the speech of the Prophet (ﷺ) what is suitable for the meaning of du'a in this verse, combining both senses, in the hadith of al-Nu'man ibn Bashir, who said:

"I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say: 'Du'a is worship,' then he recited, ﴿And your Lord said, 'Call upon Me; I will respond to you. Indeed, those who are too proud to worship Me will enter Hell, humbled.'﴾"

It was related by al-Tirmidhi, who said: "This is a hasan sahih hadith." Indeed, his saying "Du'a is worship" requires that the two realities be identical, and if du'a is worship, then worship is necessarily du'a.

So "du'a" is used for a servant's asking Allah for his need, which is its meaning in the language, and it is used for the worship of Allah by way of kinaya (metonymy, an indirect expression), because worship does not lack the invocation of the one worshipped, through calling upon his greatness and humbly turning to him. This usage is less common than the first. By "worship" in the terminology of the Qur'an is meant singling out Allah in worship, that is, acknowledging His Oneness.

"Istijaba" (response) is used for giving the one who asks what he asked for, and this is its most famous usage. It is also used for the effect of accepting worship through forgiving prior polytheism and through obtaining reward for the acts of faith. The meaning of the verse, in the sense of asking Allah for a need, fits the response being conditional on that request, subject to the will of Allah, or upon fulfilling the conditions for accepting the request, and giving something better than it in this world, or giving a substitute for it in the Hereafter. Its meaning in the sense of singling out Allah in worship is that they should repent of polytheism; the response then is the acceptance of that, since the acceptance of repentance from polytheism is certain.

Since the verse combined the two verbs, while there is a difference in how widely each usage is current, we know that the intended meaning contains something resembling al-ihtibak (a rhetorical device in which each of two parallel terms is given a meaning that is understood from the other): it stated the well-known meaning for both verbs, then followed with His saying, ﴿Indeed, those who are too proud to worship Me﴾. From this we know that what is meant is du'a and worship, and that "response" is intended to mean the acceptance of du'a and the attainment of the effect of worship. Thus the verb "ud'uni" (call upon Me) is used in both of its meanings by way of the generality of the homonym ('umum al-mushtarak).

The verb "astajib" (I will respond) is used in its literal and metaphorical senses, and the indicator is what you have known, along with the conciseness and comprehensiveness of the speech.

Naming Allah by the attribute "Lord" (Rabb), in construct with the pronoun of the addressees, indicates, through this attribute and its annexation, the obligation to comply with His command, because it is the right of lordship that the one who is lord be obeyed in what he commands, since the one who is lorded over (al-marbub) is bound to obey his lord. For this reason, with this attribute, He did not digress into a reminder of His blessings or an allusion to the perfections of His essence.

The clause, ﴿Indeed, those who are too proud to worship Me will enter Hell﴾, is a ta'lil (causal explanation) of the command to invoke, a causal explanation that conveys a warning against refusing to invoke Allah when one turns to invoking idols, as He, the Exalted, said, ﴿That is because when Allah alone was invoked, you disbelieved; but when others were associated with Him, you believed﴾ [Ghafir: 12]. The polytheists would not humble themselves to Allah except when they did not expect their partners to respond, as He, the Exalted, said, ﴿Then when He delivers you to the land, you turn away﴾ [Al-Isra': 67]. The meaning of this causal explanation of the command to invoke, by way of this warning, is that Allah does not love for His servants what leads them to punishment, as He, the Exalted, said, ﴿And He does not approve for His servants disbelief﴾ [Az-Zumar: 7]. Thus the verse contains evidence that Allah asks His servants to call upon Him in their needs. There is no disagreement among the Muslims concerning the legitimacy of du'a; the disagreement is only over whether it benefits in turning back the decree (al-qadar) or not, and this is a disagreement between us and the Mu'tazila. There is no proof against them in the verse, because they interpreted the meaning of "astajib lakum" (I will respond to you). His saying, the Exalted, ﴿And when My servants ask you concerning Me, indeed I am near﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 186], has already preceded in Surat al-Baqarah. Using the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) here indicates the causal explanation.

"Dakhirin" (humbled) is a ḥal (circumstantial state) of the pronoun in "sayadkhulun" (they will enter), meaning "humiliated." "Dakhara," like "managa" and "fariha," means: became small and humbled. His saying, ﴿prostrating to Allah while they are humbled﴾ [An-Nahl: 48], has already preceded in Surat an-Nahl.

The majority read "sayadkhulun" with a fatha on the ya' and a damma on the kha'. Abu Ja'far and Ruways from Ya'qub read it with a damma on the ya' and a fatha on the kha', in the passive voice (bina' lil-na'ib), meaning: "the angels of punishment will cause them to enter Hell."

The Name of Allah may be a substitute (badal) for "your Lord" in ﴿And your Lord said﴾ [Ghafir: 60]. This follows the name "Allah" with the proper name in order to fulfil two rights: the right of His being worthy to be obeyed by virtue of lordship (rububiyyah) and servitude (ubudiyyah), and the right of His being worthy of obedience by virtue of the attributes of perfection that the proper name Allah encompasses. For this reason, along with the description of the Lord mentioned earlier, nothing of His blessings or perfections is mentioned, by relying on what is required by the right of lordship. With the proper name, some of His bounty and favour is mentioned, and then the name is described by the relative pronoun and its clause, indicating some of His attributes and hinting at the reason for the command to worship Him. The sentence then becomes an explanatory resumptive sentence (isti'naf bayani), arising from the strengthening of the command through calling upon Him.

[p. 184]

The Name of Allah may also be the subject (mubtada'), with the relative clause as its description, and the predicate being His saying ﴿That is Allah, your Lord﴾ [Ghafir: 64], and the sentence ﴿Indeed Allah is full of bounty﴾ would then be a parenthetical interjection (mu'taridah). Or the Name of Allah may be the subject and the relative clause the predicate.

Treating the sentence as a new resumptive sentence is better than treating the Name as a substitute, because it is more fitting for drawing attention to their poor gratitude and to the context of enumerating proofs, and more fitting with His saying ﴿Allah is He who made the earth for you a place of settlement﴾ [Ghafir: 64]. The sentence would then stand in the position of giving a reason for the sentence ﴿Indeed, those who disdain My worship will enter Hell, humbled﴾ [Ghafir: 60], meaning: they brought that punishment upon themselves, because they denied the blessing of Allah when He made for them the night and the day.

On all these considerations, this verse records for people a division into those who are thankful for a blessing and those who are ungrateful for it, just as the preceding verse recorded their division into those who believe in the oneness of Allah and those who disbelieve in it.

This verse serves as a reminder of Allah's blessing upon creation, as is required by the lam of causation in His saying ﴿for you﴾, and as is required by the concluding phrase ﴿Indeed Allah is full of bounty toward mankind, but most of mankind are not grateful﴾.

Within the reminder of the blessing is woven an argument for His being alone in disposing of creation and in governing it, which is inseparable from the true nature of divinity (uluhiyyah).

The argument begins with the proofs of the heavenly phenomena and their effects reaching the earthly phenomena, and these are the locus of the blessing through night and day. These are two great creations that point to the immense power of their Creator, Regulator, and the One who made them succeed one another. Most of the interests of this world and of its people are bound up with them. Among the interests of the world is the achieving of balance between light and darkness, and between heat and cold, so that the earth is suitable for the interests of those upon it, producing pasture and ripening fruits. Among the interests of the world's inhabitants is the rest of humans and animals at night, in order to restore the nervous energy that the work of the senses and the body wearies during the day. Thus the energy returns to the nervous system of the whole body and to the senses. Were it not for the darkness of the night, sleep would not be complete, and the return of energy would be slow and feeble, and the nervous strength would soon decline and deteriorate, so that a person would not enjoy a long life.

[p. 185]

Among them is the dispersal of people and animals during the day and the clear perception of beings by light. By this, the affairs of people are accomplished in their works, through which the order of society is maintained, in cities and deserts, in settled places and in travel. Man is civic by nature and strives for work and acquisition, so his need for light is essential. Were it not for light, people's conduct would be disordered and confused.

To draw attention to the importance of people's seeing by light and to the abundance of benefits they gain from it, the seeing is attributed to the day by way of rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli, a figure in which an action is attributed to something other than its actual agent, here the time in which it occurs), because of the strong connection between actions and their times. So the seeing of people is attributed to the day itself, since the day is the cause of part of it and the cause of the perfection of another part.

As for the blessing of rest at night, it is one single blessing, namely the return of energy.

In the mention of the night there is a reminder of a great sign among created things, namely the sun, from which the night arises through the withdrawal of its rays from one half of the terrestrial sphere, and the day arises through the spreading of its rays over the opposite half of the terrestrial sphere. But since the primary purpose of this verse is to bestow favour, He mentioned the night and the day without the sun. The sun has been mentioned in other verses whose principal purpose was to indicate immense power and oneness, as in His saying ﴿And the sun and the moon [He made] to run by calculation. That is the determination of the Exalted in Might, the Knowing﴾ [al-An'am: 96].

The contrast between the stated cause of the creation of night, namely the resting of people in it, and the attribution of seeing to the essence of the day by way of rational metaphor, and the sentence ﴿and it is in the day that people see﴾ (the actual agents of seeing being people in the day), indicates by ihtibak (a device in which two parts of a statement each leave out what the other states, so that both are understood together) that the night is also restful, and that the day was created so that people might see in it. The favour is equal in both. This is among the marvels of concision, together with the variety of the two styles of literal and rational metaphor. It was not reversed to say: "He made the night for you restful and the day for you to see in," so that the explicitness of the intended meaning of rest would not be lost, lest it be supposed that the rest of the night is the intensity of its darkness, as one says "a still night" (layl saji), meaning few voices in it.

[p. 186]

The discussion of night and day has already been given in Surat al-Baqarah at His saying ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth and the alternation of night and day﴾ [al-Baqarah: 164], and in other places.

The sentence ﴿Indeed Allah is full of bounty toward mankind﴾ is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiradh), which serves as a justification for the sentence ﴿Allah is He who made the night for you to rest in﴾, because bounty includes the making of night and day and other blessings, and because "mankind" includes both those addressed by "He made for you" and others among humanity.

The indefiniteness of "bounty" (fadl) is for magnification, because Allah's blessings are great and magnificent. For this reason He said "is full of bounty" (dhu fadl) and did not say "is bountiful" (mutafaddil) or "is bestowed upon" (mufaddal). He turned to the construction of dhu with fadl, because it allows the indefinite form, which conveys magnification.

He turned away from a phrase such as "for Him is bounty" to "is full of bounty" because of the honour that dhu conveys with respect to what it is attached to.

The use of the adversative particle (istidrak) with "but" (laakinna) arises from what necessarily follows from "full of bounty toward mankind", because it is fitting for people to thank their Lord for His bounty. Yet most of them were ungrateful for His blessings. What ingratitude for a blessing is greater than abandoning the worship of their Creator who has bestowed favour upon them, and worshipping that which possesses neither benefit nor harm for them?

By "most of mankind" the minority is excluded, and they are the believers, for they are a minority, as in ﴿Even if the abundance of the corrupt impresses you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 100].

The turning away from the pronoun for "mankind" in His saying ﴿but most of mankind are not grateful﴾ to the explicit noun is so that the word "mankind" is repeated when mentioning their lack of gratitude, just as it was mentioned when speaking of His bestowing favour upon them. Thus their ingratitude is recorded against them in a more explicit way.

You have already known, from what preceded, the reason for the variation in the negated verbs in His saying ﴿but most of mankind do not know﴾ [Ghafir: 57], His saying ﴿but most of mankind do not believe﴾ [Ghafir: 59], and His saying ﴿but most of mankind are not grateful﴾. He follows each purpose that is intended to be affirmed with what suits the state of those who deny it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 40, verse 62:

Page 187
﴿That is Allah, your Lord, the Creator of all things. There is no deity except Him. So how are you deluded away from the truth?﴾.

The discourse has continued on the proofs of God's exclusive divinity, from His saying ﴿That is Allah, your Lord, the Creator of all things﴾ up to His saying ﴿sincere to Him in religion﴾ [Ghafir: 65], in the manner of proofs being connected to what they are proofs for.

The demonstrative ﴿That﴾ (dhalikum) refers to the Name of Majesty (Allah) in His saying ﴿Allah is He who made the night for you that you may rest therein﴾ [Ghafir: 61]. He turned from the pronoun to the demonstrative to convey that He, may He be exalted, is known and distinguished by His actions, which He alone performs, such that when His actions are mentioned He is distinguished from all others, and so He becomes like one present and pointed to. Thus how could His divinity be confused with a supposed divinity of idols? There is no doubt for those who associate partners with Him that could mislead them, [suggesting] that what does not act like His action is a god. That is, "That is your Lord, not other than Him." In this demonstrative there is also an implicit rebuke of the stupidity of the addressees, who were confused about the reality of His divinity.

His saying ﴿Allah, your Lord, the Creator of all things. There is no deity except Him﴾ consists of four predicates about the demonstrative. It begins with the Name that comprises the attributes of divinity in summary, and follows with "your Lord" (rabbukum), i.e., He who arranged the creation of people and prepared for them what sustains their lives. Since lordship includes an aspect of creation that is specific to humans, He is the Creator of all things just as He created them. He then follows with the negation of divinity from anything other than Him. Thus the contents of these four predicates come in an ascending order, and the fourth is the conclusion of the others. Then there is placed upon them an interrogative of wonder at their turning away from worshipping Him toward worshipping others, despite the clear corruption of their turning away from His worship.

"Anna" (أنّى) is an interrogative particle about manner (kayfiyyah). Its original meaning is interrogation about place. When they make the condition (ḥāla) into the sense of a side or source of a thing, they use anna to ask about the condition. This is indicated by the Exalted's saying ﴿How can He have a son when He has no consort?﴾ [al-An'am: 101] in Surat al-An'am.

"Tu'fakun" means "you are turned away" (tuṣrafūn). It was mentioned in His saying ﴿May Allah destroy them; how are they deluded?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 30] in Surat Bara'ah. Its form is passive to indicate ambiguity due to their turning away, since the outcome of the sentence will be clarified after it.

[Page 188]

﴿Thus are turned away those who used to deny the signs of God.﴾

This clause is parenthetical (mu'tarida), serving as the reason (ta'lil) for the content of the preceding clause, which is the expression of wonder (ta'jib) at their turning away from the worship of their Lord, the Creator of them and of everything. The explanation of this contains what shows the cause of the wonder. The relative construction (al-ism al-mawsul, "those who") is used for those who are turned away, because the relative clause (al-silah) indicates the reason for the predicate and its cause. That is, their persistence in denying the signs of God, without reflection or contemplation of their meanings and proofs, stamps their souls with a turning away from knowledge of the necessity of God's oneness, exalted is He.

The demonstrative "thus" (dhalika) refers to the turning away (al-ifk) derived from the verb tu'fakun ("you are turned away"). That is: like your turning away, those who used to deny the signs of God are turned away.

It is possible that the intended meaning of "those who used to deny the signs of God" is those addressed in His saying ﴿That is God, your Lord﴾ [Ghafir: 64]. In that case the relative construction and its clause are used in place of the pronoun (izhar fi maqam al-idmar), and the meaning is: "thus you are turned away," that is, like your turning away you are turned away. The comparison then serves as an intensification, indicating that their turning away has reached the utmost limit in its very nature, such that if one who wished to make it near to the hearers sought a likeness of it, he would find no likeness clearer or more manifest in its reality than it itself. Thus he has no recourse but to liken it to itself, in the familiar manner expressed in His saying ﴿And thus We made you a middle nation﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143]. In this way, the relative clause in ﴿those who used to deny the signs of God﴾ becomes an indication of the cause of their turning away, as an explicit explanation.

It is also possible that the intended meaning of "those who used to deny the signs of God" is everyone who denied the signs of God, from among the idolaters of the Arabs and others among the polytheists and deniers. Then the cause indicated by the relative clause becomes an allusive explanation (ta'lil ta'ridi), for if turning away is the condition of all those who deny the signs of God, then this includes those (addressed) by virtue of resemblance.

The form of the present tense (al-mudari') is used to bring the state before the mind, and the verb of being (fi'l al-kawn, "used to be") is mentioned to indicate that denying the signs of God is their habit and constant practice.

This is a great principle in scientific ethics, for minds that are habituated to denial and obstinacy before reflecting upon what is known are turned away from the unveiling of scientific truths, so that what is known becomes confused for them, and they cannot distinguish between the correct and the corrupt.

This is a second resumptive clause, built on the best of the aspects by which we explained the placement of His words ﴿Allah is He who made the night for you that you might rest therein﴾ [Ghafir: 61], as already mentioned. For this reason it is not conjoined to the preceding verse, because the context is one of enumerating the proofs of His sole action and His bounty toward them, so that their folly in associating others with Him and their ingratitude for His blessings might be exposed. In the previous verse He reminded them of the effects of His power in creating the accidents subsisting in the substances of this world, namely darkness and light, and in both there are great blessings upon people. In this verse He reminded them of the effects of creating the substances of this world in forms that are a blessing to them, and of creating their own selves in forms suited to them. As for your making the Name of Majesty in His words ﴿Allah, He who made﴾ etc. a substitute (badal) for "your Lord" in ﴿Your Lord said: Call upon Me﴾ [Ghafir: 60], then the clause ﴿Allah is He who made the earth a resting-place for you﴾ becomes a fresh, initiatory resumptive clause (isti'naf ibtida'i).

The relative pronoun and its relative clause may be an attribute (sifah) of the Name of Majesty, in which case the predicate is His words ﴿That is Allah, your Lord﴾. This is the preferable reading, because the aim is to establish His divinity alone, by the evidence of what is witnessed of the perfection of His workmanship mingled with His blessing.

It is also permissible for the relative pronoun to be the predicate, in which case the predicate is used for the purpose of bestowing favour and of drawing lessons. Since the primary aim of this verse is the bestowal of favour, as indicated by His words "for you" (lakum), the earth is mentioned before the heaven, because benefit from it is perceptible. The heaven is mentioned after it, as one evokes a thing by its opposite, together with the intent of depositing in it the proofs of the science of cosmology (al-hay'ah) for those among them who have the readiness to reflect upon it and to follow its conditions, despite the variation of faculties and the succession of generations and the expansion of knowledge.

Al-qarar (stability, a fixed resting-place) is originally a verbal noun from qarra, meaning "to be still." Here it is one of the attributes of the earth, since it functions as a predicate concerning the earth. The meaning admits of the following: that He made it stable, not swaying or agitated, so that it was not like a ball of air, agitated and moving; and had it not been stable, people would have been in hardship from its turbulence and quaking, which could lead most of them to destruction. This is the sense of His words ﴿And We placed in the earth firm mountains lest it shake with them﴾ [al-Anbiya': 31] in the Surah of al-Anbiya'.

It is also possible that the meaning is: He made the earth possessing a resting-place, that is, a resting-place for you; that is, He made it a place of settlement for you, like His words, exalted is He, ﴿And We gave them refuge on a high ground, a place of stability and springs﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 50]. That is, He created it in a manner suited to settling upon it, by making it dry and not flowing. Had He willed, He would have made the surface of the earth fluid like quicksilver or like a wheel, so that a person would never cease sinking into it, rising at times and sinking at others, and would hardly remain in one state. Such is the case of the middle of the salt-marsh of al-Takamart, called Shatt al-Jarid, which separates Nafta and Nafzawa in the south of Tunisia; for in it there are stretches where, when caravans walk through them, they sink into the ground and cannot be recovered. For this reason caravans do not traverse them except with guides who know the paths of travel by means of erected markers. Thus the creation of the earth is a sign of the great power of Allah, of the subtle precision of His wisdom, and of His mercy toward human beings and animals, for whom the surface of the earth is inhabited.

Al-bina' (building) is what is raised in height upon the earth for protection from heat, cold, rain and beasts. Describing the heaven as a building proceeds by way of eloquent metaphor (al-tashbih al-baligh). The discussion of it has already been treated comprehensively at His words, exalted is He, ﴿Who made the earth for you as a bed and the heaven as a building﴾ [al-Baqarah: 22] in the Surah of al-Baqarah.

* * *

﴿And He shaped you and made your forms good, and provided you with good things﴾.

Undoubtedly, the wisdom of Allah, exalted is He, which was concerned with bringing into being the worlds surrounding human beings, in forms suited to human life and comfort, was also concerned with bringing the human being into existence in his own essence in a form suited to him for the duration of his species' survival upon the earth and under the canopy of the heaven. For this reason, after the reminder of what He prepared for him through the creation of the earth and heaven, He followed it with a reminder that He created him fulfilling his welfare and comfort.

He expressed this creation with the verb "He shaped you" (sawwarakum), because shaping (al-tasywir) is creation in a desired form that indicates care. Do you not see His words, exalted is He, ﴿We created you, then We shaped you﴾ [al-A'raf: 11]? It entails the goodness of forms. For this reason, in regard to the creation of the human being, He turned away from the verb "made" (ja'ala) to the verb "shaped" in His words "and He shaped you." It is like His words, exalted is He, ﴿Who created you, then proportioned you, then balanced you﴾ [al-Infitar: 7] ﴿in whatever form He willed﴾ [al-Infitar: 8]. Then He stated explicitly what the verb of shaping entails of perfection and beautification, in His words ﴿and made your forms good﴾.

The "fa" (then/so) in His words ﴿fa-ahsana suwarakum﴾ is a conjunctive particle joining one sentence to another and indicates sequence: He brought the human form into existence, and it came out good.

He conjoined to this lesson and favour another favour which also contains a lesson, namely that He created you in the best form, then provided you with the best sustenance. Thus He combined for you bringing into existence and sustaining. Since sustenance (al-rizq), in its outward aspect, is a desire, and since it includes the wisdom of sustaining the body with means of renewing its vital powers, and since in His words "provided you" (razaqakum) there is an allusion to the blessing of lasting existence, so that the human being is not among the beings that appear upon the earth and then vanish within a short time, He combined for him goodness of bringing into being and goodness of sustenance. He made that by which the life is sustained, namely sustenance, from among the best of good things, in contrast to the sustenance of the rest of the species of animals.

* * *

﴿That is Allah, your Lord; so blessed is Allah, the Lord of the worlds﴾.

The position of "That is Allah, your Lord" is like the position of its counterpart mentioned just before. Repeating this is an emphatic reiteration to make them face up to the folly of their opinion in worshipping other than Him, by way of allusion, as indicated by the preceding parallel in His words ﴿There is no god but He; so how are you deluded?﴾ [Ghafir: 62], and by the context of His words here ﴿There is no god but He, so call upon Him, making the religion sincerely His﴾ [Ghafir: 65].

As a consequence of what has been mentioned of His wonderful workmanship and His abundant bounty, praise of Him is initiated by what indicates His possession of the great attributes of perfection. So He said: "so blessed is Allah." The verb tabaraka is of the pattern of mufa'alah, used figuratively with the force of the root from which the verb is derived. It is derived from a fixed noun, which is barakah (blessing), and barakah is a noun denoting the increase of good. The manifestation of the Name of Majesty together with the verb tabaraka, rather than using a pronoun even though its name has preceded, is so that the sentence may be a self-standing expression of praise.

"Lord of the worlds" means the Creator of the species of rational beings: humankind, the angels, and the jinn. This description is part of the completion of the praise, because mentioning His lordship over the worlds, which include the noblest of the species of existents, brings to mind what He has bestowed upon them of the good things of bringing into being and sustaining.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 40, verse 65:

﴿He is the Living; there is no god but Him, so call upon Him, sincere in devotion to Him, the religion.﴾

This is a third resumptive statement (isti'naf) for the progression in establishing His true divinity by establishing what befits it, namely complete life. This sentence is thus a preface to the sentence ﴿there is no god but Him﴾, and the establishment of necessary life for His essence. The One who is the Lord of the worlds, who brought them into existence in the most perfect states and supplied them with what sustains them through the passage of time, is without doubt described by true life, because the one who administers creation across the long ages must necessarily be described by life. Life, despite the difficulty in defining it among the philosophers and theologians, is an existential attribute that makes whoever it subsists in capable of perception, will, and action. Its discussion has already preceded at His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿You were dead and He gave you life﴾ [al-Baqarah: 28] in Surat al-Baqarah.

If the attribution of this attribute to its bearer is preceded by non-existence, then it is contingent, transient life, like the life of the angels, the life of spirits, the life of humans, the life of animals, and the life of insects. Thus it varies among its bearers according to the variation of its strength in them, and varies within one bearer according to the variation of times, like the variation of a single person's life in youth and his life in old age, and like a person's life when active and his life when asleep. By this variation it comes to fade and then cease, and the effect of its variation appears in the variation of its effects of perception, will, and action.

If the attribution of this attribute to its bearer is eternal, not preceded by non-existence, then it is the life of the Necessary Being, glory be to Him, and it is necessary life, essential. It is the true life, because it is not subject to deficiency or cessation. Therefore the Living in truth is God, Exalted, as the form of restriction in His saying ﴿He is the Living﴾ indicates. It is a figurative restriction (qasr idda'i), disregarding the life of everything else among the living, because their life is contingent and subject to extinction and cessation.

So the position of His saying ﴿there is no god but Him﴾ is the position of the conclusion from the proof, because everyone other than Him has no necessary life; he is therefore subject to cessation, so how could he be a god who administers the world? All that is worshipped besides God falls into the following categories: that which is not at all described by life, such as idols of stone, wood, or metal, and like the stars, the sun, the moon, and trees; that which is described by contingent life that does not cease, such as the angels; and that which is described by contingent life that ceases, among the objects of human worship, such as Buddha and Brahma, not to mention the worshipped cows and serpents. He, Exalted, said ﴿And those you call upon besides God create nothing, and they are created﴾ [al-Nahl: 20], meaning none of them is able to act by bringing into existence or giving life, and he is created, i.e., subject to life. ﴿They are dead, not living, and they do not perceive when they will be resurrected﴾ [al-Nahl: 21]. He made the negation of life from them, whether presently or in their eventual state, a proof of the negation of their divinity, and made the negation of their perception of certain perceptible things a proof of the negation of their divinity.

After the clarity of the proof for His sole divinity, the command to worship Him alone, not associating anyone else with Him in worship, is derived from it, since His singular entitlement to be worshipped is established.

Du'a' (supplication): worship, because it is accompanied by request and calling at its beginning and often during it, since supplication is the sign of the soul's humbling and submission, as was mentioned earlier at His saying, ﴿Your Lord said: call upon Me, I will respond to you﴾ [Ghafir: 60], and as in His later saying ﴿Rather, we did not used to call upon anything before﴾ [Ghafir: 74].

Ikhlas (sincerity): singling out and purifying a thing from what contradicts or corrupts it.

Din (religion): dealing, and it is applied to obedience, which is what is intended here, because it is the most intense kind of dealing between the obedient and the one obeyed. The meaning: since He is the Living, not the idols, and there is no god other than Him, worship Him without associating anyone else with Him in worship.

Included in the essence of sincerity, at the primary level, is abandoning showing off (riya') in worship, because riya' is that the worshipper intends by his worship that people see him, whether this intention is purely that or mixed with the intention of drawing near to God. All of that does not escape the attainment of some share in that worship for other than God, even if that share is not in its essence. This is the meaning of what came in the hadith: "Indeed, showing off is the minor shirk."

The placement of (lahu), which relates to mukhlisin, before the object of mukhlisin is because it is the more important here, since it is more closely connected to its complement than the object is to its governing verb.

* * *

﴿Praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds.﴾

It may be an act of praising God, as is the case with such phrases in most of their usages, as already mentioned in Surat al-Fatihah. So it may be connected to the verb "call upon Him" under an implied verb of speech, meaning: saying, ﴿Praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds﴾, or: say, ﴿Praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds﴾. The indicator of the omitted element is that such a sentence is frequently used on people's tongues, so it became like a proverb for expressing praise of God. The meaning: worship Him through action and through praising Him and thanking Him.

It may also be an independent statement intended to express praise of God from Himself, as a teaching to people on how to praise Him, as has been mentioned among the aspects of its counterparts in Surat al-Fatihah.

Or it may be spoken upon the tongue of the Messenger (ﷺ), in the manner of His saying, ﴿So the last of the people who did wrong was cut off, and praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-An'am: 45], following His saying ﴿Say: Tell Me, if the punishment of God comes upon you or the Hour comes upon you, would you call upon other than God, if you are truthful?﴾ [al-An'am: 40] and the verses that follow, in Surat al-An'am.

In my view, it is permissible that al-hamd be a verbal noun brought in place of its verb with the sense of a command, meaning: praise God, Lord of the worlds. It was shifted from the accusative to the nominative to indicate permanence and stability, as was mentioned at the beginning of al-Fatihah.

Separating the sentence from the preceding speech is more suitable for the first and fourth possibilities.

﴿Say: I have been forbidden to worship those whom you invoke besides God, now that the clear proofs have come to me from my Lord, and I have been commanded to submit to the Lord of the worlds.﴾

This is a parenthetical clause (*jumla mu'tarida*, a clause inserted within the argument) placed between the proofs of Divine unity (*wahdaniyya*) drawn from the cosmic and the inner signs, so that they may act upon its requirement in themselves by worshipping God alone. It moves on to establishing the proof of Divine unity through the report of the Divine revelation, which abolishes the worship of other than God on the tongue of His Messenger ﷺ, so that he may act upon it in himself and convey it to them, and they may know that it is God's ruling concerning them, and that they have no excuse for heedlessness of it, or for failing to perfect reflection upon it, or for deficiency in drawing its conclusions, after a Messenger from God has come to them, clarifying for them various kinds of clarification, from demonstrative (*burhaniyya*) proofs and from persuasive (*iqna'iyya*) proofs brought close to understanding.

This Messenger ﷺ calls them only to what he wills for himself; he is sincere in counsel to them, and guides them to the argument, so that the rational proofs reinforce one another with the proofs of the Divine command, such that the refutation of their doctrine of associating partners (*shirk*) becomes strong.
