For what was revealed of the revelation contained rational and persuasive proofs, divine commands, admonitions and encouragements, and all of this revolves around affirming that God, exalted is He, is singular in divinity and lordship, a singularity absolute, not mixed with any trace of partnership, even apparently, as partnership mixes with many of the other attributes, such as sovereignty and ownership, praise, benefit and harm, generosity and assistance, and that is abundant.

Thus His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Say: I have been forbidden to worship those whom you invoke besides God, now that the clear proofs have come to me from my Lord﴾ is an abolition of the worship of other than God, by a statement that indicates warning and intimidation, after this had been abolished by the force of the argument concerning the intended meaning. This is an indirect indication (*dalala kinaiyya*), because the prohibition entails a warning.

He mentioned the coming of the clear proofs within this report as an allusion to other paths of proof for God's singularity in divinity, which had been repeated before the revelation of this verse. The placing of the predicate's subject, the pronoun (*inni*, "I"), before the verbal predicate serves to strengthen the ruling, like the structure: "He gives abundantly." The specification of his own self with this prohibition, rather than associating them in that matter, is in view of the purpose mentioned earlier, together with the knowledge that they are themselves forbidden from it; otherwise there would be no benefit to them in conveying this statement. The Messenger ﷺ, from the time of his upbringing, never prostrated to an idol at all, and that was a diversion by God, exalted is He, from it, by a divine inspiration (*ilham*) as a foreshadowing (*irhas*) of his prophethood.

*Lamma* is either a particle or an adverb, according to a difference among them. Whichever it is, it is a word that indicates the coincidence of the content of two clauses that follow it, which resemble the two clauses of a conditional and its consequence; for this reason they call it *lamma* of timing (*tawqitiyya*), and the occurrence of this is in past time. So His saying, ﴿now that the clear proofs have come to me from my Lord﴾ is a timing of his prohibition against worshipping other than God by the time of the coming of the clear proofs, that is, the clear proofs of revelation in the past; and this requires that the prohibition did not exist before the time of the coming of the clear proofs.

The intention behind attributing the state of being prohibited to the Messenger ﷺ is an allusion to the prohibition of the polytheists, for the command that he say this has no purpose except conveying it to them; otherwise there is no benefit for them in being informed that the Messenger, upon him be prayer and peace, is forbidden to worship those whom they invoke besides God. That is: since I am forbidden from that, then consider your own affair and employ your insight in it, so as to drive them to reflect upon the proofs with a gentle, subtle drive, in order to follow him in what he forbids. This is as was stated explicitly, not allusively, in the saying of Abraham, peace be upon him, to his father: ﴿O my father, indeed there has come to me of knowledge what has not come to you, so follow me; I will guide you to a straight path﴾ [Maryam: 43] ﴿O my father, do not worship Satan; indeed Satan has been, to the Most Merciful, disobedient﴾ [Maryam: 44]. The verb is built in the passive form (*nai'b al-fa'il*) to make evident that the one who prohibits is God, exalted is He, by the context of conveyance and messengership.

The meaning of "invoke" (*al-du'a*) in His saying ﴿whom you invoke﴾ may be on its literal sense of invocation, which is the speech by which one asks for a need; and it may be in the sense of worship, as was mentioned earlier in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And your Lord said: Call upon Me, I will respond to you﴾ [Ghafir: 60]. Then the deviation from saying "that I worship those whom you worship" is for variety of expression (*tafannun*).

The *min* in His saying ﴿from my Lord﴾ is for origin (*ibtida'iyya*). The genitive governed by *min* was made an attribute of "Lord" (*rabb*) joined to the first-person pronoun, rather than making its object a pronoun returning to the Divine name (Allah), in order to show (the noun) in a place where the pronoun would be expected, contrary to what the apparent structure requires, to instil awe in the hearts of those addressed by the allusion, so that they know that this prohibition and the coming of the clear proofs are from the side of their Lord and their Lord's Lord, so they cannot do otherwise than obey Him. For this reason He reinforced it by attaching "Lord" to all, in His saying ﴿and I have been commanded to submit to the Lord of the worlds﴾, that is, your Lord and the Lord of others besides you, so there is no turning away for you from His obedience.

*Islam* means submission (*al-inqiyad*) by word and deed, and its verb is transitive; its object is frequently omitted, so it is treated as intransitive. Its underlying form is: "he submitted himself," or "his essence," or "his face," as is stated explicitly in such sayings as His, exalted is He, ﴿Say: I have submitted my face to God﴾ [Al 'Imran: 20]. Among its uses as intransitive is His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Say: I have submitted my face to God﴾ [Al 'Imran: 20] in the Surah of Al 'Imran, and His saying, exalted is He, ﴿When his Lord said to him, "Submit," he said, "I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds"﴾ [al-Baqara: 131] in the Surah of al-Baqara. Likewise it is here.

﴿He is the One who created you from dust, then from a drop of semen, then from a clinging clot, then He brings you forth as a child, then [He lets you live] that you reach your maturity, then that you become elders. Among you is one who dies before that, and [He lets you live] that you reach a specified term, and perhaps you will understand.﴾

[p. 198]

This is the fourth resumptive sentence (istinaf) after the sentence ﴿He is the Living﴾ [Ghafir: 65] and what branches from it, all of which arise from one another. This is a reminder of the blessing of bringing into existence, which is a blessing because existence is a dignity, while non-existence receives no care.

Within it is embedded the proof for the originative creation (ibda').

The discussion of the stages of human creation has already been presented in Surat al-Hajj, and part of it was discussed in Surat Fatir.

Al-tifl (the child) is a noun that applies to the singular, the dual, and the plural, for the masculine and the feminine. God Most High said: ﴿or the children who have not yet attained knowledge of women's private matters﴾ [al-Nur: 31]. It may also be inflected for number, so one says: tifl, tiflan, and atfal.

The lams in His words ﴿then that you reach your maturity﴾ and what is conjoined to it with thumma are connected to an omitted element, whose estimated form is: "then He leaves you [to live]," or "then He brings you into being, that you reach your maturity." These are lams of causation (ta'lil), used in the sense of "until," because the end intended by God resembles the cause in what it leads to. A parallel to this was discussed in Surat al-Hajj.

His words ﴿and that you reach a specified term﴾ are conjoined to ﴿that you become elders﴾, meaning that elderly age has an end, which is the specified term, that is, death, so there is no stage after elderly age. As for the term appointed for those who die before reaching elderly age, it is understood from His words ﴿among you is one who dies before that﴾ that "before that" refers to some of these stages, i.e., he dies before he comes out as a child, which is the miscarriage, or before he reaches maturity, or he dies before he becomes an elder.

Because it is connected only to what follows it, it was conjoined with waw and not with thumma, as the other prepositional phrases were conjoined. The meaning is that God has decreed the extinction of generations and has created them with other generations. So the living one's end is perishing, however long his life lasts. And since He created him in a state that inevitably leads to perishing, He knew that among the ends in that creation is that they reach a specified term.

Qabl is built on the ḍamma, with the intention of the meaning of the omitted genitive complement, i.e., "before what has been mentioned." Al-ashudd: strength in the body, which lies between eighteen and thirty years, and it was discussed in Surat Yusuf.

Shuyukh: the plural of shaykh, who is one who has reached the age of fifty to eighty. It was discussed at His words ﴿and this is my husband, an old man﴾ [Hud: 72] in Surat Hud.

In shuyukh the shin may be pronounced with a ḍamma, and this was the reading of Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Hafs from 'Asim, Abu Ja'far, Ya'qub, and Khalaf. It may also be pronounced with a kasra, and this was the reading of Ibn Kathir, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i.

His words ﴿and perhaps you will understand﴾ are conjoined to ﴿and that you reach a specified term﴾. The meaning is that among what God intends by creating humans in the stated state is that in that form there be a sign for individuals of the existence of this Creator who produced this wondrous creation, and of His singularity in divinity, and that nothing other than Him deserves the attribute of divinity. Whoever among people understands this has been guided to what was intended by it, and whoever does not understand this is like one lacking intellect. For this reason, the verb ta'qiluna is not given an object or a prepositional complement, because it is treated as intransitive, meaning: in the hope that you may have intellects. This is what God intends by that creation, and it is part of His wisdom that He made the wondrous creation a cause for many matters.

Fifth resumption (*istinaf*). Its placement is appropriate in relation to His saying ﴿He it is who created you from dust﴾ [Ghafir: 67], through His saying ﴿then He brings you out as a child﴾ [Ghafir: 67], and on to ﴿and among you is one who is taken in death before, so that you may reach a specified term, and perhaps you will reason﴾ [Ghafir: 67]. For among the first things one hopes they will understand is that wondrous disposal, namely the creation of life in a human being when He forms him after he was a lifeless body, and the creation of death in him when his term ends after he was living and acting by his own strength and management.

So the meaning of ﴿He gives life﴾ is that He brings the created thing into existence as living. The meaning of ﴿and causes death﴾ is that He annihilates life from the one who was living, and this is the locus of the lesson.

As for the possibility of restoring life after death, it is understood by the indication of rational analogy (*qiyas al-tamthil al-'aqli*, analogical reasoning by comparison), and it is not the explicit wording of the verse. The purpose is to express gratitude for life, following His saying before this, ﴿He it is who created you from dust﴾ [Ghafir: 67], through His saying ﴿then He brings you out as a child﴾ [Ghafir: 67].

In His saying ﴿He gives life and causes death﴾ [al-Dukhan: 8] there is the rhetorical embellishment called *tibaq* (antithesis).

Following upon this statement is an announcement that when He wills a matter of creative existence, whether giving life, causing death, or something else, He is able to do it without hesitation or effort, merely by the connection of His power to the object of power. That connection is the directing of His power toward bringing into existence or annihilating. Thus the *fa'* in His saying ﴿when He decrees a matter﴾ is the *fa'* of deriving the announcement of what follows from the announcement of what precedes it.

His saying *kun* (be!) is an analogy for the connection of power to the object of power without delay, without preparation, without exertion or treatment, like the situation of one who wants another to perform a task and so does nothing more than direct a command to him. The utterance issuing from the speaker is among the swiftest and easiest of human acts, and for bringing this close to understanding, the briefest verb was chosen, *kun*, which is composed of two letters, one moving and one still.

[p. 200]

﴿Have you not considered those who dispute concerning the signs of Allah, how they are turned away?﴾ ﴿Those who denied the Book and that with which We sent Our messengers. They will soon know,﴾ ﴿when the shackles will be around their necks and the chains, they will be dragged,﴾ ﴿in the scalding water, then in the Fire they will be burned.﴾

This surah is built upon refuting the disputation of those who dispute concerning the signs of Allah, a disputation of denial and evasion (al-tawarruk), as was mentioned earlier at the beginning of the surah, since its opening included the words ﴿None dispute concerning the signs of Allah except those who disbelieve﴾ [Ghafir: 4]. This recurred five times in it. He thus drew attention to refuting their disputation in every occasion of refutation, for He began refuting it in general after the first three verses with His words ﴿None dispute concerning the signs of Allah except those who disbelieve﴾ [Ghafir: 4], then refuted it with His words ﴿Those who dispute concerning the signs of Allah without any authority having come to them, it is greatly hateful in the sight of Allah﴾ [Ghafir: 35], then with His words ﴿Indeed, those who dispute concerning the signs of Allah without any authority having come to them, there is nothing in their breasts except pride﴾ [Ghafir: 56], then with His words ﴿Have you not considered those who dispute concerning the signs of Allah, how they are turned away?﴾.

All of this is an indication that what drives them to dispute the signs of Allah is what the Qur'an contains of refutation of polytheism. Therefore, after each method of refuting their polytheism, He follows it with reproach of their disputation concerning the signs of Allah. So the clause ﴿Have you not considered those who dispute concerning the signs of Allah﴾ is a resumptive clause (musta'anifah) expressing astonishment at their turning away from belief after those clear proofs.

The interrogative is used for taqrir (affirmation through a negative question), and although it is negated in form, its meaning is affirmation, as mentioned more than once before, including at His words ﴿He said, "Have you not believed?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 260] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The verb "seeing" (al-ru'yah) is cognitive (ilmiyyah), and its action is suspended by the interrogative with ﴿how they are turned away?﴾. Anna (أنّى) here means "how" (kayfa), and it is used to express astonishment, like His words ﴿How can I have a son when no man has touched me?﴾ [Al 'Imran: 47]. That is: Have you seen the strangeness of their turning away from belief in the Qur'an by a turning force whose origin is not clear? For this reason the verb ﴿yusrafun﴾ is built in the passive voice, because the cause of their turning away from the signs is none other than themselves.

It is also possible that anna means "where" (ayna), i.e., "Do you not marvel from where a turner turns them away from faith, so that they dispute the signs of Allah, even though the pretexts for their turning away from faith are absent, given what has been repeated of the proofs of the horizons and of themselves, and what they witnessed of the end of those who disputed the signs of Allah before them?" This is like the speaker who marvels at someone's action and says, "Where are you being taken?"

Building the verb ﴿yusrafun﴾ in the passive on this view is for astonishment at the turning force that turns them, which is not located in any place other than their own selves.

The phrase ﴿those who denied the Book﴾ is in apposition (badal) to ﴿those who dispute﴾, because the two relative clauses apply to one thing: denial is what the disputation is, and "the Book" is the Qur'an.

The conjunction in ﴿and that with which We sent Our messengers﴾ may be on its original basis, which requires difference, so the meaning would be: "and that with which We sent Our messengers" of Books before the Qur'an. Their denial of what the messengers were sent with would then mean their denial of all religions, as in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿They did not measure Allah with His true measure when they said, "Allah has not sent down anything upon a human."﴾ [al-An'am: 91]. It is also possible that it refers to denial of the Resurrection: when Muhammad (ﷺ) brought the affirmation of the Resurrection, perhaps they asked the People of the Book about it, and they affirmed it, so the polytheists rejected all the laws for that reason.

It is also possible that the conjunction is one of synonymy, whose purpose is emphasis, and "Our messengers" refers to Muhammad (ﷺ), as in His saying, ﴿The people of Noah denied the messengers﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 105], meaning the single messenger Noah. Yet in the conjunction there is an additional benefit beyond what is in the conjoined term: that what the Messenger (ﷺ) brought includes many admonitions and much guidance that is not from the Qur'an.

Their threat is consequent upon their denial, with what they will meet on the Day of Resurrection, so it is said ﴿They will soon know﴾, [p. 202] i.e., they will soon find the punishment they used to dispute about, and they will know it. He expressed their finding the punishment by knowing it, in view of their continued ignorance of the Resurrection and their obstinacy after understanding what the Messenger (ﷺ) said. So they were warned that what they had been ignorant of they would come to realize on that day, like the saying of people: "You will know from him what you do not know." Abu 'Ali al-Basir said:

"So you will blame your opinion regarding those whom you preferred over me, and you will know from them what you did not know."

The object of ﴿they know﴾ is omitted because it is indicated by ﴿denied the Book﴾, i.e., they will realize what they denied.

The adverbial clause in ﴿when the shackles are around their necks﴾ is connected to (they know), i.e., they will know at that time. The normal function of "idh" is to be a noun for past time, but here it is used for future time by the indication of "soon" (sawfa). So it is either a metaphorical usage through the relation of generality, or a subsidiary metaphor (isti'arah tab'iyyah) likening the certainly occurring future time to the past. This has been repeated. Among its examples is its being followed by "yawm" (day), as in His saying ﴿On that day it will report its news﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 4], and His saying ﴿On that day the believers will rejoice in the victory of Allah﴾ [al-Rum: 4]. The first thing they will know, when the shackles are around their necks, is that they will certainly realize the occurrence of the Resurrection.

The word "al-aghlal" is the plural of "ghull", with a dammah on the ghayn, and it is a ring of leather or iron encircling the neck, to which a chain of iron is attached, or a leather strap by which the criminal or captive is held.

The word "al-salasil" is the plural of "silsilah", with a kasrah on both sins, and it is a collection of thick rings of iron joined one to another.

Among the matters I have seen: one day, in his lesson on tafsir, Shaykh Ibn 'Arafah was asked: "Could this verse be a basis for what the rulers of the Maghrib, may Allah set them right, do in placing criminals in shackles and chains, by analogy with Allah's punishments?" Just as they derived some forms of punishment from the actions of the people of Lot, such as stoning with stones or throwing from a height. He answered in the negative, because placing a shackle on the neck is a kind of imagery, and the criminal is only bound by the hand. He said: "They only drew analogy from Allah's act in this world, and one may not draw analogy from His conduct in the Hereafter, because the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade burning with fire, and said: 'Only the Lord of Might punishes with it.'"

[p. 203] The clause ﴿they are dragged﴾ and ﴿in the scalding water﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "their necks" or from the pronoun in "they know".

Al-sahb means dragging, and it combines pain and humiliation. Al-hamim is the most intense heat.

The conjunction "thumma" (then) conjoins the clause ﴿in the Fire they are burned﴾ to the clause ﴿they are dragged in the scalding water﴾. The normal function of "thumma" when it conjoins clauses is a graded delay (al-tarakhi al-rutbi), since their being burned by the Fire is more severe in their punishment than being dragged over the Fire. So it is an ascent in describing the punishment which was summarized by His words ﴿they will soon know﴾. The burning by fire occurs right after the dragging, whether with a delay or without one.

Al-sajr means filling the oven with fuel to strengthen the fire within it. So ascribing the verb ﴿they are burned﴾ to their pronoun is a metaphorical ascription, because what is actually set aflame is their place in Hell. The purpose of ascribing the burning to them is to emphasize the connection of the burning to them. Or it is a subsidiary metaphor, likening them to the oven in which the fire settles in their interiors, as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿By which that which is in their bellies and their skins will be melted﴾ [al-Hajj: 20].

All of this is an indication that what drives them to dispute the signs of Allah is what the Qur'an contains of refutation of polytheism. Therefore, after each method of refuting their polytheism, He follows it with reproach of their disputation concerning the signs of Allah. For this reason the verb ﴿yusrafun﴾ is built in the passive voice, because the cause of their turning away from the signs is none other than themselves.

It is also possible that anna means "where" (ayna), i.e., "Do you not marvel from where a turner turns them away from faith, so that they dispute the signs of Allah, even though the pretexts for their turning away from faith are absent, given what has been repeated of the proofs of the horizons and of themselves, and what they witnessed of the end of those who disputed the signs of Allah before them?" This is like the speaker who marvels at someone's action and says, "Where are you being taken?"

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 40, verse 73–76:

﴿Then it will be said to them, "Where are those you used to associate with God?"﴾ ﴿They will say, "They have vanished from us; rather, we did not used to call upon anything before." Thus does God lead astray the disbelievers.﴾ ﴿That is because you used to exult in the land without right, and because you used to be insolent.﴾ ﴿Enter the gates of Hell, to abide therein. Evil is the abode of the arrogant.﴾

Thumma (then) here denotes a sequence of rank (al-tarakhi al-rutbi) without doubt, because this statement is made to them before they enter the Fire, as evidenced by the fact that among what occurs at the end of the speech is "Enter the gates of Hell," and entering the gates of Hell comes before being dragged into its boiling water and being cast into its fire. This saying is an escalation in their rebuke and in the public declaration of the folly of their opinions before the people of the gathering, which is more painful to the soul than physical pain. Also, this saying is a preface to imposing the punishment upon them, since it includes an explanation of the cause of the punishment: the worship of idols, and their arrogance on earth through their disbelief and insolence. It is also an escalation in describing their states, which indicate their punishment, since it rises from the description of their recompense for their association (with God), which is something not surprising to follow from shirk, to the description of their belittling of their gods which they used to worship. That is strange among their conditions, and more indicative of the falsity of the divinity of their idols, and this is the important purpose of the calamities that were imposed upon them in this surah. Thus the position of the clause conjoined by thumma here is like its position in the verse of Abu Nuwas:

"Say: if he ruled, then his father ruled before him, and before him his grandfather ruled long before."
From the point that his grandfather's rule established his father's rule and led to his own rule. This usage is found abundantly.

Qila (it was said) is formulated in the past tense because its occurrence is certain, so it is as if it has occurred and passed; likewise the verb qalu "dallu" (they said "they have vanished").

The one who says to them is a speaker by God's permission. Ayna (where) is an interrogative about the place of a thing whose place is unknown, and the interrogation here is used to alert them to their error and disgrace in the place of standing, for they used to claim that they worshipped the idols so that they would be intercessors for them before God's wrath. When the punishment was decreed upon them and they found no intercessors, they were reminded of what they used to claim, and it was said to them: "Where are those you used to associate with God?" They then hastened to answer before the end of the statement that was addressed to them. The meaning of dallu (they have vanished) is "they are absent," like His saying: "When we have vanished into the earth, shall we indeed be in a new creation?" [al-Sajdah: 10], meaning: we have been hidden in the dust. Then it became apparent to them and they knew that the idols would not benefit them. So they turned away from their saying "they have vanished from us," and said: "Rather, we did not used to call upon anything before," meaning: in the world we did not used to call upon anything that would avail us. So the negation of calling upon anything here refers to the negation of calling upon anything of consequence, as you say: "I thought that so-and-so was something, but when I tested him, he was nothing"; if you have tested him, you did not find any good in him. And in the hadith: "The Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about soothsayers, and he said: 'They are nothing.'" Meaning: they are not anything of consequence in what people seek them for. 'Abbas ibn Mirdas said:

"Indeed I was in war a man of protection, yet I was given nothing and I was not withheld."

This was mentioned earlier at His saying, "You are not on anything until you establish the Torah and the Gospel" [al-Ma'idah: 68], in Surat al-'Uqud, since the meaning is not to deny that they worshipped anything, because that contradicts their saying "they have vanished from us," which requires an implicit acknowledgment of their worship.

Many exegetes explained their saying "Rather, we did not used to call upon anything before" as a denial of idol-worship after having acknowledged it, due to their agitation from terror; so it is like His saying: "Then their trial was only that they said: 'By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists.'" [al-An'am: 23].

It is possible that they had two statements in that position. All of this is before they are gathered into the Fire together with their idols, for then they will be alike, as He said: "Indeed you and what you worship besides God are the fuel of Hell." [al-Anbiya': 98].

The clause "Thus does God lead astray the disbelievers" is an intervening concluding clause (tadhyil mu'tarid) between the parts of the saying addressed to them. The meaning of the demonstrative is wonder at their misguidance, i.e., like their misguidance, God leads astray the disbelievers. By "the disbelievers" is meant the disbelievers in general, so this is not the use of an apparent noun in the place of a pronoun.

The comparison in His saying "Thus does God lead astray the disbelievers" conveys the comparison of God's leading astray of all the disbelievers with His leading astray of those who dispute the signs of God. So the clause "Thus does God lead astray the disbelievers" is a concluding clause, meaning: like the leading astray of those who dispute the signs of God, God leads astray all the disbelievers. Thus the leading astray of those who dispute is the thing compared, and the leading astray of all the disbelievers is the thing compared to. The comparison is a metonymy for the fact that the leading astray of those who dispute the signs of God has reached the strength of its kind, such that every kind of hidden error is likened to it; and it is a metonymy for the fact that the disputing of these people concerning the signs of God is the greatest disbelief.

The comparison proceeds on its basic principle, which is attaching a deficient thing to a complete one in an attribute, and it is not of the kind of "And thus We made you a middle nation" [al-Baqarah: 143], nor is it the counterpart of his earlier saying "Thus are turned away those who used to deny the signs of God" [Ghafir: 63].

His saying "That is because you used to exult..." completes the saying addressed to them at the time when the shackles are on their necks. The demonstrative refers to what they are in of punishment.

In both places "ma" is a verbal noun (masdariyyah), meaning: that is caused by your exultation and your insolence, which were yours in the world. And "al-ard" (the land) is used absolutely for the world.

Al-farah (exultation) is gladness and a person's contentment with his states; it is an inner emotional state. Al-maraḥ is what appears on the exultant one of movements in his walk, his gaze, his dealings with people, his speech, and his arrogance; it is an outward bearing.

"Without right" is governed by each of (tafrahun and tamrahun): meaning, you exult in what pleases you of falsehood and you swagger with falsehood. So among the effects of their exultation in falsehood is their presumption against the Messenger (ﷺ), and among the insolence in falsehood is their mockery of the Messenger (ﷺ) and the believers. God said: "And when they pass by them, they wink at one another" [al-Mutaffifin: 30]; "And when they return to their people, they return jesting" [al-Mutaffifin: 31]. So whenever exultation is mentioned as forbidden in the Qur'an, what is meant is this category of it, like His saying: "When his people said to him: 'Do not exult; indeed God does not love the exultant.'" [al-Qasas: 76], not every exultation, for God granted the believers a favour through exultation in His saying: "On that day the believers will rejoice in the victory of God" [al-Rum: 4-5].

Between tafrahun and tamrahun there is a muharraf paronomasia (jinas).

The clause "Enter the gates of Hell" may be a resumptive explanatory clause (isti'naf bayani), because when they heard the rebuke and the reproach and became certain that no intercessor would avail them, they waited to see what would be commanded concerning them, so it was said to them: "Enter the gates of Hell." It may also be a substitutive clause of inclusion (badal ishtimal) from the clause "That is because you used to exult..." etc., since what the demonstrative refers to is the punishment witnessed by them, and it includes their entry into the gates of Hell and their abiding therein.

Entering the gates is a metonymy for being in Hell, because gates are only made so that one may pass through them to a house or the like.

"Khalidin" (abiding) is a circumstantial clause of anticipation (hal muqaddarah), meaning: their abiding being decreed.

Following this is "Evil is the abode of the arrogant," and the object of the dispraise is omitted, because the mention of Hell indicates it, meaning: "Evil is the abode of the arrogant: Hell." The verb bi'sa did not take the feminine ta' because its agent apparently is "mathwa" (abode); for what matters is the attribution of the verb of dispraise or praise to the noun mentioned after them. As for the noun of the object of praise/dispraise, it is in the position of explanation after a general statement, so it is a subject whose predicate is omitted, or the predicate of an omitted subject. For this reason the construction of ni'ma and bi'sa is counted among the means of amplification (itnab).

"Al-mathwa" is the place of dwelling, and "al-thawa" is lasting residence. The word mathwa was chosen over "mudkhal" (entrance), which would suit "udkhulu," because mathwa is more indicative of eternity, so it is more fitting for their distress.

By "al-mutakabbirin" (the arrogant) is primarily meant those addressed, because they disputed the signs of God out of arrogance in their breasts, as He said: "Indeed those who dispute the signs of God without authority that has come to them, there is in their breasts only pride, which they will never attain." [Ghafir: 56]; and because their arrogance stems from their exultation.

The apparent noun "al-mutakabbirin" was used instead of their pronoun to indicate that among the causes of their falling into the Fire is their arrogance toward the Messengers. And so that every person characterised by arrogance has a share of deserving punishment if he does not repent and his good deeds do not outweigh his bad deeds, if he is one of the people of faith.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 40, verse 73–76:

﴿Then it will be said to them, "Where are those you used to associate with God?"﴾ ﴿They will say, "They have vanished from us; rather, we did not used to call upon anything before." Thus does God lead astray the disbelievers.﴾ ﴿That is because you used to exult in the land without right, and because you used to be insolent.﴾ ﴿Enter the gates of Hell, to abide therein. Evil is the abode of the arrogant.﴾

Thumma (then) here denotes a sequence of rank (al-tarakhi al-rutbi) without doubt, because this statement is made to them before they enter the Fire, as evidenced by the fact that among what occurs at the end of the speech is "Enter the gates of Hell," and entering the gates of Hell comes before being dragged into its boiling water and being cast into its fire. This saying is an escalation in their rebuke and in the public declaration of the folly of their opinions before the people of the gathering, which is more painful to the soul than physical pain. Also, this saying is a preface to imposing the punishment upon them, since it includes an explanation of the cause of the punishment: the worship of idols, and their arrogance on earth through their disbelief and insolence. It is also an escalation in describing their states, which indicate their punishment, since it rises from the description of their recompense for their association (with God), which is something not surprising to follow from shirk, to the description of their belittling of their gods which they used to worship. That is strange among their conditions, and more indicative of the falsity of the divinity of their idols, and this is the important purpose of the calamities that were imposed upon them in this surah. Thus the position of the clause conjoined by thumma here is like its position in the verse of Abu Nuwas:

"Say: if he ruled, then his father ruled before him, and before him his grandfather ruled long before."
From the point that his grandfather's rule established his father's rule and led to his own rule. This usage is found abundantly.

Qila (it was said) is formulated in the past tense because its occurrence is certain, so it is as if it has occurred and passed; likewise the verb qalu "dallu" (they said "they have vanished").

The one who says to them is a speaker by God's permission. Ayna (where) is an interrogative about the place of a thing whose place is unknown, and the interrogation here is used to alert them to their error and disgrace in the place of standing, for they used to claim that they worshipped the idols so that they would be intercessors for them before God's wrath. When the punishment was decreed upon them and they found no intercessors, they were reminded of what they used to claim, and it was said to them: "Where are those you used to associate with God?" They then hastened to answer before the end of the statement that was addressed to them. The meaning of dallu (they have vanished) is "they are absent," like His saying: "When we have vanished into the earth, shall we indeed be in a new creation?" [al-Sajdah: 10], meaning: we have been hidden in the dust. Then it became apparent to them and they knew that the idols would not benefit them. So they turned away from their saying "they have vanished from us," and said: "Rather, we did not used to call upon anything before," meaning: in the world we did not used to call upon anything that would avail us. So the negation of calling upon anything here refers to the negation of calling upon anything of consequence, as you say: "I thought that so-and-so was something, but when I tested him, he was nothing"; if you have tested him, you did not find any good in him. And in the hadith: "The Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about soothsayers, and he said: 'They are nothing.'" Meaning: they are not anything of consequence in what people seek them for. 'Abbas ibn Mirdas said:

"Indeed I was in war a man of protection, yet I was given nothing and I was not withheld."

This was mentioned earlier at His saying, "You are not on anything until you establish the Torah and the Gospel" [al-Ma'idah: 68], in Surat al-'Uqud, since the meaning is not to deny that they worshipped anything, because that contradicts their saying "they have vanished from us," which requires an implicit acknowledgment of their worship.

Many exegetes explained their saying "Rather, we did not used to call upon anything before" as a denial of idol-worship after having acknowledged it, due to their agitation from terror; so it is like His saying: "Then their trial was only that they said: 'By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists.'" [al-An'am: 23].

It is possible that they had two statements in that position. All of this is before they are gathered into the Fire together with their idols, for then they will be alike, as He said: "Indeed you and what you worship besides God are the fuel of Hell." [al-Anbiya': 98].

The clause "Thus does God lead astray the disbelievers" is an intervening concluding clause (tadhyil mu'tarid) between the parts of the saying addressed to them. The meaning of the demonstrative is wonder at their misguidance, i.e., like their misguidance, God leads astray the disbelievers. By "the disbelievers" is meant the disbelievers in general, so this is not the use of an apparent noun in the place of a pronoun.

The comparison in His saying "Thus does God lead astray the disbelievers" conveys the comparison of God's leading astray of all the disbelievers with His leading astray of those who dispute the signs of God. So the clause "Thus does God lead astray the disbelievers" is a concluding clause, meaning: like the leading astray of those who dispute the signs of God, God leads astray all the disbelievers. Thus the leading astray of those who dispute is the thing compared, and the leading astray of all the disbelievers is the thing compared to. The comparison is a metonymy for the fact that the leading astray of those who dispute the signs of God has reached the strength of its kind, such that every kind of hidden error is likened to it; and it is a metonymy for the fact that the disputing of these people concerning the signs of God is the greatest disbelief.

The comparison proceeds on its basic principle, which is attaching a deficient thing to a complete one in an attribute, and it is not of the kind of "And thus We made you a middle nation" [al-Baqarah: 143], nor is it the counterpart of his earlier saying "Thus are turned away those who used to deny the signs of God" [Ghafir: 63].

His saying "That is because you used to exult..." completes the saying addressed to them at the time when the shackles are on their necks. The demonstrative refers to what they are in of punishment.

In both places "ma" is a verbal noun (masdariyyah), meaning: that is caused by your exultation and your insolence, which were yours in the world. And "al-ard" (the land) is used absolutely for the world.

Al-farah (exultation) is gladness and a person's contentment with his states; it is an inner emotional state. Al-maraḥ is what appears on the exultant one of movements in his walk, his gaze, his dealings with people, his speech, and his arrogance; it is an outward bearing.

"Without right" is governed by each of (tafrahun and tamrahun): meaning, you exult in what pleases you of falsehood and you swagger with falsehood. So among the effects of their exultation in falsehood is their presumption against the Messenger (ﷺ), and among the insolence in falsehood is their mockery of the Messenger (ﷺ) and the believers. God said: "And when they pass by them, they wink at one another" [al-Mutaffifin: 30]; "And when they return to their people, they return jesting" [al-Mutaffifin: 31]. So whenever exultation is mentioned as forbidden in the Qur'an, what is meant is this category of it, like His saying: "When his people said to him: 'Do not exult; indeed God does not love the exultant.'" [al-Qasas: 76], not every exultation, for God granted the believers a favour through exultation in His saying: "On that day the believers will rejoice in the victory of God" [al-Rum: 4-5].

Between tafrahun and tamrahun there is a muharraf paronomasia (jinas).

The clause "Enter the gates of Hell" may be a resumptive explanatory clause (isti'naf bayani), because when they heard the rebuke and the reproach and became certain that no intercessor would avail them, they waited to see what would be commanded concerning them, so it was said to them: "Enter the gates of Hell." It may also be a substitutive clause of inclusion (badal ishtimal) from the clause "That is because you used to exult..." etc., since what the demonstrative refers to is the punishment witnessed by them, and it includes their entry into the gates of Hell and their abiding therein.

Entering the gates is a metonymy for being in Hell, because gates are only made so that one may pass through them to a house or the like.

"Khalidin" (abiding) is a circumstantial clause of anticipation (hal muqaddarah), meaning: their abiding being decreed.

Following this is "Evil is the abode of the arrogant," and the object of the dispraise is omitted, because the mention of Hell indicates it, meaning: "Evil is the abode of the arrogant: Hell." The verb bi'sa did not take the feminine ta' because its agent apparently is "mathwa" (abode); for what matters is the attribution of the verb of dispraise or praise to the noun mentioned after them. As for the noun of the object of praise/dispraise, it is in the position of explanation after a general statement, so it is a subject whose predicate is omitted, or the predicate of an omitted subject. For this reason the construction of ni'ma and bi'sa is counted among the means of amplification (itnab).

"Al-mathwa" is the place of dwelling, and "al-thawa" is lasting residence. The word mathwa was chosen over "mudkhal" (entrance), which would suit "udkhulu," because mathwa is more indicative of eternity, so it is more fitting for their distress.

By "al-mutakabbirin" (the arrogant) is primarily meant those addressed, because they disputed the signs of God out of arrogance in their breasts, as He said: "Indeed those who dispute the signs of God without authority that has come to them, there is in their breasts only pride, which they will never attain." [Ghafir: 56]; and because their arrogance stems from their exultation.

The apparent noun "al-mutakabbirin" was used instead of their pronoun to indicate that among the causes of their falling into the Fire is their arrogance toward the Messengers. And so that every person characterised by arrogance has a share of deserving punishment if he does not repent and his good deeds do not outweigh his bad deeds, if he is one of the people of faith.

﴿So be patient. Indeed, the promise of Allah is true. And whether We show you part of what We promise them or We take you in death, to Us they will be returned.﴾

Earlier in the surah there was already what contains consolation for the Prophet ﷺ regarding the harm and the determined aversion he received from the polytheists, beginning from His saying at the beginning of the surah ﴿Let not their movement throughout the land deceive you﴾ [Ghafir: 4], then His saying ﴿Have they not traveled through the land and observed how was the end of those before them?﴾ [Ghafir: 21], then His saying ﴿Indeed, We will surely support Our messengers﴾ [Ghafir: 51], then

صفحة ٢٠٨
His saying ﴿So be patient. Indeed, the promise of Allah is true, and ask forgiveness for your sin﴾ [Ghafir: 55], and so on. Here, then, He grounds upon all that preceded, both explicit and allusive, the command of Allah to the Prophet ﷺ to be patient over what he encounters from them. This is like a repetition of His saying earlier ﴿So be patient. Indeed, the promise of Allah is true, and ask forgiveness for your sin﴾ [Ghafir: 55]. Its earlier counterpart came after the promise of victory in His saying ﴿Indeed, We will surely support Our messengers and those who believe in the worldly life and on the day when the witnesses stand﴾ [Ghafir: 51], then His saying ﴿And We had certainly given Moses guidance and caused the Children of Israel to inherit the Scripture﴾ [Ghafir: 53], and so on. When the discourse had completed what Allah had inflicted upon the deniers of worldly punishment, the discourse shifted to mention what they will face in the Hereafter, with His saying ﴿Those who denied the Book and that with which We sent Our messengers—they are going to know﴾ [Ghafir: 70], when ﴿the shackles will be around their necks and the chains﴾ [Ghafir: 71], and the verses. Then He followed it with His saying ﴿So be patient. Indeed, the promise of Allah is true﴾, returning to the beginning, since the command to be patient is grounded upon what was implied by His saying ﴿Let not their movement throughout the land deceive you﴾ [Ghafir: 4], ﴿The people of Noah denied before them﴾ [Ghafir: 5], and the verses, then His saying ﴿And warn them of the approaching Day, when hearts will be at the throats﴾ [Ghafir: 18], then His saying ﴿Have they not traveled through the land and observed﴾ [Ghafir: 21] and what follows. So when the promise of retribution against the deniers of the Prophet ﷺ in this world and the Hereafter was established, He followed it with His saying ﴿So be patient. Indeed, the promise of Allah is true. And whether We show you part of what We promise them﴾. The suitability of the command to be patient after that is that it be an allusion to victory for him. For this reason, the conditional sentence whose two parts are uncertain, whether He shows him some of what Allah has threatened them with or whether he does not see it, is grounded upon the command to be patient. The answer to the condition holds in both states, and it is the meaning of ﴿to Us they will be returned﴾, that is, they cannot escape punishment. Undoubtedly, one of the two uncertainties is that the Prophet ﷺ sees their punishment in this world.

For this reason, the emphasis with ﴿inna﴾ in His saying ﴿Indeed, the promise of Allah is true﴾ [Ghafir: 55] has its place, since the Prophet ﷺ and the believers were slow in perceiving the victory, as He, Exalted, said ﴿And they were shaken until the Messenger and those who believed with him said, "When is the help of Allah?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 214]. So they were treated as one who doubts it, and so His promise was emphasized with the particle of emphasis.

The use of the present tense in His saying ﴿yurja'un﴾ (they are returned) serves to indicate renewal, and so it implies a return to Allah in this world.

His saying ﴿fa-immā nurīnnaka﴾ is a conditional, in which the conditional particle ﴿in﴾ is joined with the superfluous particle ﴿mā﴾ for emphasis, and therefore the energetic nūn (nūn al-tawkīd) attached to the verb of the condition. Joined to it by ﴿aw﴾ is ﴿aw natawaffayannaka﴾, which is a second verb of condition.

The clause ﴿fa-ilaynā yurja'ūn﴾ is the answer to the second verb of condition, because the meaning is that it is its answer. As for the first verb of condition, its answer is omitted and indicated by the beginning of the speech, which is His saying ﴿Indeed, the promise of Allah is true﴾. Its answer is estimated as: ﴿whether We show you part of what We promise them, that is well; or We take you in death, then to Us they will be returned﴾, meaning that they cannot escape from what We promise them.

The parallel of these two conditionals has preceded in Surah Yunus, except that in Surah Yunus it is ﴿ilaynā marji'uhum﴾ [Yunus: 46], while in Surah Ghafir it is ﴿ilaynā yurja'ūn﴾. The difference between the two verses is variation in expression. Also, what is in Yunus required threatening them that Allah is Witness over what they do, that is, over what both groups do, from His saying ﴿And among them are those who listen to you﴾ [Yunus: 42] and His saying ﴿And among them are those who look at you﴾ [Yunus: 43]. So the closing was achieved by His saying ﴿over what they do﴾ [Yunus: 46]. Here, however, the closing corresponds to the condition, so it required formulating the return in the present form ending in waw and nun, and since "their return" is defined by the genitive construction, it implies the known return, which is their return in the Hereafter, unlike His saying "yurja'ūn," which implies a renewed return, as you know.

The meaning is: they are situated within the grip of Our power in this world, whether that happens during your life, like the punishment of the Day of Badr, or after your death, like their killing on the Day of Yamamah. As for the punishment of the Hereafter, that is established for them all the more so. This is like His saying ﴿Or We show you that which We promised them, for indeed We are Able over them﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 42].

The fronting of the prepositional phrase in His saying ﴿fa-ilaynā yurja'ūn﴾ is for the sake of the verse-ending (ri'āyah lil-fāṣilah) and for emphasis.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 40, verse 78:

﴿And We certainly sent messengers before you; of them are those We have related to you, and of them are those We have not related to you. And it was not for any messenger to bring a sign except by the permission of Allah. So when the command of Allah comes, judgment will be passed in truth, and the falsifiers will then lose.﴾

We mentioned, at His saying ﴿None dispute in the signs of Allah except those who disbelieve﴾ [Ghafir: 4], at the beginning of this surah, that among the forms of their disputing about the signs is their showing a lack of conviction in the miracle of the Qur'an, so they would propose signs as they wished, with the aim of confounding the Messenger ﷺ. When the detailed refutation of their misguidance had concluded, through clear proofs, reminders of blessings, warnings with intimidation and encouragement, and the coining of parables from the conditions of the nations that denied, and then the promise to the Messenger ﷺ and the believers of victory and the fulfilment of the promise, this was followed by a reinforcement of the Messenger ﷺ, that his situation was no different from the situation of the messengers before him: they did not bring signs of their own accord, nor in response to the desires of their opponents; rather, the signs are with Allah, who manifests whichever of them He wills, in accordance with His will which runs in line with His knowledge and wisdom. In this there is an implicit rebuttal of those who dispute about the signs of Allah, and an alert to them regarding the error of their assumption that the messengers should stand up to debate the obstinate.

The most important purpose of this verse is His saying ﴿And it was not for any messenger to bring a sign except by the permission of Allah﴾. As for His saying ﴿And We certainly sent messengers before you﴾ etc., it is like an introduction to the purpose, to affirm the generality of His saying ﴿And it was not for any messenger to bring a sign except by the permission of Allah﴾. Yet it also conveys, by its placement, an independent meaning of refuting their disputation, for they used to say ﴿Allah did not send down anything upon a human being﴾ [al-An'am: 91] and say ﴿Why was an angel not sent down to him?﴾ [al-An'am: 8]. Their claims were thus crushed by what is known through mass transmission (tawatur) regarding the repeated sending of messengers across many eras and nations.

Allah has sent messengers and prophets whose number none knows but Allah the Exalted, because some of them Allah informed His Prophet ﷺ about, and some of them He did not inform him about, since there is no perfection in informing him about those He did not inform him about. Of those he was informed about, some were mentioned by name in the Qur'an, and some Allah informed him about through revelation other than the Qur'an. Some of them are mentioned in authentic reports, with or without specification. In a hadith: "Allah sent a prophet named 'Abbud, a black slave." And in a hadith: the mention of Hanzalah ibn Safwan, the prophet of the people of al-Rass; and the mention of Khalid ibn Sinan, the prophet of Banu 'Abs. And in a hadith: "A prophet was bitten by an ant, so he burned its settlement, and he was rebuked for that." People can hardly count their number, due to the distance of their times, the multiplicity of their nations, and the remoteness of their regions, which is beyond the reach of human knowledge and which the pens of historians and the reports of storytellers cannot enumerate. Of knowledge concerning some of them and some of their nations there has been obtained what suffices for drawing lessons regarding good and evil, and for encouragement and warning.

Mentioned in the Qur'an by name as messengers are fifteen: Nuh, Ibrahim, Lut, Isma'il, Ishaq, Ya'qub, Yusuf, Hud, Salih, Shu'ayb, Musa, Harun, 'Isa, Yunus, and Muhammad ﷺ. And twelve prophets: Dawud, Sulayman, Ayyub, Zakariyya, Yahya, Ilyas, al-Yasa', Idris, Adam, Dhu'l-Kifl, Dhu'l-Qarnayn, Luqman, and a female prophet, Maryam. Mentioned in general terms without naming is the companion of Musa, known in the Sunnah as Khadir, and the prophet of the Children of Israel, who is Samuel (Samwil), and Tubba'.

Muslims are not obliged to know anyone other than Muhammad ﷺ. However, the prophets who are mentioned in the Qur'an with the explicit description of prophethood, belief in their prophethood is obligatory for whoever reads the verses in which they are mentioned, and their number is twenty-five among messengers and prophets. His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿That was Our argument which We gave Ibrahim against his people﴾ [al-An'am: 83], up to His saying "and Lut", includes the names of eighteen of them, and the names of seven others are mentioned in other verses. Someone has gathered them in verse:

It is obligatory on every person of responsibility to know the prophets in detail who are known,
In that argument of Ours, eight of them; after ten, seven remain, and they are:
Idris, Hud, Shu'ayb, Salih, and likewise
Dhu'l-Kifl, Adam; by the Chosen One they have been sealed.

Know that concerning Yusuf being a messenger there is a difference of opinion, which I explained at His saying ﴿And Yusuf had already come to you before with clear proofs﴾ [Ghafir: 34] in this surah; and that concerning the prophethood of al-Khadir, Luqman, Dhu'l-Qarnayn and Maryam there is also a difference of opinion. I have chosen to affirm their prophethood because Allah mentioned of some of them that He addressed them, and mentioned of some that He gave them wisdom, which is well known in connection with prophethood, and of some that the angels spoke to them. Belief is obligatory only in the occurrence of messengership and prophethood in general terms.

It is not obligatory upon the community to believe in the messengership of any specific individual except Muhammad ﷺ, or whoever's prophethood has reached among the Muslims the level of certainty through its mass transmission, such as Musa, 'Isa, Ibrahim and Nuh.

But whoever comes across the mention of a prophet's prophethood with that description explicitly in the Qur'an, it is incumbent upon him to believe in what he knows of it.

What is established by solitary reports (akhbar al-ahad) does not make belief in it obligatory, because beliefs are not made obligatory by conjecture; but that is instruction, not an obligation of belief.

The indefinite form "messengers" (rusulan) conveys magnification and multiplicity, meaning: We sent messengers whose number is great and whose station is great.

The conjunction of "And it was not for any messenger..." with "wa" rather than "fa" indicates that this sentence stands independently by itself, due to the great meaning it contains, worthy of not being subordinate to something else; and the connection between the two sentences is sufficiently indicated by the position of one relative to the other.

The "ayah" is the miracle. The "idhn of Allah" is the command of creation by which Allah creates the extraordinary event to make it a sign of the Messenger's truthfulness.

The meaning of a messenger bringing a sign is his challenge to his people that Allah will support him with a sign which He specifies, like the words of Salih, peace be upon him: ﴿This is the she-camel of Allah, a sign for you﴾ [al-A'raf: 73], and the words of Musa, peace be upon him, to Pharaoh: ﴿Even if I bring you something clear?﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 30] and so on.

And the words of 'Isa, peace be upon him: "﴿That I create for you from clay like the form of a bird, then I breathe into it and it becomes a bird by the permission of Allah﴾" [Al 'Imran: 49], and the words of Muhammad ﷺ: ﴿Then bring a surah like it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 23].

The "ba'" in (بِآيَةٍ) is the ba' of transitivity for the verb ya'ti, while the "ba'" in (بِإذْنِ اللَّهِ) is the ba' of causation, entering upon an exception from omitted causes in the "istithna' mufarragh" construction, meaning: it was not for him to bring a sign by any cause among the causes except by the permission of Allah the Exalted.

This is a negation of what they cling to of proposals and pretexts.

Following it is His saying ﴿So when the command of Allah comes, judgment will be passed in truth﴾, meaning: so when the command of Allah comes, by the manifestation of a sign through the Messenger, the truthfulness of the Messenger becomes apparent, and that would be a judgment from Allah the Exalted for His Messenger in truth against his deniers. Thus the permission of Allah is His creative command to create a sign and make it manifest.

As for His saying ﴿So when the command of Allah comes﴾, "al-amr" means the decree and determination, like His saying ﴿The command of Allah has come, so do not seek to hasten it﴾ [al-Nahl: 1] and His saying ﴿or a command from Him﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 52]; it is the overwhelming event for people, as in the words of 'Umar when Abu Qatadah said to him on the day of Hunayn, "What is the matter with the people, that they were routed and fled?" 'Umar said, "The command of Allah."

In the shift from "idhn Allah" (the permission of Allah) to "amr Allah" (the command of Allah) there is an implicit indication that what Allah will manifest of the permission for Muhammad ﷺ are signs of punishment for his obstinate opponents. Among them: the sign of hunger for seven years until they ate carrion; the sign of the sword on the day of Badr, when He uprooted the chieftains of the deniers; and the sign of the Confederates, about which He said ﴿O you who believe, remember the blessing of Allah upon you when hosts came against you, so We sent upon them a wind and hosts you did not see﴾ [al-Ahzab: 9], then He said ﴿And Allah repelled those who disbelieved in their rage; they gained no good. And Allah sufficed the believers in battle, and Allah is ever Powerful and Exalted in Might﴾ [al-Ahzab: 25].

﴿And He brought down those of the People of the Scripture who supported them from their fortresses and cast terror into their hearts; a party you killed and a party you took captive﴾ [al-Ahzab: 26]. ﴿And He caused you to inherit their land and their homes and their wealth and a land you had not trodden; and ever is Allah, over all things, Competent﴾ [al-Ahzab: 27].

In the choice of mentioning "qudiya bil-haqq" (judgment was passed in truth) specifically, rather than other expressions such as "zahara al-haqq" (the truth became manifest) or "tabayyana al-sidq" (truthfulness became clear), there is a reinforcement of the implicit allusion in "amr Allah" that it is a command of retribution against the deniers.

Therefore He conjoined to it ﴿and the falsifiers will then lose﴾, meaning: those who disputed with falsehood in order to refute the truth with it will lose.

Loss is used metaphorically for the occurrence of harm to one who sought gain, like the loss of a merchant who sought profit but his capital was gone. Its meaning has been mentioned more than once before, including His saying ﴿So their commerce did not profit﴾ [al-Baqarah: 16] at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah. "Hunalika" originally is a demonstrative noun for place, and it is used here metaphorically to indicate the time expressed by "idha" in His saying ﴿So when the command of Allah comes﴾.

In this metaphor there is a subtle rhetorical point, namely the allusion that the falsifiers among the Quraysh would be struck by the sign in a place on earth, which is the place of Badr and other sites where the sword was applied against them. Thus the signs of Muhammad ﷺ were a proof against his obstinate opponents stronger than the heavenly signs such as thunderbolts or wind, and stronger than the earthly signs such as drowning and the earth swallowing, because those were with their participation and involvement, so that their defeat would be more decisive for their argument and more humiliating for them, akin to the sign of Musa's staff alongside the staves of the magicians.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 40, verses 79–80:

﴿It is Allah who made the cattle for you, that you may ride some of them and eat from some of them.﴾ ﴿And for you in them are benefits, and that you may reach by them a need in your breasts, and upon them and upon the ships you are carried.﴾

This is a transition from the favour (imtinan) shown to people through what He subjected for their sake of the order of the upper and lower worlds, and through what He granted them of bringing things into existence and its development, and the kindnesses toward them in all of that, and what is embedded in it of evidence that He, exalted is He, alone has sole control. How, then, could one turn away from worshipping Him to those who associate with Him other gods? It moves to the favour of what He subjected for them of camels, for their many benefits, both particular and general. So the sentence is a fresh resumption (isti'naf) of the sixth kind.

The discussion of how it opens is like the discussion of how its earlier counterparts open, with the Name of Majesty or with a pronoun referring to it.

"Al-an'am" (the livestock) means camels, sheep, goats and cattle. Here, what is meant is specifically camels, because of His saying ﴿that you may reach by them a need﴾ and His saying ﴿and upon them you are carried﴾. Camels were the majority of their means of livelihood.

"Al-ja'l" (making, appointing) means placing, enabling and preparing. It is interpreted in each context according to what suits it. The purpose of the favour is to bring their souls closer to monotheism, because it is the nature of people of honour to feel shame before a benefactor.

Embedded within the favour is an argument for the fineness of the craftsmanship and the far-reaching wisdom, as indicated by His saying ﴿and He shows you His signs﴾ [Ghafir: 81], meaning that in all of that.

[Page 215]

The lam in "lakum" is the lam of causation (ta'lil), meaning "for your sake." It is a general favour which, upon reflection, includes all the benefits in camels that they have, and which they know when they recall and count them.

Then this generality was explained in some detail by mentioning the most important of the blessings in camels, in His saying ﴿that you may ride some of them﴾ up to ﴿you are carried﴾.

So the lam in ﴿that you may ride some of them﴾ is the lam of purpose (kay), and it is connected to "ja'ala" (He made), meaning "for your riding."

The "min" in both places here is partitive (tab'id), and it describes an omitted noun indicated by "min", meaning "a part of them," that is, what is prepared for journeys from the mounts. The particle "min" is connected to "tarkabu" (you ride). The connection of partitive "min" to the verb is a weak connection, and this is what led al-Taftazani to say that "min" in such a construction is a noun meaning "part" (ba'd). This was mentioned earlier at His saying ﴿And among the people is one who says, "We believe in Allah"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 8] in Surat al-Baqarah.

Riding here is intended as riding for ease from the fatigue of the legs in a near need, as indicated by its being contrasted with His saying ﴿and that you may reach by them a need in your breasts﴾.

The clause ﴿and from them you eat﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to "al-an'am," or it is coordinated with the meaning of the clause ﴿that you may ride some of them﴾, because it has the force of saying "you ride from them." It is a resumption to explain the generality in ﴿He made the cattle for you﴾. On both considerations, it falls within the scope of what the lam of purpose governs, so its meaning is: "and that you may eat from them."

The clause ﴿And for you in them are benefits﴾ is coordinated with the clause ﴿and from them you eat﴾. The meaning, also on the basis of the causal reading, is as if it were said: "and that you may gather their benefits, which have been made for you." He changed the style of causation only for variety in speech and to refresh the listener, so that the particle of causation would not be repeated many times.

"Al-manafi'" (benefits) is the plural of "manfa'a", which is a noun of place from "al-naf'" (benefit). It is the thing from which one benefits, that is, which is made useful.

So the benefits in this verse are intended to include what stands in contrast to the benefits of eating their meat, mentioned in His saying ﴿and from them you eat﴾: such as benefiting from their wool, their milk, their price, and their equivalents in blood-money and dowries. Likewise, benefiting from their hides by making tents and other things from them, and by sitting upon them. Likewise, benefiting from the beauty of their appearance to the eyes in pasture and in their return. The benefits also include the riding mentioned in His saying ﴿that you may ride some of them﴾. So the mention of benefits after ﴿that you may ride some of them﴾ is a generalization after a specification, like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and I have in it other uses﴾ [Taha: 18] after His saying ﴿It is my staff, upon which I lean﴾ [Taha: 18]. Here He mentioned what is most common and well known among them, then mentioned something similar to it in commonness, which is eating from them. Then He returned to the generality of benefits, and then He specified from the benefits the journeys, because the intensity of need for camels during journeys makes riding them for travel a matter of great concern.

[Page 216]

Since the benefits are not confined to the parts of the livestock, the prepositional phrase connected to them is introduced with "fi" (in) rather than "min" (from), because "fi" here denotes figurative containment (zarfiyya majaziyya), by contextual indication. So it includes everything that is regarded as what is contained within the livestock. This is like the saying of Sabra ibn 'Amr al-Faq'asi, one of the poets of al-Hamasa, mentioning what he took of camels as blood-money for a relative:

We favour our equals with them, and we humiliate others with them, and we drink their price, and we gamble.

The verb "li-tablughu" (that you may reach) indicates that the need which is in the breasts is a need in a distant place, which its owner seeks.

"Al-hajah" (need) means intention and resolve.

"Al-sudur" (breasts) is used to mean the minds (uqul), following common usage, just as "al-qulub" (hearts) is used to mean minds.

He followed the favour of the livestock with the favour of the ships, because of its connection with His saying ﴿that you may reach by them a need in your breasts﴾. So He said ﴿and upon them and upon the ships you are carried﴾. This is a transition from the favour of making the livestock to the favour of the blessing of riding in ships on seas and rivers. The intended matter is His saying ﴿and upon the ships you are carried﴾. As for His saying ﴿and upon them﴾, it is a preparation for it, and it is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraḍ) with the parenthetical waw, repeating the favour. Furthermore, it may include carrying loads on camels, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and it carries your loads﴾ [al-Nahl: 7], in which case the attribution of carrying to the pronoun of people is by predominance (taghlib).

[Page 217]

The aspect of the favour of ships is that it is a favour of what Allah composed in the human being of planning and intelligence, by which he reached useful inventions according to the differing ages and generations, as was mentioned earlier in Surat al-Baqarah at His saying ﴿and the ships that run in the sea with what benefits people, there are signs﴾ [al-Baqarah: 164]. There we explained that the Arabs used to sail the Red Sea in trade, and they also sailed the rivers. Al-Nabigha said, describing the Euphrates:

It keeps the boatman, from its fear, holding fast to the pole, after exhaustion and distress.

The combination of travel by camels and travel by ships is a subtle combination, for camels are "ships of the land," and the ancients called them that. Al-Zamakhshari said this in his commentary on Surat al-Mu'minun.

He said "wa 'ala al-fulk" (and upon the ships), not "wa fi al-fulk" (and in the ships), as in His saying ﴿So when they board the ships﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 65], for the sake of parallelism and harmony with "wa 'alayha" (and upon them). The preposition "'ala" was repeated before "al-fulk" because it is the intended object of mention, and the mention of "wa 'alayha" served as a preparation for it, so it came in its pattern.

The fronting of the prepositional phrases in His saying ﴿and from them you eat﴾ and His saying ﴿and upon them and upon the ships﴾ is for the sake of observing the rhyme (fasila), together with attention to what is the intended matter in the context.

The fronting of "lakum" (for you) before "al-an'am" (the livestock), although the object is more closely connected to its verb than the prepositional phrase, is for the purpose of emphasizing those who are favoured.

As for the fronting of the two prepositional phrases in His saying ﴿And for you in them are benefits﴾, it is for the sake of attention to those upon whom the favour is bestowed and to the Benefactor by whom it is bestowed, since this is the primary aim of His saying ﴿It is Allah who made the cattle for you﴾.
