The connection of partitive "min" to the verb is a weak connection, and this is what led al-Taftazani to say that "min" in such a construction is a noun meaning "part" (ba'd). This was mentioned earlier at His saying ﴿And among the people is one who says, "We believe in Allah"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 8] in Surat al-Baqarah.

Riding here is intended as riding for ease from the fatigue of the legs in a near need, as indicated by its being contrasted with His saying ﴿and that you may reach by them a need in your breasts﴾.

The clause ﴿and from them you eat﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to "al-an'am," or it is coordinated with the meaning of the clause ﴿that you may ride some of them﴾, because it has the force of saying "you ride from them." It is a resumption to explain the generality in ﴿He made the cattle for you﴾. On both considerations, it falls within the scope of what the lam of purpose governs, so its meaning is: "and that you may eat from them."

The clause ﴿And for you in them are benefits﴾ is coordinated with the clause ﴿and from them you eat﴾. The meaning, also on the basis of the causal reading, is as if it were said: "and that you may gather their benefits, which have been made for you." He changed the style of causation only for variety in speech and to refresh the listener, so that the particle of causation would not be repeated many times.

"Al-manafi'" (benefits) is the plural of "manfa'a", which is a noun of place from "al-naf'" (benefit). It is the thing from which one benefits, that is, which is made useful.

So the benefits in this verse are intended to include what stands in contrast to the benefits of eating their meat, mentioned in His saying ﴿and from them you eat﴾: such as benefiting from their wool, their milk, their price, and their equivalents in blood-money and dowries. Likewise, benefiting from their hides by making tents and other things from them, and by sitting upon them. Likewise, benefiting from the beauty of their appearance to the eyes in pasture and in their return. The benefits also include the riding mentioned in His saying ﴿that you may ride some of them﴾. So the mention of benefits after ﴿that you may ride some of them﴾ is a generalization after a specification, like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and I have in it other uses﴾ [Taha: 18] after His saying ﴿It is my staff, upon which I lean﴾ [Taha: 18]. Here He mentioned what is most common and well known among them, then mentioned something similar to it in commonness, which is eating from them. Then He returned to the generality of benefits, and then He specified from the benefits the journeys, because the intensity of need for camels during journeys makes riding them for travel a matter of great concern.

[Page 216]

Since the benefits are not confined to the parts of the livestock, the prepositional phrase connected to them is introduced with "fi" (in) rather than "min" (from), because "fi" here denotes figurative containment (zarfiyya majaziyya), by contextual indication. So it includes everything that is regarded as what is contained within the livestock. This is like the saying of Sabra ibn 'Amr al-Faq'asi, one of the poets of al-Hamasa, mentioning what he took of camels as blood-money for a relative:

We favour our equals with them, and we humiliate others with them, and we drink their price, and we gamble.

The verb "li-tablughu" (that you may reach) indicates that the need which is in the breasts is a need in a distant place, which its owner seeks.

"Al-hajah" (need) means intention and resolve.

"Al-sudur" (breasts) is used to mean the minds (uqul), following common usage, just as "al-qulub" (hearts) is used to mean minds.

He followed the favour of the livestock with the favour of the ships, because of its connection with His saying ﴿that you may reach by them a need in your breasts﴾. So He said ﴿and upon them and upon the ships you are carried﴾. This is a transition from the favour of making the livestock to the favour of the blessing of riding in ships on seas and rivers. The intended matter is His saying ﴿and upon the ships you are carried﴾. As for His saying ﴿and upon them﴾, it is a preparation for it, and it is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraḍ) with the parenthetical waw, repeating the favour. Furthermore, it may include carrying loads on camels, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and it carries your loads﴾ [al-Nahl: 7], in which case the attribution of carrying to the pronoun of people is by predominance (taghlib).

[Page 217]

The aspect of the favour of ships is that it is a favour of what Allah composed in the human being of planning and intelligence, by which he reached useful inventions according to the differing ages and generations, as was mentioned earlier in Surat al-Baqarah at His saying ﴿and the ships that run in the sea with what benefits people, there are signs﴾ [al-Baqarah: 164]. There we explained that the Arabs used to sail the Red Sea in trade, and they also sailed the rivers. Al-Nabigha said, describing the Euphrates:

It keeps the boatman, from its fear, holding fast to the pole, after exhaustion and distress.

The combination of travel by camels and travel by ships is a subtle combination, for camels are "ships of the land," and the ancients called them that. Al-Zamakhshari said this in his commentary on Surat al-Mu'minun.

He said "wa 'ala al-fulk" (and upon the ships), not "wa fi al-fulk" (and in the ships), as in His saying ﴿So when they board the ships﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 65], for the sake of parallelism and harmony with "wa 'alayha" (and upon them). The preposition "'ala" was repeated before "al-fulk" because it is the intended object of mention, and the mention of "wa 'alayha" served as a preparation for it, so it came in its pattern.

The fronting of the prepositional phrases in His saying ﴿and from them you eat﴾ and His saying ﴿and upon them and upon the ships﴾ is for the sake of observing the rhyme (fasila), together with attention to what is the intended matter in the context.

The fronting of "lakum" (for you) before "al-an'am" (the livestock), although the object is more closely connected to its verb than the prepositional phrase, is for the purpose of emphasizing those who are favoured.

As for the fronting of the two prepositional phrases in His saying ﴿And for you in them are benefits﴾, it is for the sake of attention to those upon whom the favour is bestowed and to the Benefactor by whom it is bestowed, since this is the primary aim of His saying ﴿It is Allah who made the cattle for you﴾.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 40, verse 81:

﴿And He shows you His signs, so which of the signs of Allah do you deny?﴾

It is conjoined to the clause "for you" (lakum) concerning the cattle, meaning: Allah is the One who shows you His signs. This is a transition from the multiple acts of favour mentioned earlier in His saying ﴿It is Allah who made the night for you that you may rest therein﴾ [Ghafir: 61], ﴿It is Allah who made the earth a place of settlement for you﴾ [Ghafir: 64], ﴿It is He who created you from dust﴾ [Ghafir: 67], ﴿It is Allah who made the cattle for you﴾ [Ghafir: 79]. Those were mentioned in the context of favour, as a reminder to give thanks,

Page 218

so here He alerts that in those favours there are signs indicating what is due to Allah of oneness, power and wisdom.

For this reason His saying ﴿And He shows you His signs﴾ serves the function of a concluding generalisation (tadhyil), because of the generality in His saying "His signs" (ayatihi), since the definite plural made definite by a genitive attachment (al-jam' al-mu'arraf bi'l-idafah) is one of the forms of generality. That is: He shows you His signs in the favours mentioned and others, and in everything that indicates the obligation of His oneness, the confirmation of His messengers, and the rejection of obstinacy regarding the signs of their truthfulness that they bring to you.

The present tense has been used for the showing of the signs, since it indicates renewal (tajaddud), because whenever a person benefits from some favour, he knows what it contains of indication of the oneness of its Creator, His power and His wisdom.

The "showing" (ira'ah) here is visual, and it is used figuratively for knowledge of Allah's attributes, since the path to that knowledge is witnessing those varied states; from that witnessing the intellect moves to inference. In this there is an indication that the indication of the existence of the Creator, His oneness and His power is demonstrative (burhaniyyah), leading to certainty and necessity.

The attribution of the signs to the divine name (damir al-jalalah) serves to increase their esteem and to guide to excellence in intellectual reflection on their proofs. As for their coming from Allah and that their attribution is of the kind that carries the sense of the agent, this is derived from the attribution of the verb "shows you" to His pronoun, may He be exalted.

Following upon the showing of the signs comes an interrogative of denunciation addressed to them, on account of their denial of what those signs indicate.

"Ayy" (which): an interrogative noun by which one seeks to distinguish one thing from its counterpart within what it is attached to. Here it is used in denial that any of Allah's signs could be denied to the exclusion of the other signs, which implies that all the signs are suitable for indicating Allah's oneness and power, and there is no room for claiming that it is hidden, and that they have no excuse for failing to benefit from any one of the signs.

Page 219

The more common usage, when "ayy" is attached to a noun feminine in form, is that the taa' marbutah is not added to it, relying on the femininity of what it is attached to. This is because, in nouns that are not adjectives, the usual practice is not to distinguish masculine from feminine by the taa', as in "himar" (donkey), so one does not say "himarah" for the female. "Ayy" is a noun and is increased in ambiguity by what it contains, so only the genitive attached to it clarifies it. For this reason he said here ﴿fa-ayya ayati Allah﴾ rather than "fa-ayyata ayati Allah", because adding the feminine marker to "ayy" in such a case is rare. Feminine use of "ayy" occurs contrary to the usual practice in the verse of al-Kumayt:

"By which book, or by which sunnah, do you see their love as a shame upon me, and reckon it so?"

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 40, verses 82–83:

﴿Have they not travelled through the earth and seen how was the end of those before them? They were more numerous than them, and greater in strength and in the traces they left upon the earth. Yet what they used to earn did not avail them.﴾ ﴿So when their messengers came to them with clear proofs, they exulted in the knowledge they had, and there befell them that which they used to mock.﴾

This interrogative follows immediately His words ﴿And He shows you His signs﴾ [Ghafir: 81], which implies that it is parallel to the preceding continuation, namely ﴿So which of God's signs will you deny?﴾ [Ghafir: 81]. This implies that the travelling asked about, whose neglect is reproached, is a journey in which there are signs and proofs of God's existence and His oneness. Both continuations are connected to His words ﴿And that you may attain thereon a need in your breasts, and upon them and upon the ship you are carried﴾ [Ghafir: 80]. This is the occasion for the transition to admonition through the lesson of the traces of the nations whom God uprooted when they denied His messengers and rejected His signs and blessings.

By this there is achieved a repetition of the reproach found in His words before this: ﴿Have they not travelled through the earth and seen how was the end of those who were before them? They were stronger than them in might﴾ [Ghafir: 21], and so the earlier passage was a transition following verses of warning and threat, while this one is a transition following verses of favour and argument. In both transitions there is admonition, threat and warning. It indicates that if they are not among those whom blessings restrain from ingratitude to their Giver, as is the case with noble souls, then let them be among those whom fear of seizure restrains, as is the case with base souls. Let them place themselves where they choose from between the two courses.

As for the saying ﴿Have they not travelled through the earth﴾ up to ﴿and traces upon the earth﴾, it is like its counterpart earlier in this surah, except that the wording differs in joining the clause ﴿Have they not travelled﴾ between this verse, which is joined by the particle fa' for consequence, because it follows what may serve as the basis for the denial of their failure to reflect upon the end of those before them. This differs from its counterpart before it, which came after their being warned of the Day of the Imminent (Yawm al-Azifa).

The clause ﴿Yet what they used to earn did not avail them﴾ is parenthetical (mu'tarida), and the fa' is for consequence upon His words ﴿they were more numerous than them﴾. It is like His words, exalted is He, ﴿This, so let them taste it: boiling water and dark, cold liquid﴾ [Sad: 57], and the saying of 'Antara:

And indeed you have alighted, so do not think other than that
I am to you in the position of a loving, honoured one.

The benefit of this parenthetical clause is the hastening to convey that their multitude, their strength, their fortresses and their gardens did not avail them anything against the might of God.

The clause ﴿So when their messengers came to them with clear proofs﴾ up to the end of the verse is consequent upon the clause ﴿they were more numerous than them﴾, meaning: they remained so until God's messengers came to them with clear proofs, but they did not believe them, so they saw Our might. Al-Zamakhshari made it function as an explanation and elucidation of His words ﴿did not avail them﴾, but what I have followed is better, and the position of the fa' supports it.

As for "lamma" (when), in the sense of temporal limit, it conveys the meaning that God did not change the great blessings they had until they denied His messengers.

The answer to "lamma" is the clause ﴿they exulted in the knowledge they had﴾ and what is joined to it.

Know that the commentators have taken various paths in explaining this verse, some of which al-Tabari related from some early commentators. Al-Zamakhshari reduced them to six, al-Kashf inclined to one of them, and Abu Hayyan to another, but there is no need to cite them.

The path that is preferred is that here there are ten pronouns, all plural third-person pronouns, and that some of them necessarily return to ﴿those before them﴾, and that the proper arrangement of the discourse requires that the pronouns be coherent and not disjointed, so it is necessary that they refer to one single antecedent.

Thus those who ﴿exulted in the knowledge they had﴾ are those to whom their messengers came with clear proofs, and they are those upon whom there befell what they used to mock, and those who saw God's might. Thus we need only explain the meaning of ﴿they exulted in the knowledge they had﴾.

Exultation here is a metonymy for its effect, which is arrogance (al-izdiha'), as in His words, exalted is He, ﴿When his people said to him: do not exult﴾ [al-Qasas: 76], meaning in what you are in. Here it is a metonymy for their clinging to what they were upon. The meaning is that they disputed with the messengers, rebuffed the proofs, and turned away from reflection. What they had of knowledge is their inherited beliefs from the people of error among their forefathers.

Mujahid said: they said to their messengers, "We are more knowledgeable than you; we will not be resurrected and we will not be punished." End.

The application of the word "knowledge" to their belief is mockery and a going along with their own assumption; otherwise it is ignorance.

al-Suddi said: ﴿they exulted in the knowledge they had﴾ "through their ignorance," meaning that it belongs to the same category as His words, exalted is He, ﴿Say: Have you any knowledge that you can bring forth for us? You follow only conjecture, and you do only guess﴾ [al-An'am: 148].

"Haqa bihim": it encompassed them. It is said: haqa yahiqu haqan, when it encircles. Here it is used figuratively for severity from which there is no relief, because that which encircles a thing leaves it no opening.

And ﴿what they used to mock﴾ is the extirpation and the punishment. The meaning is that their messengers threatened them with punishment, so they mocked the punishment, meaning its occurrence. The mention of the verb of being (kana) is an indication that mocking the threats of the messengers was a habit of theirs. And the use of yastahziun in the present tense conveys the repetition of their mockery.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 40, verse 84:**

﴿So when they saw Our punishment, they said, "We believe in God alone, and we reject what we used to associate with Him."﴾ ﴿But their faith did not benefit them when they saw Our punishment.﴾ [Ghafir: 85].

The position of the clause ﴿when they saw Our punishment﴾ within His words ﴿Then when their messengers came to them with clear proofs﴾ [Ghafir: 83] is like the position of the clause ﴿when their messengers came to them﴾ [Ghafir: 83] within His words ﴿they were more numerous than them﴾ [Ghafir: 82]. This is because the function of *lamma* (when, as a particle of time) is to indicate the time at which what precedes it ends. That is, the calling of the messengers to them continued, and their denial and mockery continued, until they saw Our punishment, and then they said, "We believe in God alone."

[p. 222]

*Al-ba's* (severe distress, affliction) is intensity in what is disliked, and it encompasses all kinds of punishment, as in God's words ﴿Never did We send a prophet to a town but We seized its people with adversity and hardship, so that they might humble themselves﴾ [al-A'raf: 94], and ﴿Why, when Our punishment came to them, did they not humble themselves?﴾ [al-An'am: 43]. So that *ba's* here has the meaning of *ba'sa'* (hardship). Do you not see that He says "they humbled themselves," and here He says ﴿their faith did not benefit them when they saw Our punishment﴾ [Ghafir: 85]? Thus *al-ba's* here is the punishment that breaks the normal course of things and announces annihilation. When they saw it, they knew that it was the punishment they had been warned of.

This is followed by His words ﴿their faith did not benefit them when they saw Our punishment﴾ [Ghafir: 85], meaning: when they witnessed the punishment, faith no longer benefited them, because God does not accept faith at the descent of His punishment.

He turned away from saying "then their faith did not benefit them" to His words ﴿it did not benefit them﴾ [Ghafir: 85], because the verb *kana* (to be) indicates that its predicate is firmly established for its subject. So when the intention was to negate the establishment of benefit for them after its time had passed, He employed the negation of the verb *kana*, whose predicate is ﴿benefit them﴾.

The meaning is that faith after seeing the flashes of punishment does not benefit its possessor as faith at the moment of the death rattle (*al-gharghara*) benefits, nor as faith at the rising of the sun from its west, as is stated in the authentic hadith. The explanation of this will come after it.

[p. 223]

The accusative of "sunnata Allah" (God's way) is a substitute for the absolute object (al-maf'ul al-mutlaq), since "sunnah" is a verbal noun (ism al-masdar) of "sanna," and it stands in place of its verb. The sense is: "God has ordained that as a sunnah." The clause is a resumed explanatory clause (isti'naf bayani), answering the question of one who asks: why did faith not benefit them when they did believe? The answer is that this is a decree God set for the earlier nations, informed them of it, and made it a condition upon them. It is an enduring pattern among His servants: faith does not benefit the disbeliever except before the descent of punishment (al-ba's). The only exception God made to this is the people of Yunus, as He said: ﴿Why was there no town that believed so that its faith benefited it, except the people of Yunus? When they believed, We removed from them the punishment of disgrace in the life of this world﴾ [Yunus: 98].

[p. 224 is not present; continuing]

[p. 223, continued]

This is God's ruling concerning al-ba's in the sense of punishment that breaks custom and is a clear sign. As for the ba's that is customary, and is a hidden sign, such as the punishment of the sword's ba's, with which God gave victory to His Messenger on the day of Badr and the day of the Conquest of Makkah: whoever believes upon seeing it, like Abu Sufyan ibn Harb when he saw the army of the Conquest, or believes after escaping it, like the faith of the Quraysh on the day of the Conquest after the sword was lifted from them, his faith is complete, like the faith of Khalid ibn al-Walid, Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith ibn Abd al-Muttalib, and Abdullah ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Sarh after his apostasy.

The reason faith is not accepted when the punishment of total annihilation (isti'sal) descends, while it is accepted when the sword's ba's descends, is that the punishment of annihilation is the approach of destruction and the departure from the world. Bringing faith at that point does not achieve the purpose for which faith was made obligatory, which is that believers become a party and helpers for His religion and helpers for His messengers. What benefit is the faith of a people among whom nothing remains but a weak breath of life? Their faith at that time is like the acknowledgment of sins by the people of the Gathering, and it is not a time for action. God said concerning Pharaoh: ﴿When drowning overtook him, he said: I believe that there is no god except the One in whom the Children of Israel believe, and I am of the Muslims﴾ [Yunus: 90]. ﴿Now? And you had disobeyed before and were among the corrupters﴾ [Yunus: 91], meaning that there was no longer any time to make up for his disobedience and corruption. God also said: ﴿On the day when some of the signs of your Lord come, no soul will benefit from its faith if it had not believed before or earned good through its faith﴾ [al-An'am: 158]. His words ﴿or earned good through its faith﴾ point to the wisdom behind no one benefiting from their faith at that hour. What befell the people of Yunus was a state intermediate between the appearance of the ba's and the awareness of it, when its signs became apparent, as we explained in the commentary on Surat Yunus.

The clause ﴿and there the disbelievers lost﴾ serves as a summary (fadhlaka) of His words ﴿So their faith did not benefit them when they saw Our ba's﴾. With it, the purpose of the surah is announced as concluded.

"Hunalika" is a demonstrative of place, used metaphorically to indicate time, meaning: they lost at the time they saw Our ba's, when their lives and their authority had ended, and they came to await a lasting punishment in the future.

The shift from the pronoun in ﴿those who were before them, they were stronger than them﴾ [Ghafir: 21] to the explicit noun "the disbelievers" indicates that the cause of their loss is disbelief in God. This is an excuse for the polytheists of Quraysh.

[p. 224]

The style of Surat Ghafir.

Its style is that of argument and proof for the truthfulness of the Qur'an and that it was sent down from God, the refutation of the error of the deniers, the presenting of the deniers' case by the nations that denied, and the warning of them against persisting in their error and the encouragement of them to reflect so that they may be guided.

It opens with the two disjoined letters of the alphabet, because the first of its aims is that the Qur'an is from God. In the two letters of the alphabet there is an allusion to their inability to produce its equal after it challenged them, and so they did not do it, as was mentioned at the opening of Surat al-Baqarah.

In this opening there is an arousing of curiosity about what follows, to draw attention to it.

The attributes applied to the name of the One who sent down the Qur'an contain an allusion that it does not resemble human speech, because it is the speech of the All-Mighty, the All-Knowing, and an allusion to the ease of their turning away from disbelief, and a warning of punishment for persistence. All of that is part of the excellence of the opening.

Then it moved from allusion and symbol to the explicit description of the error of the obstinate and their comparison with the earlier nations whom God uprooted.

The most excellent of the earlier messengers, Musa, is singled out for mention, with a nation from among the greatest of the earlier nations, the people of Egypt. This was extended because of the strong similarity of their condition to that of the polytheists of the Arabs in their self-admiration, and in the scarcity of believers among them, such as the believer of Pharaoh's family. Interspersed with this is the steadfastness of Musa and the steadfastness of the believer of Pharaoh's family, as an allusion to the comparison with the steadfastness of Muhammad (ﷺ) and Abu Bakr. Then it moved on to argument for the Oneness of God and the vastness of His power to restore the dead.

It concludes with mention of the people of error among the earlier nations, whom their self-admiration and their confidence in their ignorance destroyed, so their ears were deafened to hearing the proofs of truth, and their eyes were blinded to reflecting upon the signs in creation, so they thought they were in a perfection that lacked nothing, while they had need of the perfection. Then the punishment befell them. In this there is a "return of the last to the first" (radd al-'ajuz 'ala al-sadr). God warned the polytheists against sliding into the pit of the earlier ones, by stating that the sunnah of God among His servants is respite, then requital. That was a comprehensive word for the purpose, announcing the end of the discourse, and so it was a fine conclusion.

[p. 225]

Interspersed throughout all of this are digressions and transitions: mention of the praise of the Highest Assembly for the believers and their censure of the disbelievers; mention of what they will come to of punishment and regret; a depiction of the difference between believers and disbelievers; a depiction of the state of the disbelievers in the Hereafter; the affirmation of the believers in their faith, and that God supports His Messenger and the believers in this world and the Hereafter; the command to them to be patient and to rely upon God; and that the condition of the Messenger (ﷺ) is like that of the messengers before him in facing denial, and that he brings signs which God caused to come through his hands, not the demands of the obstinate.

[p. 226]

[p. 227]

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surat Fussilat.

It is called "Ha Mim al-Sajdah," with "Ha Mim" added to "al-Sajdah," as we mentioned at the beginning of Surat al-Mu'min. It is so titled in Sahih al-Bukhari and in Jami' al-Tirmidhi, because it is distinguished from the surahs that open with the letters "Ha Mim" by having in it a prostration of the Qur'an.

Al-Bayhaqi recorded in Shu'ab al-Iman from Khalil ibn Murrah that "the Messenger of God (ﷺ) would not sleep until he recited: Tabarak (al-Mulk), and Ha Mim al-Sajdah."

It is called in most of the Eastern mushafs and tafsir works "Surat al-Sajdah," which is an abbreviation of their saying "Ha Mim al-Sajdah." It is not a distinction for it by the prostration itself.

These surahs are called in many tafsir works "Surat Fussilat."

Its name is well known in Tunisia and the Maghrib as "Surat Fussilat," because the phrase ﴿Its verses have been detailed﴾ [Fussilat: 3] occurs at its beginning, so it became known by it, distinguishing it from the surahs that open with "Ha Mim." Just as "Surat al-Mu'min" was distinguished by the name "Surat Ghafir" from the rest of the surahs that open with "Ha Mim."

Al-Kawashi said: It is also called "Surat al-Masabih," because of His words in it: ﴿And We have adorned the lowest heaven with lamps﴾ [al-Mulk: 5], and it is called "Surat al-Aqwat," because of His words: ﴿And He measured in it its sustenance﴾ [Fussilat: 10].

[p. 228]

Al-Kawashi said in al-Tabsirah: It is called "Sajdat al-Mu'min." The reason for this name is to distinguish it from the surah "Alif Lam Mim al-Sajdah," which is called "Surat al-Madaji'," so they attached this one to the surah before it, which is "Surat al-Mu'min," just as they distinguished "Surat al-Madaji'" by the name "Sajdat Luqman," because it comes after "Surat Luqman."

It is Makkan by consensus. It was revealed after "Surat Ghafir" and before "Surat al-Zukhruf," and it is counted as the sixty-first in the order of revelation of the surahs.

Its verses are counted as fifty-three according to the people of Madinah and the people of Makkah, fifty-two according to the people of Syria and Basrah, and fifty-four according to the people of Kufah.

* * *

Its aims.

Praising the Qur'an and pointing to their inability to produce its equal.

Mention of its guidance, and that it is protected from falsehood reaching it, and its confirmation by what was sent down to the messengers before Islam.

The polytheists' reception of it with aversion and the deafening of ears.

The refutation of the polytheists' slanders against it, and their reminder that the Qur'an was revealed in their own language, so they have no excuse at all for not benefiting from its guidance.

The rebuke and reproach of the polytheists for their disbelief in the Creator of the heavens and the earth, along with an explanation of what is in their creation of proofs of His sole divinity.

The warning to them of what befell the nations that denied, of punishment in this world.

The threat to them of punishment in the Hereafter, and of the testimony of their hearing, their sight and their skins against them.

The warning to them against the companions who adorn disbelief for them, from among the devils and men, and that they will regret on the Day of Resurrection having followed them in this world.

[p. 229]

This is set against what the monotheists have of honor with God.

The command to the Prophet (ﷺ) to repel them with what is better, to be patient with their harshness, and to seek refuge with God from Satan.

The surah also mentions proofs that God alone created the great creations, such as the sun and the moon.

Proofs of the possibility of resurrection, that it is certain to occur, and that none knows its time except God, exalted is He.

The steadfastness of the Prophet (ﷺ) and the believers through God's support for them by the descent of angels with revelation, and with good tidings for the believers.

Interspersed in this are various parables about the beginning of the creation of worlds, and lessons from the changing fortunes of the people of polytheism.

And the mention of the giving of zakat.
